data.body: Operator 2026-10-22: the goal is CONSISTENCY between ids generated by different agents for the same project. Measured on this log (836 bugs, 464 fix tasks): 677 bug ids are the machine form B<hash> but 159 are agent-chosen slugs (B-ci-gate-prints-passed-with-failing-tests...), 385 fix tasks are fix-B<hash> but 79 are fix-B-<slug>; task ids use dozens of ad-hoc prefixes. Cause: --id lets every agent invent a shape. Add [ids].enforce = off|warn|refuse (default warn): a caller-supplied id for a machine-minted kind (bug, lesson, research, decision, memory, job, fix task) must match the pattern derived from its template, else it is minted instead or refused with the right form; an explicit slug stays allowed only where the template says caller-named. 'ddflow doctor' lists nonconforming existing ids (they are never renamed: recorded ids are immutable). Tests: warn, refuse, minted fallback, doctor.
data.title: Id conformance: an explicit id must match its kind's [ids] template (warn/refuse by knob), ddflow doctor lists existing nonconforming ids

data.body: Tasks and phases are caller-named (D-id-schemes-final covers imported ones only), so parallel agents pick different shapes (US-, RQM-, SPEC-, PI-, ACF-, LS-, SU- were each chosen by the researching agent; older phases use B-uni, P-agent..., fix-B...). Add an optional 'id_prefix' on a phase (set by phase add, a preset, or the org vocabulary) and have 'ddflow task add --phase P' with no id mint the next free <prefix>-<seq> through the id service (next_seq, taken-key check across worktrees), and with an explicit id warn or refuse a non-conforming prefix per [ids].enforce. Print the convention in the claim/brief charter so agents follow it, and in 'ddflow plan check' (warn on a plan whose task ids break the phase prefix). chunk_findings.detail: `_overwritten` treats any non-zero merge output containing the literal substring `would be overwritten by merge` as a pre-merge dirty-tree refusal. Git can emit that substring as part of a path in a normal conflicted merge: if a tracked file or directory is named `would be overwritten by merge` and both sides modify it, `git merge` exits non-zero and prints a conflict message such as `CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in would be overwritten by merge`. `_overwritten` returns true, `_merge_retrying_stash` returns `GIT_REFUSED` with `attempted=False`, and the merge gate therefore does not record a real conflicted merge; it incorrectly claims the branch was not judged. The predicate should be anchored to git’s actual local-changes/untracked-files error rather than the bare phrase.

chunk_findings.detail: The new fallback overrides *every* review exclusion, not just lockfile/chore exclusions. Given `review.exclude_globs = ["*.pem"]` (or an ad-hoc `--exclude "*.pem"`), and a change whose only modified file is `server.pem`, `gone.files` is non-empty and `kept.strip()` is empty, so the function returns the full diff containing the private-key changes to rubber_duck/critic. The same secret is correctly excluded when the commit also contains one unrelated non-excluded file, so the leak depends on whether an unrelated file is present. The comment assumes the excluded content is a safe lockfile, but the code does not check that, silently defeating privacy/security exclusions.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/review_exclude.py:113

chunk_findings.detail: The change makes `review.exclude_globs` ineffective whenever every changed file is excluded: it sends the full excluded diff to reviewers. The test asserts this behavior directly (`"LOCKED" in kept`) and the mixed-file test asserts that an excluded generated file’s contents are sent to the reviewer (`"GENERATED_MARK" in seen.read_text()`). Given a repo config with `[review].exclude_globs = ["*.pem"]` and a change that only modifies `server.pem`, the same code path returns the private key diff to the external reviewer, violating the exclusion and potentially leaking secrets. The fix should preserve exclusion semantics (e.g., send only file names/metadata or record a special no-content review), not send excluded file bodies.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_lockfile_only_item.py:33

chunk_findings.detail: The test is named `..._naming_them`, but it does not actually assert that the excluded file is named. It only checks that the review text contains the generic substring `"excluded from review"`. An implementation could emit a review text like `All changed files are excluded from review.` without ever listing `x.py`; the test would still pass because `out.exit == 0`, the full diff contains `GENERATED_MARK`, and the generic substring is present. This leaves the promised “naming them” behavior unguarded.

chunk_findings.detail: When `it.landed_paths` is set, the landed diff is filtered and then returned as `sorted(restricted) or paths`. If the restriction matches none of the current changed paths, the function silently returns the full landed diff. For example, if an item has `landed_paths=["docs/**"]` but its stored `landed_before..landed_after` range no longer changes anything under that restriction (e.g. after the recorded range is amended/edited without revalidating the restriction), `restricted` is empty and the function returns the whole mixed commit, including code paths. That makes the docs-only item look code-changing again and reintroduces the exact bug this field is meant to fix, while contradicting the new docstring’s “never the whole commit’s” guarantee.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/completion.py:changed_paths

chunk_findings.detail: `check_paths` validates each restriction glob by calling `_touches(item, [p])`, which tests `p` as if it were a concrete path against the item’s declared globs, not as a glob that must be contained by them. A broader restriction glob can therefore pass. For an item declared with `docs/*`, passing `docs/**` is accepted because the literal pattern string `docs/**` matches the declared glob `docs/*`, but `changed_paths` later uses `inside("docs/sub/a.md", "docs/**")`, which is true while `inside("docs/sub/a.md", "docs/*")` is false. The restriction then lets undeclared paths be reported as the item’s changed paths, defeating the stated guarantee that a restriction “it never declared could [not] hide code.”

chunk_findings.detail: When `it.landed_paths` is set, the landed diff is filtered and then returned as `sorted(restricted) or paths`. If the restriction matches none of the current changed paths, the function silently returns the full landed diff. For example, if an item has `landed_paths=["docs/**"]` but its stored `landed_before..landed_after` range no longer changes anything under that restriction (e.g. after the recorded range is amended/edited without revalidating the restriction), `restricted` is empty and the function returns the whole mixed commit, including code paths. That makes the docs-only item look code-changing again and reintroduces the exact bug this field is meant to fix, while contradicting the new docstring’s “never the whole commit’s” guarantee.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/completion.py:changed_paths

chunk_findings.detail: `check_paths` validates each restriction glob by calling `_touches(item, [p])`, which tests `p` as if it were a concrete path against the item’s declared globs, not as a glob that must be contained by them. A broader restriction glob can therefore pass. For an item declared with `docs/*`, passing `docs/**` is accepted because the literal pattern string `docs/**` matches the declared glob `docs/*`, but `changed_paths` later uses `inside("docs/sub/a.md", "docs/**")`, which is true while `inside("docs/sub/a.md", "docs/*")` is false. The restriction then lets undeclared paths be reported as the item’s changed paths, defeating the stated guarantee that a restriction “it never declared could [not] hide code.”
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/landed.py:check_paths

chunk_findings.detail: When `it.landed_paths` is set and the recorded landed range changes no path matching the restriction, the new code returns `[]`. The function’s own contract says `None` is the only “git cannot say” result and it must “never” return an empty “nothing changed” list, so callers are entitled to treat a returned list as a known non-empty set of changed paths. For example, an item with `landed_paths=["docs/**"]` whose `landed_before..landed_after` range changed only `src/app.py` now causes `changed_paths()` to return `[]`. A docs-only check that follows the documented `None`-vs-list contract and tests `all(is_doc(p) for p in paths)` will evaluate `all([])` as `True`, classifying the item as docs-only and skipping the full pipeline—the exact behavior the change is supposed to prevent. Returning an empty list does not itself “fail closed”; it only fails closed if every consumer explicitly rejects empty lists, which contradicts the function’s stated invariant.

chunk_findings.detail: The new fallback overrides *every* review exclusion, not just lockfile/chore exclusions. Given `review.exclude_globs = ["*.pem"]` (or an ad-hoc `--exclude "*.pem"`), and a change whose only modified file is `server.pem`, `gone.files` is non-empty and `kept.strip()` is empty, so the function returns the full diff containing the private-key changes to rubber_duck/critic. The same secret is correctly excluded when the commit also contains one unrelated non-excluded file, so the leak depends on whether an unrelated file is present. The comment assumes the excluded content is a safe lockfile, but the code does not check that, silently defeating privacy/security exclusions.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/review_exclude.py:113

chunk_findings.detail: The change makes `review.exclude_globs` ineffective whenever every changed file is excluded: it sends the full excluded diff to reviewers. The test asserts this behavior directly (`"LOCKED" in kept`) and the mixed-file test asserts that an excluded generated file’s contents are sent to the reviewer (`"GENERATED_MARK" in seen.read_text()`). Given a repo config with `[review].exclude_globs = ["*.pem"]` and a change that only modifies `server.pem`, the same code path returns the private key diff to the external reviewer, violating the exclusion and potentially leaking secrets. The fix should preserve exclusion semantics (e.g., send only file names/metadata or record a special no-content review), not send excluded file bodies.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_lockfile_only_item.py:33

chunk_findings.detail: The test is named `..._naming_them`, but it does not actually assert that the excluded file is named. It only checks that the review text contains the generic substring `"excluded from review"`. An implementation could emit a review text like `All changed files are excluded from review.` without ever listing `x.py`; the test would still pass because `out.exit == 0`, the full diff contains `GENERATED_MARK`, and the generic substring is present. This leaves the promised “naming them” behavior unguarded.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_exclude.py:111

chunk_findings.detail: `excluded_outright` recomputes the exclusion with `patterns(cfg, repo)` using the default `tags=None`, `exclude=""`, and `include_pinned=False`, while the actual review exclusion in `apply` is computed from `patterns(cfg, repo, tags, exclude, include_pinned)`. Given a repo with no `[review].exclude_globs` but a review invoked with an ad-hoc exclusion such as `apply(diff_of_only_uv_lock, cfg, repo, say, ev, exclude="uv.lock")`, `apply` drops the only file and records the exclusion, but `excluded_outright(cfg, repo, ["uv.lock"])` sees no patterns and returns `False`. If `complete` uses this function to decide whether to demand an independent reviewer, the same lockfile-only item still cannot complete, so the gate is inconsistent with the exclusion path it is supposed to mirror.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/review_exclude.py:84

chunk_findings.detail: The new `excluded_outright` policy is defined only by `review.exclude_globs`, and the test asserts that any entirely excluded change is “outright excluded.” Combined with the stated completion behavior (“a change made entirely of excluded files needs no cross-family reviewer”), this bypasses reviewer independence for arbitrary excluded paths, not just lockfiles/chores. chunk_findings.detail: The new fallback overrides *every* review exclusion, not just lockfile/chore exclusions. Given `review.exclude_globs = ["*.pem"]` (or an ad-hoc `--exclude "*.pem"`), and a change whose only modified file is `server.pem`, `gone.files` is non-empty and `kept.strip()` is empty, so the function returns the full diff containing the private-key changes to rubber_duck/critic. The same secret is correctly excluded when the commit also contains one unrelated non-excluded file, so the leak depends on whether an unrelated file is present. The comment assumes the excluded content is a safe lockfile, but the code does not check that, silently defeating privacy/security exclusions.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/review_exclude.py:113

chunk_findings.detail: The change makes `review.exclude_globs` ineffective whenever every changed file is excluded: it sends the full excluded diff to reviewers. The test asserts this behavior directly (`"LOCKED" in kept`) and the mixed-file test asserts that an excluded generated file’s contents are sent to the reviewer (`"GENERATED_MARK" in seen.read_text()`). Given a repo config with `[review].exclude_globs = ["*.pem"]` and a change that only modifies `server.pem`, the same code path returns the private key diff to the external reviewer, violating the exclusion and potentially leaking secrets. The fix should preserve exclusion semantics (e.g., send only file names/metadata or record a special no-content review), not send excluded file bodies.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_lockfile_only_item.py:33

chunk_findings.detail: The test is named `..._naming_them`, but it does not actually assert that the excluded file is named. It only checks that the review text contains the generic substring `"excluded from review"`. An implementation could emit a review text like `All changed files are excluded from review.` without ever listing `x.py`; the test would still pass because `out.exit == 0`, the full diff contains `GENERATED_MARK`, and the generic substring is present. This leaves the promised “naming them” behavior unguarded.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_exclude.py:111

chunk_findings.detail: The new independence bypass is keyed only on `RX.excluded_outright(...)`, which by the function’s own contract is true when *every* changed path matches a review exclusion (`[review].exclude_globs` / pin files). It is not limited to lockfiles or chore-class files. Given a project with `[review].exclude_globs = ["*.pem"]` and a task whose only changed path is `server.pem`, `changed_paths(repo, it)` returns `["server.pem"]`, `RX.excluded_outright` returns true, so `needs_independent_reviewer` returns false and `_independence` adds no blocker. The item can therefore complete with no independent reviewer and without `--force`. This is a new defect of the rewritten code: it fixes the lockfile-only case by suppressing reviewer independence for any fully excluded change, including sensitive or otherwise non-lockfile files that an operator merely excluded from automated review.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/completion.py:196

chunk_findings.detail: `excluded_outright` calls `patterns(cfg, repo)` with default `tags`, `exclude`, and `include_pinned`, while the actual exclusion path in `apply` calls `patterns(cfg, repo, tags, exclude, include_pinned)`. Therefore the new predicate does not faithfully answer “would the review exclusion drop every path?” for any review that uses ad-hoc or tag-scoped exclusions. For example, with `[review].exclude_globs` empty but a review run with `--exclude uv.lock` (or `apply(..., exclude="uv.lock")`), a diff whose only changed file is `uv.lock` returns empty `kept` and non-empty `gone.files`, so the review should be treated as entirely excluded/UNAVAILABLE. But `excluded_outright(cfg, repo, ["uv.lock"])` returns `False` because `patterns(cfg, repo)` sees no patterns. If `complete` uses this helper to waive the independent-reviewer requirement, the lockfile-only item remains blocked under the same ad-hoc exclusion, and the predicate can similarly disagree with tag-specific exclusion settings.

chunk_findings.detail: The failure branch adds the promise “the next clean delta then passes” whenever `GD.triage_counts` reports `untriaged > 0`, without checking that the gate’s failed record is actually the held pass. For a gate whose failed record has no `held_pass` evidence, `_held_and_settled` returns `None`, so `_unchanged_delta` will never release it; any later unchanged delta stays failed. Example: gate record `outcome="failed"`, `evidence={}` (no `held_pass`), triage counts `{"findings": 2, "untriaged": 1}`. An unchanged delta returns exit `REFUSED` and a reason saying triage will make the next clean delta pass, but the release path requires `held_pass`, so triage cannot unblock it. This contradicts the intended “only the hold is released” behavior and can cause an agent to triage and retry an unchanged delta expecting a pass that is impossible.

chunk_findings.detail: The new flag is set for any review that ends with `outcome == "failed"` and has any truthy `held` value. It does not check that the current review itself was clean and the failure was caused only by the held findings (for example, that `best.status` was `"passed"` and `_hold` changed it to failed). Thus a failed delta that has its own non-hold failure while older findings are also held records `held_pass=True`. Later, when an unchanged delta consults that evidence to decide whether the hold can be released, a failed delta that is “not the hold” is treated as releasable — exactly the case named by the added regression test `test_a_failed_delta_that_is_not_the_hold_is_never_released`. A concrete scenario is: a gate has held finding H; a delta review fails because of a new non-held failure F while H is still held; `held` is truthy, so the evidence is marked `held_pass=True`. After H is settled, the unchanged-delta path can release the gate even though the non-hold failure from that review remains, allowing the gate to pass without a real review of the failure.

chunk_findings.detail: In the combined-review path, the per-gate `_record` call has already persisted `rec.outcome` before `_link_refuted` is called. If `_link_refuted` finds digests already refuted on another gate, it only appends `review.triaged` log events and prints a message; it does not recompute the held count or update the just-recorded outcome. Thus a combined review whose only held findings are previously refuted digests is still recorded as failed. For example, if the item has `triage["critic"][d] = {"verdict": "refuted", ...}` and the combined review for `rubber_duck` produces `chunk_findings=[d]` with `rec.outcome="fail"`, the code records `rubber_duck = fail`, then logs the auto-refuted triage and continues, leaving the gate failed—exactly the re-raised-refuted failure the change intends to fix.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/review.py:2127-2137 (combined-review recording branch)

chunk_findings.detail: The fake reviewer fixture emits a fixed `STATUS: FINDINGS 1` whenever stdin contains the substring `FIND`, rather than the number of findings it actually emitted. If a reviewer chunk contains both `FINDA` and `FINDB` (the script explicitly handles this by printing two `FINDING` lines), the output claims one finding while providing two; if the review prompt contains `FIND` for a clean chunk, it claims one finding while providing none. This makes the regression test depend on a parser that ignores the required status count and can produce false-positive/negative finding counts, so the test fixture is not a valid reviewer output.

chunk_findings.detail: The ended-session fallback ignores later sessions that declared no model and can therefore return a stale model. For example, if the same agent has session S1 started with `--model old` and then ended, followed by a later session S2 started without a model and then ended, `_session_model` finds no open session, the `declared` list filters out S2 because `s.model` is empty, and the function returns `old` with source `"session"`. A `complete` call without `--model` is then attributed to the model from the older closed session, not the latest session/identity declaration, and the CLI/result/durable event claim the model came from “the agent’s session” even though the latest session did not declare that model.

chunk_findings.detail: The new path restriction is verified only when `edit.landed_paths` is supplied. If an item already has `landed_paths` and the operator later records or corrects the landing with `update --landed <range>` without also supplying `--landed-paths`, the `edit.landed is not None` branch records the new `landed_before`/`landed_after` and never calls `LD.check_paths` against the existing `landed_paths`. The item can then keep a path restriction that is not inside the newly recorded landing range, while `changed_paths` still reports only those paths; the doc-only pipeline can therefore run for a landing whose changed files do not contain the item’s recorded docs. Existing `landed_paths` should be revalidated, cleared, or the landing change should require a new path restriction.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items.py:update (landed_paths handling)

chunk_findings.detail: When `landed_paths` is set, `changed_paths` can return an empty list even though git successfully reported changed files for the landed range. For example, with `landed_before..landed_after` changing only `src/x.py` and `landed_paths=['docs/y.md']`, `CH.changed_paths` returns `['src/x.py']`, but the filter returns `[]`. The function’s documented contract says it returns `None` when git cannot say and “never an empty ‘nothing changed’”; returning `[]` here makes a failed path restriction look like a successful empty change set. Callers that rely on the non-empty invariant and classify docs-only with `paths is not None and all(is_doc(p) for p in paths)` will see the empty list as vacuously docs-only, so a range that no longer holds any of the item’s restricted work can get the doc pipeline instead of failing closed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/completion.py:changed_paths

chunk_findings.detail: The failure branch adds the promise “the next clean delta then passes” whenever `GD.triage_counts` reports `untriaged > 0`, without checking that the gate’s failed record is actually the held pass. For a gate whose failed record has no `held_pass` evidence, `_held_and_settled` returns `None`, so `_unchanged_delta` will never release it; any later unchanged delta stays failed. Example: gate record `outcome="failed"`, `evidence={}` (no `held_pass`), triage counts `{"findings": 2, "untriaged": 1}`. An unchanged delta returns exit `REFUSED` and a reason saying triage will make the next clean delta pass, but the release path requires `held_pass`, so triage cannot unblock it. This contradicts the intended “only the hold is released” behavior and can cause an agent to triage and retry an unchanged delta expecting a pass that is impossible.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/review.py:_unchanged_delta

chunk_findings.detail: The new flag is set for any review that ends with `outcome == "failed"` and has any truthy `held` value. It does not check that the current review itself was clean and the failure was caused only by the held findings (for example, that `best.status` was `"passed"` and `_hold` changed it to failed). Thus a failed delta that has its own non-hold failure while older findings are also held records `held_pass=True`. Later, when an unchanged delta consults that evidence to decide whether the hold can be released, a failed delta that is “not the hold” is treated as releasable — exactly the case named by the added regression test `test_a_failed_delta_that_is_not_the_hold_is_never_released`. A concrete scenario is: a gate has held finding H; a delta review fails because of a new non-held failure F while H is still held; `held` is truthy, so the evidence is marked `held_pass=True`. After H is settled, the unchanged-delta path can release the gate even though the non-hold failure from that review remains, allowing the gate to pass without a real review of the failure.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/review.py:2297 (`evidence["held_pass"] = True`)

chunk_findings.detail: The test does not actually isolate the `held_pass` marker it claims to test. After the full review, finding 1 is left untriaged; the delta adds finding 2, and the test triages only finding 2. The final unchanged delta can stay failed solely because finding 1 remains untriaged, so an implementation that ignored the `held_pass` marker but still required all findings to be settled would also pass. To test the stated invariant, the test must settle all findings (e.g. also triage finding 1, or start from a clean full review) while `held_pass` is absent, then assert that the unchanged delta does not flip the failed delta to passed.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_delta.py:test_a_failed_delta_that_is_not_the_hold_is_never_released

chunk_findings.detail: The new fallback overrides *every* review exclusion, not just lockfile/chore exclusions. Given `review.exclude_globs = ["*.pem"]` (or an ad-hoc `--exclude "*.pem"`), and a change whose only modified file is `server.pem`, `gone.files` is non-empty and `kept.strip()` is empty, so the function returns the full diff containing the private-key changes to rubber_duck/critic. The same secret is correctly excluded when the commit also contains one unrelated non-excluded file, so the leak depends on whether an unrelated file is present. The comment assumes the excluded content is a safe lockfile, but the code does not check that, silently defeating privacy/security exclusions.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/review_exclude.py:113

chunk_findings.detail: The change makes `review.exclude_globs` ineffective whenever every changed file is excluded: it sends the full excluded diff to reviewers. The test asserts this behavior directly (`"LOCKED" in kept`) and the mixed-file test asserts that an excluded generated file’s contents are sent to the reviewer (`"GENERATED_MARK" in seen.read_text()`). Given a repo config with `[review].exclude_globs = ["*.pem"]` and a change that only modifies `server.pem`, the same code path returns the private key diff to the external reviewer, violating the exclusion and potentially leaking secrets. The fix should preserve exclusion semantics (e.g., send only file names/metadata or record a special no-content review), not send excluded file bodies.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_lockfile_only_item.py:33

chunk_findings.detail: The test is named `..._naming_them`, but it does not actually assert that the excluded file is named. It only checks that the review text contains the generic substring `"excluded from review"`. An implementation could emit a review text like `All changed files are excluded from review.` without ever listing `x.py`; the test would still pass because `out.exit == 0`, the full diff contains `GENERATED_MARK`, and the generic substring is present. This leaves the promised “naming them” behavior unguarded.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_exclude.py:111

chunk_findings.detail: `excluded_outright` recomputes the exclusion with `patterns(cfg, repo)` using the default `tags=None`, `exclude=""`, and `include_pinned=False`, while the actual review exclusion in `apply` is computed from `patterns(cfg, repo, tags, exclude, include_pinned)`. Given a repo with no `[review].exclude_globs` but a review invoked with an ad-hoc exclusion such as `apply(diff_of_only_uv_lock, cfg, repo, say, ev, exclude="uv.lock")`, `apply` drops the only file and records the exclusion, but `excluded_outright(cfg, repo, ["uv.lock"])` sees no patterns and returns `False`. If `complete` uses this function to decide whether to demand an independent reviewer, the same lockfile-only item still cannot complete, so the gate is inconsistent with the exclusion path it is supposed to mirror.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/review_exclude.py:84

chunk_findings.detail: The new `excluded_outright` policy is defined only by `review.exclude_globs`, and the test asserts that any entirely excluded change is “outright excluded.” Combined with the stated completion behavior (“a change made entirely of excluded files needs no cross-family reviewer”), this bypasses reviewer independence for arbitrary excluded paths, not just lockfiles/chores. For example, with `[review].exclude_globs = ["*.pem"]`, a change whose only modified file is `server.pem` makes `excluded_outright(..., ["server.pem"])` true on the same code path as `["uv.lock"]`, so `complete` can skip the independent-reviewer check and complete the change without any reviewer. The superseded leak finding does not answer this: the diff may no longer be sent to reviewers, but the secret modification can still pass completion unreviewed.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_lockfile_only_item.py:27

chunk_findings.detail: The test docstring promises that the unavailable review “says why (naming the excluded file)”, but the assertion only checks the generic substring `"excluded file(s)"`. An implementation can return a reason such as `"All changed files are excluded from review."` without ever listing `uv.lock`, and the test still passes. Thus the regression test does not actually enforce the “naming the excluded file” behavior it claims to cover.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_lockfile_only_item.py: `test_a_lockfile_only_change_is_unavailable_not_leaked`

chunk_findings.detail: The added assertion makes a transient review exclusion a completion waiver. With no `[review].exclude_globs`, a change that only touches `app.py` can be reviewed with `--exclude app.py` (or any pattern matching all changed files); `apply` drops the only file and calls `excluded_outright(..., exclude="app.py")`, which now returns True, as pinned by this test. The review gates then record UNAVAILABLE, and per the docstring `complete` will not demand an independent reviewer, so the change completes without any review. The previous fix only made the predicate mirror the review's inputs; it did not restrict the waiver to persistent project exclusions or lockfile/chore, so the reviewer-independence bypass remains and is now reachable from an ad-hoc CLI flag.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_lockfile_only_item.py:33

chunk_findings.detail: The rewritten predicate iterates `paths` twice. For a one-shot iterable (a generator), `if not paths` is always false, the first `all(... for p in paths)` consumes the iterator, and the second `all(_hit(...) for p in paths)` then iterates an empty sequence and is vacuously true. Thus `excluded_outright(cfg, repo, iter([]))` returns True whenever `patterns(cfg, repo)` is non-empty, even though the function is documented to be true only for a non-empty set of paths; more generally, `excluded_outright(cfg, repo, iter(["uv.lock"]))` can return True without actually verifying that the configured exclusion hits `uv.lock`, because the second check sees no items. The previous implementation iterated `paths` only once; this change can falsely waive reviewer independence if a caller supplies a lazily produced iterable such as `filter(...)` or `map(...)` rather than a list.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/review_exclude.py:excluded_outright

chunk_findings.detail: The rewritten test now claims to verify that the review “records UNAVAILABLE,” but the only assertions are `out.exit == 2` and that the fake reviewer did not receive `SECRET_ISH`. The event-log/gate-outcome assertion that the previous triage said would pin the completion-crucial `UNAVAILABLE` record is not present in this file. An implementation can return exit 2 for some unrelated unavailable condition, or return exit 2 without writing the `rubber_duck`/`critic` UNAVAILABLE event that `complete` inspects, and this test will still pass, so the regression test does not actually pin the behavior needed to close the completion bug.

chunk_findings.detail: The combined-review path auto-links already-refuted digests only after the gate result has already been recorded, and it never recomputes the outcome from the linked digests. If an item has digest `X` refuted on another gate, and a combined review for this gate returns `rec.outcome="fail"` with `ev["chunk_findings"]=[{"digest": "X", ...}]`, the code calls the preceding `_record(... evidence=ev, gates=gates)` with the failing outcome, then `_link_refuted` logs `X` as refuted and prints `recorded ... = fail`. The gate still fails even though its only finding was already refuted; unlike the non-combined path, it does not adjust held/outcome, so the reported bug remains for combined reviews.

chunk_findings.detail: `mine = it.triage.get(gate, {})` is captured once and is never updated when the function appends a new triage log entry. If the same digest appears more than once in `findings` (for example, duplicate `chunk_findings` from a combined review), the first occurrence is linked, but the second still sees `digest not in mine` and appends another `review.triaged` entry for the same gate/digest. Example: `findings=[Finding(digest="X"), Finding(digest="X")]`, `it.triage={"other": {"X": {"verdict": "refuted", "probe": "..."}}}`, `gate="rubber_duck"` produces two refuted triage entries for `rubber_duck:X`, and the returned `linked` list contains `"X"` twice, so the later `held = max(0, held - len(linked))` can decrement the held count more times than there are distinct settled findings.

chunk_findings.detail: The first test asserts that the `rubber_duck` review outcome is `"failed"` even though it immediately asserts that all `rubber_duck` findings are already refuted and `untriaged == 0`. In the scenario it constructs, the critic has refuted both findings and `rubber_duck` raises byte-identical findings; the stated fix is to make those already-refuted claims settle the round rather than fail the gate. If `api.review(...).data["outcome"]` is the gate outcome (as `_gui` treats it when deciding whether triage is needed), a correct auto-link fix should not return `"failed"` for this round, so this assertion fails. If the implementation instead leaves the outcome failed as the test requires, the gate still fails and the reported bug is not fixed.

"passed" ...)` flips the gate to passed. This releases a failure that was not the hold’s “next clean delta passes” promise and bypasses the originally recorded failure condition.

chunk_findings.detail: The test is renamed to claim that the unchanged delta “counts no round,” but it never checks the actual round counter (`_ev(repo)["delta_rounds"]`). It only checks that the refusal text contains `"No round was counted"` and that no reviewer was invoked (`_calls(seen) == calls`). If an implementation increments `delta_rounds` on the unchanged delta while still emitting the new `"No round was counted"` message, this test passes even though the exact bug (an unchanged delta burning a round) has returned.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_delta.py:test_nothing_changed_since_the_reviewed_head_counts_no_round_and_names_full

chunk_findings.detail: The test claims the unchanged delta counts no round and the gate stays failed, but it does not capture `delta_rounds` after the held delta before the unchanged review, nor does it assert the gate outcome remains failed after the refusal. For example, if the held clean delta failed to count a round (`delta_rounds == 0`) and the unchanged refusal then counted one (`delta_rounds == 1`), the final assertion `_ev(repo)["delta_rounds"] == 1` would still pass, so the test does not isolate the “unchanged delta spent no round” claim. Similarly, an implementation that writes a passed gate outcome but returns `REFUSED` with the expected reason strings would pass this test.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_delta.py:test_an_unchanged_delta_with_findings_still_untriaged_stays_failed_and_counts_no_round

chunk_findings.detail: The new test is presented as the probe that a failed delta without the `held_pass` marker is never released, but it does not exercise the path that needed that guard. The delta fails because it introduced its own finding (`FINDME-B`), so its recorded `delta_findings` are non-empty. The earlier concern was that a failed delta with `review_kind == "delta"` and an empty `delta_findings` list, but no actual hold marker, could be treated as the held clean delta and released. This test never reaches that condition: even the pre-fix logic described in the earlier finding would refuse because `delta_findings` is not falsey. Thus the test does not prove the `held_pass`-marker refutation; a regression for that case needs a failed clean delta with empty `delta_findings` and no `held_pass` (for example a max-rounds failure) whose findings are then settled.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_delta.py:test_a_failed_delta_that_is_not_the_hold_is_never_released

Given a state where agent `a` has an older still-open session `s1` with `started_at=1`, `model="old"`, and a newer session `s2` with `started_at=2`, `model=""`, `ended_at=3`, a `complete` without `--model` returns `("old", "session")` and the CLI prints “author model: old (from the agent’s session)”. The newer model-less session should supersede the older declaration and cause `complete` to refuse, but the open-session shortcut re-attributes the stale model.

chunk_findings.detail: `_held_and_settled` decides that a failed gate is the special “clean delta held over untriaged earlier findings” case only from `review_kind == "delta"` and a falsey `delta_findings`; it never verifies that the recorded failure is actually the `_hold` failure. Given a failed gate whose evidence happens to contain `{"review_kind": "delta", "delta_findings": []}` for a different reason (for example a max-rounds failure or any other clean-delta failure), and `GD.triage_counts(...)` returning something like `{"findings": 1, "untriaged": 0, "refuted": 0, "confirmed": 1}`, an unchanged `review --delta` enters `_unchanged_delta`, `_held_and_settled` returns counts, and `GD.record(... "passed" ...)` flips the gate to passed. This releases a failure that was not the hold’s “next clean delta passes” promise and bypasses the originally recorded failure condition.

chunk_findings.detail: The test is renamed to claim that the unchanged delta “counts no round,” but it never checks the actual round counter (`_ev(repo)["delta_rounds"]`). It only checks that the refusal text contains `"No round was counted"` and that no reviewer was invoked (`_calls(seen) == calls`). If an implementation increments `delta_rounds` on the unchanged delta while still emitting the new `"No round was counted"` message, this test passes even though the exact bug (an unchanged delta burning a round) has returned.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_delta.py:test_nothing_changed_since_the_reviewed_head_counts_no_round_and_names_full

chunk_findings.detail: The test claims the unchanged delta counts no round and the gate stays failed, but it does not capture `delta_rounds` after the held delta before the unchanged review, nor does it assert the gate outcome remains failed after the refusal. For example, if the held clean delta failed to count a round (`delta_rounds == 0`) and the unchanged refusal then counted one (`delta_rounds == 1`), the final assertion `_ev(repo)["delta_rounds"] == 1` would still pass, so the test does not isolate the “unchanged delta spent no round” claim. Similarly, an implementation that writes a passed gate outcome but returns `REFUSED` with the expected reason strings would pass this test.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_delta.py:test_an_unchanged_delta_with_findings_still_untriaged_stays_failed_and_counts_no_round

chunk_findings.detail: The new test is presented as the probe that a failed delta without the `held_pass` marker is never released, but it does not exercise the path that needed that guard. The delta fails because it introduced its own finding (`FINDME-B`), so its recorded `delta_findings` are non-empty. The earlier concern was that a failed delta with `review_kind == "delta"` and an empty `delta_findings` list, but no actual hold marker, could be treated as the held clean delta and released. This test never reaches that condition: even the pre-fix logic described in the earlier finding would refuse because `delta_findings` is not falsey. Thus the test does not prove the `held_pass`-marker refutation; a regression for that case needs a failed clean delta with empty `delta_findings` and no `held_pass` (for example a max-rounds failure) whose findings are then settled.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_delta.py:test_a_failed_delta_that_is_not_the_hold_is_never_released

chunk_findings.detail: The added assertions still do not isolate the unchanged delta’s round count. If the held clean delta undercounted `delta_rounds` as `0` and the unchanged refusal then incremented it to `1`, the final assertion would still pass even though the unchanged delta burned a round, which is the behavior the test claims to forbid. chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_delta.py:test_an_unchanged_delta_with_findings_still_untriaged_stays_failed_and_counts_no_round

chunk_findings.detail: The new test is meant to prove that a markerless held delta can be released by an unchanged delta without burning a round, but it only checks the final counter (`_ev(repo)["delta_rounds"] == 1`) after the release. It never captures `delta_rounds` immediately after the held clean delta, unlike the neighbouring unchanged-delta test. If a regression caused the held clean delta to leave `delta_rounds` at `0` and the unchanged markerless review to increment it to `1`, all assertions in this test would still pass, so the test would not detect the exact “unchanged delta counts a round” regression it is supposed to guard.

chunk_findings.detail: The new wave-loop text gives contradictory termination rules. It says the session “keeps driving until nothing actionable is left,” but then says “Stop ONLY where the question tool says so,” and enumerates only `AskUserQuestion`, operator approval, policy decisions, and un-settleable review findings. Given a phase where all tasks have merged and `ddflow next --json` returns no ready items and no in-flight leases, the agent has no defined behavior: stopping violates “Stop ONLY where the question tool says so,” while continuing violates “until nothing actionable is left” and can lead to repeated `next` polling or an unnecessary operator prompt.

chunk_findings.detail: The new fallback overrides *every* review exclusion, not just lockfile/chore exclusions. Given `review.exclude_globs = ["*.pem"]` (or an ad-hoc `--exclude "*.pem"`), and a change whose only modified file is `server.pem`, `gone.files` is non-empty and `kept.strip()` is empty, so the function returns the full diff containing the private-key changes to rubber_duck/critic. The same secret is correctly excluded when the commit also contains one unrelated non-excluded file, so the leak depends on whether an unrelated file is present. The comment assumes the excluded content is a safe lockfile, but the code does not check that, silently defeating privacy/security exclusions.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/review_exclude.py:113

chunk_findings.detail: The change makes `review.exclude_globs` ineffective whenever every changed file is excluded: it sends the full excluded diff to reviewers. The test asserts this behavior directly (`"LOCKED" in kept`) and the mixed-file test asserts that an excluded generated file’s contents are sent to the reviewer (`"GENERATED_MARK" in seen.read_text()`). Given a repo config with `[review].exclude_globs = ["*.pem"]` and a change that only modifies `server.pem`, the same code path returns the private key diff to the external reviewer, violating the exclusion and potentially leaking secrets. The fix should preserve exclusion semantics (e.g., send only file names/metadata or record a special no-content review), not send excluded file bodies.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_lockfile_only_item.py:33

chunk_findings.detail: The test is named `..._naming_them`, but it does not actually assert that the excluded file is named. It only checks that the review text contains the generic substring `"excluded from review"`. An implementation could emit a review text like `All changed files are excluded from review.` without ever listing `x.py`; the test would still pass because `out.exit == 0`, the full diff contains `GENERATED_MARK`, and the generic substring is present. This leaves the promised “naming them” behavior unguarded.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_exclude.py:111

chunk_findings.detail: The new independence bypass is keyed only on `RX.excluded_outright(...)`, which by the function’s own contract is true when *every* changed path matches a review exclusion (`[review].exclude_globs` / pin files). It is not limited to lockfiles or chore-class files. Given a project with `[review].exclude_globs = ["*.pem"]` and a task whose only changed path is `server.pem`, `changed_paths(repo, it)` returns `["server.pem"]`, `RX.excluded_outright` returns true, so `needs_independent_reviewer` returns false and `_independence` adds no blocker. The item can therefore complete with no independent reviewer and without `--force`. This is a new defect of the rewritten code: it fixes the lockfile-only case by suppressing reviewer independence for any fully excluded change, including sensitive or otherwise non-lockfile files that an operator merely excluded from automated review.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/completion.py:196

chunk_findings.detail: `excluded_outright` calls `patterns(cfg, repo)` with default `tags`, `exclude`, and `include_pinned`, while the actual exclusion path in `apply` calls `patterns(cfg, repo, tags, exclude, include_pinned)`. Therefore the new predicate does not faithfully answer “would the review exclusion drop every path?” for any review that uses ad-hoc or tag-scoped exclusions. For example, with `[review].exclude_globs` empty but a review run with `--exclude uv.lock` (or `apply(..., exclude="uv.lock")`), a diff whose only changed file is `uv.lock` returns empty `kept` and non-empty `gone.files`, so the review should be treated as entirely excluded/UNAVAILABLE. But `excluded_outright(cfg, repo, ["uv.lock"])` returns `False` because `patterns(cfg, repo)` sees no patterns. If `complete` uses this helper to waive the independent-reviewer requirement, the lockfile-only item remains blocked under the same ad-hoc exclusion, and the predicate can similarly disagree with tag-specific exclusion settings.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/review_exclude.py:92

chunk_findings.detail:
Threading `tags`/`exclude`/`include_pinned` makes the predicate agree with the review invocation, but it still returns true for any change whose every path matches `[review].exclude_globs`, not just lockfile/chore-class paths. The completion independence bypass (in `completion.py`, unchanged in this manifest) keys on this predicate, so with a project config `[review]
exclude_globs = ["*.pem"]` and a task whose only changed path is `server.pem`, `excluded_outright(cfg, repo, ["server.pem"])` returns true and the item can complete without an independent reviewer. The prior triage fix only addressed ad-hoc/tag input fidelity; it does not restrict the bypass to the lockfile/chore cases the bug was meant to unblock.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/review_exclude.py:excluded_outright

chunk_findings.detail: The generated-class test treats any path matched by the `pinned` list as generated (`or _hit(p, [], pinned)`). Since `pins.toml` is project configuration and `_hit` also treats a trailing-slash entry as a directory prefix, a non-generated file can be placed into the exempt class by adding it to `pins.toml`. Given a repo whose `pins.toml` contains `server.pem` (or `secrets/`) and whose `[review].exclude_globs` is empty or `["*.pem"]`, `excluded_outright(cfg, repo, ["server.pem"])` returns true: the `generated` all() passes via the pinned branch, `pats or pinned` is true, and the final `_hit` passes via the same pinned entry. Completion then waives reviewer independence for a change that only touches a non-generated, privacy-pinned file, even though it matches neither `GENERATED_EXCLUDE_DEFAULTS` nor `LOCKFILES`. This reintroduces a config-set privacy waiver through pins.

data.claim: The record line printed for a findings verdict (`--outcome failed --reviewed-sha <sha> --model <m>`) carries no --reason, and ddflow's own gate-record contract refuses outcome failed with no reason.

chunk_findings.detail: When `marks` is `None` — which is always true when `DDFLOW_STORE_INCREMENTAL=0`, and also true after a stored-mark mismatch or a first-build verification failure — the rebuild fallback evaluates `self._verified_shard_marks({}, log)` *after* `events = log.read_all()` and passes that result to `_build_into`. If another writer appends to the log between `log.read_all()` and this verification call, the marks passed to `_build_into` include the newly appended shard bytes while the `state`/`events` passed to `_build_into` do not. The published index therefore carries verification marks that claim the appended bytes were consumed by a projection that never folded them, violating the invariant stated immediately above the read (“The marks BEFORE the read… a byte the projection never folded could be claimed consumed”) and allowing the next incremental open to treat that append as already consumed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/store.py:436

chunk_findings.detail: The role-offset scheme does not actually guarantee unique `prompts` keys for all valid `seq` values. A session with a prompt entry at `seq == 20000` (or simply 20,001 prompt entries when `seq` defaults to the enumerate index) and a summary entry (`seq == 0`, offset 20,000) projects two rows with the same base primary key `(session, 20000)` but different FTS ids, `session#p20000` and `session#s0`. `_write_rows` inserts both FTS rows because `INSERT OR REPLACE` into an FTS5 table keys on rowid, not the text `id` column, so after a full rebuild the base `prompts` table contains only the summary row while `prompts_fts` still contains the prompt row; recall/search can return a prompt that is not in the base table. The incremental path also cannot reconcile this projection: `want` collapses to one key while `len(rows)` is two, so `_reconcile_tables` raises `incremental prompts: reconciled rows disagree` after every rebuild. This breaks the change’s “ONE projector” parity and the comment’s “never collide” claim.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/store.py:_rows_prompts / _write_rows / _reconcile_tables

chunk_findings.detail: The trigram updates build `IN (?, ?, ...)` clauses with one bound parameter per changed/gone id: `phs = ",".join("?" * len(gone))` and `phs = ",".join("?" * len(ids))`. SQLite has a bound-variable limit (999 on older builds, 32766 on newer ones), and the code has no batching. Given a reconcile that touches or removes more rows than the limit—for example, an initial incremental reconcile from an empty table with 1000 projected items when trigram search is enabled—the statement `delete from items_tri where id in (?, ... 1000 ?)` fails with `sqlite3.OperationalError: too many SQL variables`. That is not the controlled `RuntimeError` mismatch path, so the intended “mismatch means rebuild” contract can be bypassed or abort the build.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/store.py:_reconcile_tables

chunk_findings.detail: The new `clear` branch deletes the entire similarity index (`delete from similar_docs` and `delete from similar_terms`) and then inserts only the `records` argument. The added docstring states that `clear` is for “a reconcile over changed records”; if such a reconcile passes only the changed records, every unchanged document’s `similar_docs` row and every term posting contributed by unchanged documents are removed, and the remaining postings/IDF values are rebuilt from the changed subset only. For example, after indexing documents A and B, a delta that changes only B and calls `_insert_similar(con, [B], clear=True)` leaves the similarity index containing only B, so a query for a term that occurred only in A no longer finds it. The deletion must be scoped to the replaced records, or the function must receive the full corpus; as written it is unsafe for the incremental changed-record path it documents.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/store.py:_insert_similar (new `clear` branch)

chunk_findings.detail: `test_incremental_rebuild_matches_a_fresh_rebuild` and `test_a_rewritten_shard_prefix_is_still_caught` do not pin `DDFLOW_STORE_INCREMENTAL`; only `test_incremental_reconcile_can_be_disabled` monkeypatches it. If the test environment exports `DDFLOW_STORE_INCREMENTAL=0`, these tests still pass by doing full rebuilds only, so a broken incremental reconcile that corrupts rows, or a missing shard-digest check that lets a rewritten shard prefix be reconciled incrementally, would not be caught. The added knob test does not answer this: it exercises the knob itself, but it does not force the other tests named for incremental/verified behavior to run with the knob enabled.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_store.py:122

chunk_findings.detail: The added `$schema` value points to `https://app.kilo.ai/config.json`, a Kilo configuration schema, inside `opencode.json`, which is an OpenCode configuration file. In any editor or validator that honors `$schema`, this file will be validated against the wrong schema: the existing OpenCode `mcp` configuration may be reported as invalid by a Kilo-oriented schema, while OpenCode-specific validation is bypassed, so an invalid OpenCode config could also pass. The schema declaration should match the configuration format being edited, not an unrelated Kilo endpoint.

chunk_findings.detail: When `marks` is `None` (knob disabled, stored marks failed verification, or `_reconcile` raised), the fallback full rebuild computes the marks to persist with `self._verified_shard_marks({}, log)` **after** `events = log.read_all()` and after `state = fold(events, strict=False)`. The comment immediately above explicitly says marks must be taken before the read because “marked afterwards, a byte the projection never folded could be claimed consumed.” Given a concurrent append between `log.read_all()` returning and the `_verified_shard_marks({}, log)` call, `_build_into` receives marks covering the newly appended word while the `state` it writes does not contain that word. On the next incremental rebuild, those marks verify, the delta is empty, and `_reconcile` can return the old projection, permanently omitting the appended word.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/store.py:Store.rebuild

chunk_findings.detail: The incremental path still decides whether `similar_docs` is current by comparing only the ordered list of `digest` values. That cannot establish “same rows” for the similarity table: any non-digest row content written by `_insert_similar` is ignored. For example, if the existing `similar_docs` contains a row such as `(ord=1, id=1, digest=D)` and the new projection record has `(ord=1, id=2, title="x", body="y")` with the same digest `D`, the query returns `[D]`, the computed digest list is `[D]`, and the `!=` test is false, so `_insert_similar(..., clear=True)` is not called. The stale row for the deleted/changed doc identity remains, which can make similarity results return a non-existent id and violates the same-rows parity that licenses skipping a full rebuild. The same digest-only comparison also misses changed ordering/identity columns such as `ord` if those are stored as row values.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/store.py:_reconcile

chunk_findings.detail: With `clear=True`, the function unconditionally executes `delete from similar_docs` and `delete from similar_terms`, then inserts only the rows in the supplied `records` list. The added docstring says this is for “a reconcile over changed records,” so the documented use is to pass a subset of records. For example, if `similar_docs` currently contains docs A and B, and a reconcile calls `_insert_similar(con, [record_B], clear=True)` after B changed, the commit leaves `similar_docs` and `similar_terms` containing only B; all postings and document-frequency information for unchanged doc A are lost. The deletion should be limited to the records being replaced, or the caller must pass the complete current record set; as written, the documented incremental use wipes unchanged similarity-index rows.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/store.py:_insert_similar

chunk_findings.detail: `_dump` builds each table oracle with `select * from {t}` and no `ORDER BY`, then the tests compare the resulting lists with `==`. SQLite does not guarantee row order for an unordered query, and the incremental path can change physical row order when it deletes and reinserts rows (for example, an FTS/postings row in `similar_docs` can receive a new rowid while unchanged rows keep their old rowids). A fresh rebuild after `store.path.unlink()` can insert the same logical rows in a different physical order, so `assert _dump(store) == kept` can fail even though the rows are logically identical. This is the previously reported `_dump` ordering issue; the current test still does not add an `ORDER BY` or otherwise make the comparison order-insensitive.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_store.py:_dump

chunk_findings.detail: The enabled branch only asserts that `Store._reconcile` was called; it does not assert that the enabled rebuild’s result actually came from the reconcile path. Given a `Store.rebuild` implementation such as “if the knob is enabled, call `self._reconcile(...)` for verification, then unconditionally call `self._build_into(...)` and return that result,” this test still passes: the enabled assertion sees `calls` nonempty, the disabled assertion sees `_reconcile` not called when `DDFLOW_STORE_INCREMENTAL=0`, and the parity checks still pass because the unconditional full build produces correct rows. Thus the test does not pin that the enabled/default path actually uses the incremental result. This is the previously reported finding 12 and remains unaddressed.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_store.py:test_incremental_reconcile_can_be_disabled

chunk_findings.detail: The new helper still relies on `not W.dirty(...)` as the only proof that the checkout is clean, but Git’s dirty check does not report changes hidden by `assume-unchanged` or `skip-worktree`. The earlier finding’s triage probe discusses a phase-exemption overshoot, not this hidden-index case, so the hole still holds. For example, with a merged item whose `merged_sha` is in the base history, if the primary or kept worktree has `HEAD^{tree}` equal to the merged tree and an operator/agent runs `git update-index --assume-unchanged tests/test_a.py` and then modifies that file, the ancestry checks pass, `HEAD^{tree}` still equals the merged tree, `W.dirty` returns false, and `_at_merged_tree` returns true. `item_tree` then accepts that checkout as the merged tree and records a gate outcome for the merged item even though the tests actually run against modified content. The same can happen with sparse checkout: a tracked test file may be skipped/absent while `HEAD^{tree}` and `W.dirty` still make the checkout look like the merged tree.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/gates.py:_at_merged_tree

chunk_findings.detail: The new unconditional phase exemption accepts any phase with `merged_sha` before checking whether the checkout actually stands at the merged tree. Given a phase item whose merge is recorded (`it.kind == "phase"`, `it.merged_sha` set) but whose primary/kept worktree has been reverted, checked out away from `merged_sha`, or is dirty, this function returns `""` immediately when called with `gate="implement"`, `result="passed"`, and `has_note=False`. The non-phase path would call `_at_merged_tree`, reject the reverted/dirty/moved checkout, then fall through to `rev-list --count base..HEAD` and refuse the passed implement gate. Thus a merged phase can claim a reverted or dirty primary as the merged outcome, contrary to the behavior the added revert/dirty regression tests are meant to enforce.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/gates.py:1011

chunk_findings.detail: The previously confirmed `_at_merged_tree` hole is not answered by this change. The new tests only prove that an ordinary tracked modification is rejected (`test_a_dirty_primary_is_not_the_merged_tree`); they do not exercise `assume-unchanged` or `skip-worktree` states, which are exactly the states that make Git’s committed-tree equality plus the normal dirty check lie. Given a merged item whose primary checkout is at `it.merged_sha`, an operator or agent can run `git update-index --assume-unchanged tests/test_critical.py` and then modify that file (or sparse-checkout/skip a tracked test-affecting file). `git rev-parse HEAD^{tree}` still equals the merged tree and `W.dirty`/`git status` still reports clean, so `_at_merged_tree` can still admit the checkout as “at the merged tree” and `gate run T1 unit_tests` can record `passed` for T1 while the working tree actually being measured is not the merged tree.

chunk_findings.detail: The new index-mark guard is fail-open: it refuses the checkout only when `marked.ok` is true and a marked line is seen. If `git ls-files -v` exits non-zero, the guard is skipped and the old `W.dirty` + `git diff --quiet` path can still return `True`. Under an `assume-unchanged` (or `skip-worktree`) mark, both `git status`/`W.dirty` and `git diff --quiet` can report clean even though the working file differs from HEAD. Given a merged item whose `HEAD^{tree}` equals `merged_sha^{tree}`, but whose primary checkout has a tracked file modified and marked `assume-unchanged`, in an environment where `git ls-files -v` fails while the other git calls succeed (for example, a PATH `git` shim that rejects `ls-files -v` but returns success for `rev-parse`, `status`, and `diff --quiet`), `_at_merged_tree` skips the mark check and returns `True`, admitting a checkout that does not actually stand at the merged tree. The docstring’s “no checkout whose index carries a mark can be PROVEN … and none is admitted” requires failing closed when the mark scan itself fails, e.g. `if not marked.ok: return False`, rather than `if marked.ok and any(...)`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/gates.py:_at_merged_tree

chunk_findings.detail: In the `sort == "severity"` path, the function re-calls `view_list(..., limit=0, offset=0)` and copies that fresh outcome into `base`, then overwrites `offset`, `rows`, `shown`, `truncated`, and `next`, but it never overwrites `limit` with the caller’s requested `lim`. Because `fresh` was fetched with `limit=0`, the returned outcome’s `data["limit"]` is whatever the engine records for that whole-set fetch (typically `0` or `MAX_LIMIT`), not the page limit the caller actually requested. For example, a bug-list call requesting `limit=2` can return two rows while `data["limit"]` still says `0` (or `MAX_LIMIT`), so any client that uses the returned `limit` to determine page size or pagination behavior receives incorrect metadata.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/bugs.py:finish_bug_list

chunk_findings.detail: `ddflow_list` is a generic list tool, but the MCP dispatcher applies the bug-specific `finish_bug_list` post-processing to every `ddflow_list` call without checking `args["kind"]`. The schema change also advertises `sort` for the whole list tool, so an MCP client can call `ddflow_list(kind="task", sort="severity")` and pass argument validation; the dispatcher then routes the non-bug result through `finish_bug_list`, bypassing the CLI/list-engine convention that non-bug kinds refuse `sort` (as asserted by `test_list_refuses_sort_for_kinds_that_do_not_take_it`). Depending on `finish_bug_list`’s tolerance, this either silently accepts/ignores an invalid sort for a non-bug kind or applies bug-list-specific processing to non-bug rows, whereas the same CLI request should be refused. The MCP path should restrict this finishing step to `kind == "bug"` or pass `kind` so the same refusal is enforced.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py:_finish_list_read

chunk_findings.detail: These tests verify severity ordering with the same `KB.severity_rank` helper that the implementation uses, instead of independently asserting the intended critical..low order. For example, if `severity_rank` were implemented with unset/empty severity as rank `0` and critical as rank `3` (the opposite of the stated intent), `finish_bug_list` could order rows unset -> medium -> high -> critical, and the assertion `keys == sorted(keys)` would still pass because it merely checks that rows are sorted by that same wrong rank function. The CLI repagination test would also pass: the first row would be the unset-severity bug, and `KB.severity_rank(body["rows"][0]["severity"]) == 0` would be true even though the critical bug is not first. The tests should assert the actual expected severity/title order, e.g. critical before high before medium before unset.

chunk_findings.detail: The severity re-cut treats the caller’s `limit` as a numeric page size even when that limit is the engine’s “all rows” sentinel `0`, which is exactly the value this function itself passes to `view_list` to fetch the whole matched set (`limit=0, offset=0`). If a bug list request asks for the whole set with `limit=0, offset=0` and `sort="severity"`, then `off, lim = 0, 0`, so the page is `full[0:0]`. For a non-empty matched set the returned outcome has `total > 0`, `rows=[]`, `shown=0`, `truncated=True`, and `next=0`; a client following `next` will loop forever and the first page is empty. The re-cut needs to handle the whole-set sentinel (for example, use `full[off:]` when `lim == 0`) or normalize the caller’s limit before slicing.

chunk_findings.detail: When `sort="severity"`, the function re-fetches the bug list with `limit=0`, but the engine normalizes `limit=0` to its `MAX_LIMIT`, so `full` contains at most `MAX_LIMIT` rows while `base["total"]` remains the full match count. If a caller asks for a page whose offset is at or beyond that capped fetch, the page is empty but still advertised as truncated with a non-advancing `next`. For example, with `MAX_LIMIT=500` and 600 matching bugs, a request for `offset=500, limit=10, sort="severity"` produces `full` of length 500, `page = full[500:510] == []`, `base["shown"] == 0`, `base["truncated"] == (600 > 500)`, and `base["next"] == 500`. Requesting `next=500` again returns the same empty page, so rows beyond the cap are unreachable and pagination can loop. This is not answered by the earlier `limit=0` probe, which only exercised offset 0.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/bugs.py:finish_bug_list

chunk_findings.detail: The new MCP tests never exercise the bug-list shaping path. `test_mcp_list_tool_declares_the_sort_argument` only asserts that the `ddflow_list` schema has a `sort` property, and `test_mcp_list_serves_the_non_bug_sort_refusal` calls `_finish_list_read` with `kind="task"`. If `_finish_list_read` failed to call `KB.finish_bug_list` for `kind="bug"` or ignored the `sort` argument, an MCP `ddflow_list` call such as `{"kind": "bug", "sort": "severity"}` would return rows without the required severity ordering and without `severity`, `fix_task`, and `needs`, but every test in this file would still pass. The stated intent requires the MCP bug list to carry the same fields and ordering as the CLI/API bug list, so the MCP bug path is untested.

With 1123 matching bugs and a request for `offset=1000, limit=10, sort="severity"`, the re-fetched `full` list contains only the first 1000 rows, so the requested page is empty (`rows=[]`, `shown=0`) yet the response still reports `truncated=True` and `next=1000`. The caller cannot advance past the cap, and later pages are silently missing even though `total` says more bugs exist.

chunk_findings.detail: The new severity paging loop fixes the normal capped-fetch case, but it does not handle the case where the loop takes its `break` branch (`if not chunk: break  # said the cap, gave less`). When that branch is taken, `full` is shorter than `fresh.data["total"]`, but the function still copies `fresh.data` into `base` and computes `truncated`/`next` from the stale total. For example, if the first `view_list(..., limit=0, offset=0)` reports `total=1001` and returns 1000 rows (`stride=1000`), and the next `view_list(..., offset=1000, limit=1000)` returns an empty chunk, `full` has 1000 rows while `base["total"]` remains 1001. A caller asking for `offset=1000, limit=10` gets `rows=[]`, `shown=0`, `truncated=True`, and `next=1000`: the result says more rows remain, but the next offset cannot advance past the short fetched set. The break branch should adjust `total` (or at least `truncated`/`next`) to reflect the rows actually fetched.

For example, with `LIST_MAX_LIMIT=1000` and 1123 matching bugs, `ddflow list bugs --sort severity --offset 1000 --limit 10` gets an empty row slice from the capped full fetch while still reporting the full total, so the CLI can show an empty page with `truncated=True` and a non-advancing `next` value (e.g. `next=1000`). chunk_findings.detail: `_fixing_item` short-circuits on `rec.fix_task` before it can fall back to the found item. If a bug record has `fix_task` set to an id that is not present in `st.items` (the state `_missing_fix_source` explicitly describes as “its fix task … is not in the queue”), the function returns `st.items.get(rec.fix_task)` and never checks `rec.item`. For example, with a bug whose `fix_task="fix-x"` is missing from the store but whose `item="found-y"` names a found item with a worktree (or a `landed_before`/`landed_after` pair), `_fixing_item` returns `None`, `_verify_regression` then returns `"needs-fix-task"`, and `ddflow bug fixed` refuses the close even though a valid pre-fix source exists. This contradicts the stated contract that a source exists when there is a found item with a worktree or landing pair.

subject: Bug list sorting by severity with dependency edges for CLI and MCP

chunk_findings.detail: When `sort="severity"`, the function fetches the whole matched set but, if a later page fetch returns no rows while the first fetch's `total` is still larger (the case its own comment calls “said the cap, gave less”), it breaks out and then builds the returned outcome from `base = dict(fresh.data)` without lowering `total` to the number of rows actually fetched. `truncated` and `next` are therefore computed from a stale total. For example, with an engine cap/limit of 2, a first fetch reporting `total=3` and returning 2 rows, a second fetch at offset 2 returning no rows, and a caller page of `offset=0, limit=2`, `finish_bug_list` returns `total=3`, `shown=2`, `truncated=True`, and `next=2`. The next call at offset 2 repeats the same full fetch, gets an empty page, and again returns `truncated=True, next=2`, so the CLI/MCP never reaches the end of the list. The early-stop path should make `total` agree with `len(full)` (or otherwise correct the advertised total).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/bugs.py:finish_bug_list

chunk_findings.detail: `finish_bug_list` is called after `view_list`, so any ordering it performs is applied only to rows already selected by the query. If the list engine’s existing `--limit`/`--offset` knobs are part of `query` (as list-rendering knobs normally are), `view_list` returns a page in the default order first, and `--sort severity` then only sorts that page. For example, with a default newest-change-first order and `--limit 10`, a critical bug outside the newest 10 will still be omitted from `ddflow list bug --limit 10 --sort severity`; severity-first ordering should have fetched/ordered it before pagination, so the command returns the wrong rows rather than the globally severity-ordered first page.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/commands/viewers_lists.py:174

chunk_findings.detail: The MCP handler calls the existing `ddflow_list` API first (`result = self._invoke(...)`) and only then applies `sort` in `_finish_list_read`; the comment explicitly says the tool’s api keeps passing only its existing filters. Therefore `sort` cannot affect any row selection already performed by the API (e.g. limit/offset or default ordering). For a call such as `ddflow_list(kind="bug", sort="severity", limit=10)` in a repo with one older critical bug and ten newer lower-severity bugs, `_invoke` asks the API for the newest 10 rows, returns the ten lower-severity bugs, and `_finish_bug_list` merely reorders that already-truncated page. The critical bug is still omitted, whereas sorting by severity before limit would include it.

chunk_findings.detail: The added `"kind",` is inserted in the middle of the command's positional argument list (the list beginning `phase`, `parent`, `title`). This changes the positional grammar for existing callers: values after `title` shift. For example, a previously valid positional call `ddflow task add T1 P1 parent "Title" "T2" "src/**" "Body"` now binds `kind="T2"`, `needs="src/**"`, `globs="Body"`, and leaves `body` unset; because `T2` is not a valid kind, the command fails, or if the value happened to be `doc`/`job` it silently files the task with the wrong kind and wrong needs/globs/body. The new tests use only `--kind`/named dict arguments, so they pass despite this regression. If `kind` must be positional, it should be appended at the end to preserve existing positional callers.

chunk_findings.detail: `_lock_wait` returns `max(float(cfg.ci.suite_wait_s), float(timeout_s))`, which makes `[ci].suite_wait_s` a floor rather than the per-run wait limit. Given `[ci].suite_wait_s = 1800` and a caller using `--timeout 60`, `_lock_wait` returns `1800`, so `SL.hold` is still allowed to wait 1800 seconds for the suite lock even though the caller authorized only a 60-second run budget. This leaves the queue wait unbounded by the smaller per-run timeout, contrary to the intent that the per-run override cover/bound the queue wait.

chunk_findings.detail: `fake_hold` is an undecorated generator function, but it is monkeypatched in as `CI.SL.hold`, which the other tests and presumably `_run_locked` use as a context manager (`with SL.hold(...)`). When `CI._run_locked` calls `with SL.hold(...)`, `fake_hold(...)` returns a bare generator object with no `__enter__`/`__exit__`, so the test fails with an `AttributeError`/`TypeError` before it can assert that `wait_s` was passed through. The fake must be wrapped with `contextlib.contextmanager` or return an actual context manager for this test to exercise `_run_locked`.

chunk_findings.detail: The new cap is applied unconditionally to every MCP `ddflow_wait`, but the stated justification only applies to calls that cannot send any progress frame (no `_meta.progressToken`). A client that does supply a progress token can have the server send heartbeats, resetting the idle timer, so a wait may safely run past 1500 s. For example, an MCP request with `_meta.progressToken` and `timeout=1800` for a condition that becomes true at t=1700 s is clamped by `_wait_timeout` to 1500 s, so the tool returns a timeout at 1500 s even though the heartbeat would have kept the call alive and the answer would have arrived at 1700 s, still below the 1800 s cutoff. This is a regression from the previous behavior where that same token-bearing wait would have succeeded.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/tools/_common.py:49

chunk_findings.detail: `_progress_will_flow` treats any positive `[mcp].progress_s` as “progress will flow,” so `_wait_timeout` uses the full `MCP_WAIT_MAX_S` cap. But a heartbeat interval at or above the client idle cutoff does not reset the idle timer strictly before that cutoff. For example, with `_meta.progressToken= [REDACTED] config `mcp.progress_s = 1800.0`, and `timeout=1800`, `_wait_timeout` returns `1800`. A wait whose condition is not satisfied until the timeout (or becomes true at `t=1800`) has no progress frame strictly before the client’s 1800-second no-frame cutoff; the first possible beat is only at/after `t=1800`, so the client can abort before the answer arrives. Such a wait should be classified as silent and capped to `MCP_WAIT_SILENT_MAX_S`; the predicate needs an upper bound such as `0 < progress_s < CLIENT_IDLE_ABORT_S` (or otherwise account for the headroom).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/tools/_common.py:_progress_will_flow

chunk_findings.detail: The new rule treats a wait as “can send progress” whenever it has a usable token and `[mcp].progress_s` is merely non-zero, but a positive `progress_s` larger than the client idle window still cannot emit any frame before the client aborts. For example, with repo config `[mcp] progress_s = 3600` and an MCP request containing `_meta.progressToken` plus `timeout=1800`, `_wait_timeout` returns the full 1800 s cap. If the waited condition becomes true at 1800 s, no `notifications/progress` can be sent before that point because the heartbeat period is 3600 s, so the client’s 1800 s idle timer can abort the call exactly where the answer is being produced. The silent cap should apply whenever no progress frame can precede the idle cutoff, not only when `progress_s == 0`.

chunk_findings.detail: The strict bound `0 < progress_s < CLIENT_IDLE_ABORT_S` only guarantees a heartbeat can land before the idle abort if the wait starts at the same moment the idle timer does. Given repo config `[mcp] progress_s = 1500.0`, an MCP request with `_meta.progressToken = [REDACTED] and `timeout = 1800`, and the wait being entered 600 s after the request with no frames sent (the same silent worker-wait the silent cap’s 600 s headroom budgets for), `_progress_will_flow` returns True because `1500 < 1800`, so `_wait_timeout` selects the full progress cap. The first heartbeat is then scheduled 1500 s after the wait starts, i.e. 2100 s after the request, so the client aborts at 1800 s before any progress frame; the call is silent even though the code treats it as progress-capable. The check must account for elapsed silent time/headroom before the wait, not just the configured interval.
