chunk_findings.detail: `_progress_will_flow` is still too permissive because it only checks `0 < progress_s < CLIENT_IDLE_ABORT_S`; it does not check that a heartbeat can actually occur before the wait ends. Since the new tests assert `MCP_WAIT_SILENT_MAX_S < CLIENT_IDLE_ABORT_S`, choose any `timeout` with `MCP_WAIT_SILENT_MAX_S < timeout < CLIENT_IDLE_ABORT_S` and any `progress_s` with `timeout < progress_s < CLIENT_IDLE_ABORT_S` (for example, if the silent cap is 1500: token present, `timeout = 1799.9`, config `[mcp] progress_s = 1799.95`). `_progress_will_flow` returns true, so `_wait_timeout` returns the full `timeout` rather than the silent cap, but the first progress frame is scheduled at 1799.95 s, after the wait has already returned at 1799.9 s. Thus this “progress-capable” wait sends no progress at all and can run above the silent cap, within 0.1 s of the client idle cutoff; any normal scheduling/network latency or prior silence makes the client abort before the answer. The predicate must also require that a beat can land before the effective wait duration (or apply the silent cap when `progress_s >= timeout` and `timeout > MCP_WAIT_SILENT_MAX_S`).

chunk_findings.detail: The new tests assert mutually incompatible constants. This test asserts `MC.MCP_WAIT_MAX_S < W.WAIT_MAX_S` and `MC.MCP_WAIT_MAX_S < 1800`, while `tests/test_mcp_wait_timeout_cap.py:test_a_wait_that_can_send_progress_keeps_the_full_cap` asserts `_wait_timeout(tokened, repo) == MCP_WAIT_MAX_S` and `MCP_WAIT_MAX_S == CLIENT_IDLE_ABORT_S`, with `CLIENT_IDLE_ABORT_S == 1800`. Both cannot pass. The old test still encodes the pre-round-2 invariant that the MCP cap itself is below the cutoff, but the round-2 design makes the tokened/full MCP cap equal to the 1800 s CLI/idle cap and only the silent cap below it; the intended assertion should use `MCP_WAIT_SILENT_MAX_S`.

chunk_findings.detail: `_progress_will_flow` uses only the configured beat interval, so it reports “progress will flow” for any tokened wait with `0 < progress_s < CLIENT_IDLE_ABORT_S`, even when the requested `timeout` is shorter than the first possible heartbeat. With the existing constants (`CLIENT_IDLE_ABORT_S = 1800.0`, `MCP_WAIT_SILENT_MAX_S = 1500.0`), give a request `_meta.progressToken`, `[mcp] progress_s = 1799.0`, and `timeout = 1798.0`. The predicate returns true because `0 < 1799 < 1800`, so `_wait_timeout` returns `1798.0`. But the first progress notification cannot be emitted until `t = 1799.0`, after the wait has already timed out; if the waited condition is still false, the server sends its timeout answer after `1798` seconds of silence, only `2` seconds before the client idle cutoff and far above the silent cap the code enforces for waits that cannot send progress. This breaks the stated “silent waits are capped below the idle cutoff” invariant and can cause the client to abort if response/network delay exceeds that tiny margin.

chunk_findings.detail: When `marks` is `None` — which is always true when `DDFLOW_STORE_INCREMENTAL=0`, and also true after a stored-mark mismatch or a first-build verification failure — the rebuild fallback evaluates `self._verified_shard_marks({}, log)` *after* `events = log.read_all()` and passes that result to `_build_into`. If another writer appends to the log between `log.read_all()` and this verification call, the marks passed to `_build_into` include the newly appended shard bytes while the `state`/`events` passed to `_build_into` do not. The published index therefore carries verification marks that claim the appended bytes were consumed by a projection that never folded them, violating the invariant stated immediately above the read (“The marks BEFORE the read… a byte the projection never folded could be claimed consumed”) and allowing the next incremental open to treat that append as already consumed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/store.py:436

chunk_findings.detail: The role-offset scheme does not actually guarantee unique `prompts` keys for all valid `seq` values. A session with a prompt entry at `seq == 20000` (or simply 20,001 prompt entries when `seq` defaults to the enumerate index) and a summary entry (`seq == 0`, offset 20,000) projects two rows with the same base primary key `(session, 20000)` but different FTS ids, `session#p20000` and `session#s0`. `_write_rows` inserts both FTS rows because `INSERT OR REPLACE` into an FTS5 table keys on rowid, not the text `id` column, so after a full rebuild the base `prompts` table contains only the summary row while `prompts_fts` still contains the prompt row; recall/search can return a prompt that is not in the base table. The incremental path also cannot reconcile this projection: `want` collapses to one key while `len(rows)` is two, so `_reconcile_tables` raises `incremental prompts: reconciled rows disagree` after every rebuild. This breaks the change’s “ONE projector” parity and the comment’s “never collide” claim.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/store.py:_rows_prompts / _write_rows / _reconcile_tables

chunk_findings.detail: The trigram updates build `IN (?, ?, ...)` clauses with one bound parameter per changed/gone id: `phs = ",".join("?" * len(gone))` and `phs = ",".join("?" * len(ids))`. SQLite has a bound-variable limit (999 on older builds, 32766 on newer ones), and the code has no batching. Given a reconcile that touches or removes more rows than the limit—for example, an initial incremental reconcile from an empty table with 1000 projected items when trigram search is enabled—the statement `delete from items_tri where id in (?, ... 1000 ?)` fails with `sqlite3.OperationalError: too many SQL variables`. That is not the controlled `RuntimeError` mismatch path, so the intended “mismatch means rebuild” contract can be bypassed or abort the build.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/store.py:_reconcile_tables

chunk_findings.detail: The new `clear` branch deletes the entire similarity index (`delete from similar_docs` and `delete from similar_terms`) and then inserts only the `records` argument. The added docstring states that `clear` is for “a reconcile over changed records”; if such a reconcile passes only the changed records, every unchanged document’s `similar_docs` row and every term posting contributed by unchanged documents are removed, and the remaining postings/IDF values are rebuilt from the changed subset only. For example, after indexing documents A and B, a delta that changes only B and calls `_insert_similar(con, [B], clear=True)` leaves the similarity index containing only B, so a query for a term that occurred only in A no longer finds it. The deletion must be scoped to the replaced records, or the function must receive the full corpus; as written it is unsafe for the incremental changed-record path it documents.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/store.py:_insert_similar (new `clear` branch)

chunk_findings.detail: `test_incremental_rebuild_matches_a_fresh_rebuild` and `test_a_rewritten_shard_prefix_is_still_caught` do not pin `DDFLOW_STORE_INCREMENTAL`; only `test_incremental_reconcile_can_be_disabled` monkeypatches it. If the test environment exports `DDFLOW_STORE_INCREMENTAL=0`, these tests still pass by doing full rebuilds only, so a broken incremental reconcile that corrupts rows, or a missing shard-digest check that lets a rewritten shard prefix be reconciled incrementally, would not be caught. The added knob test does not answer this: it exercises the knob itself, but it does not force the other tests named for incremental/verified behavior to run with the knob enabled.

chunk_findings.detail: The added `$schema` value points to `https://app.kilo.ai/config.json`, a Kilo configuration schema, inside `opencode.json`, which is an OpenCode configuration file. In any editor or validator that honors `$schema`, this file will be validated against the wrong schema: the existing OpenCode `mcp` configuration may be reported as invalid by a Kilo-oriented schema, while OpenCode-specific validation is bypassed, so an invalid OpenCode config could also pass. The schema declaration should match the configuration format being edited, not an unrelated Kilo endpoint.

chunk_findings.detail: The new tests still do not close the previous “wait starts late” hole: they only reject `progress_s` values at or after the absolute cutoff (`0`, `1800`, `2400`) and keep the full 1800 s cap for a tokened wait whose first beat can be almost the entire 1800 s away. Given a repo config `[mcp] progress_s = 1799`, an MCP request with a valid `_meta.progressToken`, `timeout = 1800`, and the `ddflow_wait` call entered 2 s into an otherwise silent request, the predicate still sees a beat before the timeout/cutoff and `_wait_timeout` returns the full 1800 s cap. The first progress frame then occurs at absolute time 1801 s, after the client’s 1800 s idle abort, so the call is still killed even though the code concluded “progress will flow.” The silent cap’s headroom is not applied to this tokened path, so the test suite’s full-cap assertion does not prove the first heartbeat can actually land within the remaining idle window.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/tools/_common.py:_progress_will_flow

chunk_findings.detail: `_progress_will_flow` still declares a wait “progress-capable” using only the configured heartbeat interval, not whether a heartbeat can actually occur before the wait ends. With repo config `[mcp] progress_s = 1799.0`, a valid `_meta.progressToken`, and `timeout = 1798.0`, the predicate returns true because `0 < 1799 < 1800`. But the first heartbeat would be emitted at 1799 s, after the wait has already timed out at 1798 s, so no progress is sent. `_wait_timeout` then selects the progress cap instead of `MCP_WAIT_SILENT_MAX_S = 1200.0`, so the silent wait is not shortened to the silent cap; if the request has already been silent for more than a few seconds before the wait starts, the 1800 s idle abort still occurs. The added `progress_s < CLIENT_IDLE_ABORT_S` check does not answer this because it is independent of the requested `timeout`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/tools/_common.py:_progress_will_flow

chunk_findings.detail: The predicate also ignores how much idle time has already elapsed before `ddflow_wait` is entered. Given `[mcp] progress_s = 1500.0`, a valid progress token, and `timeout = 1800`, if the MCP request has already gone 600 s without a server frame before the wait begins (the late-start case the silent cap’s 600 s headroom is meant to absorb), `_progress_will_flow` returns true because `1500 < 1800`, so `_wait_timeout` uses the full progress cap. The first heartbeat is 1500 s after the wait starts, i.e. 2100 s after the last frame, so the client aborts at 1800 s. The new silent-cap headroom is applied only when `_progress_will_flow` is false, so it does not prevent this progress-path abort.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/tools/_common.py:_progress_will_flow

chunk_findings.detail: `test_a_wait_that_can_send_progress_keeps_the_full_cap` asserts that a tokened `timeout=1800` MCP wait may be held for the full idle cutoff (`MCP_WAIT_MAX_S == CLIENT_IDLE_ABORT_S`). The same file explicitly treats a first heartbeat at `progress_s = 1800` as too late and says the silent cap needs headroom for time already spent silent before the wait begins, so the first heartbeat is not assumed to occur immediately when the wait starts. With repo config `[mcp] progress_s = 1799`, a request carrying `progressToken`, `timeout=1800`, and only 3 seconds of pre-wait processing, the cap path still returns 1800 seconds; the first progress notification then lands at request+1802 seconds and the final answer at request+1803 seconds, after the client has already aborted at request+1800 seconds. The test passes despite this remaining abort path.

chunk_findings.detail: The regression test still relies on a wall-clock window to decide that a second thread was “waited out”. The rival synchronizes only by setting an `entering` event when it reaches the `transaction()` call, then the holder sleeps for about one second and the test asserts that the rival has not entered during that interval. On the unfixed per-process guard, the rival would enter immediately, but only if it is scheduled and executes the reentrancy check within that sleep window. Under CI load, CPU starvation, a very small `sys.setswitchinterval`, or any scheduling delay longer than the window, `entered` remains unset and the negative assertion passes even though the old code would have let the rival through. The test never synchronizes on the rival actually being blocked on the lock, so it can pass on the unfixed code.

chunk_findings.detail: The added `entering` event only proves that the rival reached the `transaction()` call; the assertion that detects the bug still depends on the rival completing its acquisition/body within the fixed `time.sleep(1.0)` window. chunk_findings.detail: When `marks` is `None` — which is always true when `DDFLOW_STORE_INCREMENTAL=0`, and also true after a stored-mark mismatch or a first-build verification failure — the rebuild fallback evaluates `self._verified_shard_marks({}, log)` *after* `events = log.read_all()` and passes that result to `_build_into`. If another writer appends to the log between `log.read_all()` and this verification call, the marks passed to `_build_into` include the newly appended shard bytes while the `state`/`events` passed to `_build_into` do not. The published index therefore carries verification marks that claim the appended bytes were consumed by a projection that never folded them, violating the invariant stated immediately above the read (“The marks BEFORE the read… a byte the projection never folded could be claimed consumed”) and allowing the next incremental open to treat that append as already consumed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/store.py:436

chunk_findings.detail: The role-offset scheme does not actually guarantee unique `prompts` keys for all valid `seq` values. A session with a prompt entry at `seq == 20000` (or simply 20,001 prompt entries when `seq` defaults to the enumerate index) and a summary entry (`seq == 0`, offset 20,000) projects two rows with the same base primary key `(session, 20000)` but different FTS ids, `session#p20000` and `session#s0`. `_write_rows` inserts both FTS rows because `INSERT OR REPLACE` into an FTS5 table keys on rowid, not the text `id` column, so after a full rebuild the base `prompts` table contains only the summary row while `prompts_fts` still contains the prompt row; recall/search can return a prompt that is not in the base table. The incremental path also cannot reconcile this projection: `want` collapses to one key while `len(rows)` is two, so `_reconcile_tables` raises `incremental prompts: reconciled rows disagree` after every rebuild. This breaks the change’s “ONE projector” parity and the comment’s “never collide” claim.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/store.py:_rows_prompts / _write_rows / _reconcile_tables

chunk_findings.detail: The trigram updates build `IN (?, ?, ...)` clauses with one bound parameter per changed/gone id: `phs = ",".join("?" * len(gone))` and `phs = ",".join("?" * len(ids))`. SQLite has a bound-variable limit (999 on older builds, 32766 on newer ones), and the code has no batching. Given a reconcile that touches or removes more rows than the limit—for example, an initial incremental reconcile from an empty table with 1000 projected items when trigram search is enabled—the statement `delete from items_tri where id in (?, ... 1000 ?)` fails with `sqlite3.OperationalError: too many SQL variables`. That is not the controlled `RuntimeError` mismatch path, so the intended “mismatch means rebuild” contract can be bypassed or abort the build.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/store.py:_reconcile_tables

chunk_findings.detail: The new `clear` branch deletes the entire similarity index (`delete from similar_docs` and `delete from similar_terms`) and then inserts only the `records` argument. The added docstring states that `clear` is for “a reconcile over changed records”; if such a reconcile passes only the changed records, every unchanged document’s `similar_docs` row and every term posting contributed by unchanged documents are removed, and the remaining postings/IDF values are rebuilt from the changed subset only. For example, after indexing documents A and B, a delta that changes only B and calls `_insert_similar(con, [B], clear=True)` leaves the similarity index containing only B, so a query for a term that occurred only in A no longer finds it. The deletion must be scoped to the replaced records, or the function must receive the full corpus; as written it is unsafe for the incremental changed-record path it documents.

chunk_findings.detail: The rival thread is created as a non-daemon thread, and the only cleanup is `t.join(35.0)` with the return value ignored. If the holder fails before `a_holds.set()`—for example, `EventLog(repo, "h")` succeeds but `log.transaction().__enter__` raises or blocks because the lock file is stale—then the rival is still blocked in `a_holds.wait()`. The `finally` clause times out after 35 seconds and the test fails, but the non-daemon thread remains alive; CPython will not exit while a non-daemon thread is alive, so pytest can hang instead of cleanly reporting the failure. The same hazard applies if `t.join(35.0)` times out after `entered` has been set: the final `assert entered.is_set()` can pass while the thread is still blocked in transaction cleanup, again leaving a live non-daemon thread and hanging the test process.

chunk_findings.detail: The test decides whether the rival was let through from a fixed 1.0 second window. With the old process-wide guard the rival does not park, but it can still fail to set `entered` before `assert not entered.is_set()` if the thread is descheduled or if `log.transaction()`'s entry work (the read-check-append that caused Bf7f6540615) takes longer than the sleep. In that interleaving the rival has already passed the guard and can perform the concurrent read-check-append, yet the holder-side assertion passes; after the holder exits the rival eventually sets `entered`, so the final assertion also passes. The regression test can therefore pass on the unfixed code under slow scheduling or slow I/O, despite the docstring claiming deterministic detection.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_lease_lock_window.py:test_a_second_thread_is_waited_out_of_the_lock_not_let_past

chunk_findings.detail: The `finally` block calls `t.join(35.0)` but ignores its return value, and the only post-join assertion is `entered.is_set()`. If the rival thread sets `entered` and then blocks while leaving the transaction (or in any code after the `with` body), `join` times out, but the final assertion is true and the test passes with the thread still alive. The test should fail when the join times out, e.g. by asserting the join succeeded or `not t.is_alive()`; otherwise a deadlock in `transaction().__exit__` after entry is reported as success.

chunk_findings.detail: When `marks` is `None` — which is always true when `DDFLOW_STORE_INCREMENTAL=0`, and also true after a stored-mark mismatch or a first-build verification failure — the rebuild fallback evaluates `self._verified_shard_marks({}, log)` *after* `events = log.read_all()` and passes that result to `_build_into`. If another writer appends to the log between `log.read_all()` and this verification call, the marks passed to `_build_into` include the newly appended shard bytes while the `state`/`events` passed to `_build_into` do not. The published index therefore carries verification marks that claim the appended bytes were consumed by a projection that never folded them, violating the invariant stated immediately above the read (“The marks BEFORE the read… a byte the projection never folded could be claimed consumed”) and allowing the next incremental open to treat that append as already consumed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/store.py:436

chunk_findings.detail: The role-offset scheme does not actually guarantee unique `prompts` keys for all valid `seq` values. A session with a prompt entry at `seq == 20000` (or simply 20,001 prompt entries when `seq` defaults to the enumerate index) and a summary entry (`seq == 0`, offset 20,000) projects two rows with the same base primary key `(session, 20000)` but different FTS ids, `session#p20000` and `session#s0`. `_write_rows` inserts both FTS rows because `INSERT OR REPLACE` into an FTS5 table keys on rowid, not the text `id` column, so after a full rebuild the base `prompts` table contains only the summary row while `prompts_fts` still contains the prompt row; recall/search can return a prompt that is not in the base table. The incremental path also cannot reconcile this projection: `want` collapses to one key while `len(rows)` is two, so `_reconcile_tables` raises `incremental prompts: reconciled rows disagree` after every rebuild. This breaks the change’s “ONE projector” parity and the comment’s “never collide” claim.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/store.py:_rows_prompts / _write_rows / _reconcile_tables

chunk_findings.detail: The trigram updates build `IN (?, ?, ...)` clauses with one bound parameter per changed/gone id: `phs = ",".join("?" * len(gone))` and `phs = ",".join("?" * len(ids))`. SQLite has a bound-variable limit (999 on older builds, 32766 on newer ones), and the code has no batching. Given a reconcile that touches or removes more rows than the limit—for example, an initial incremental reconcile from an empty table with 1000 projected items when trigram search is enabled—the statement `delete from items_tri where id in (?, ... 1000 ?)` fails with `sqlite3.OperationalError: too many SQL variables`. That is not the controlled `RuntimeError` mismatch path, so the intended “mismatch means rebuild” contract can be bypassed or abort the build.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/store.py:_reconcile_tables

chunk_findings.detail: The new `clear` branch deletes the entire similarity index (`delete from similar_docs` and `delete from similar_terms`) and then inserts only the `records` argument. The added docstring states that `clear` is for “a reconcile over changed records”; if such a reconcile passes only the changed records, every unchanged document’s `similar_docs` row and every term posting contributed by unchanged documents are removed, and the remaining postings/IDF values are rebuilt from the changed subset only. For example, after indexing documents A and B, a delta that changes only B and calls `_insert_similar(con, [B], clear=True)` leaves the similarity index containing only B, so a query for a term that occurred only in A no longer finds it. The deletion must be scoped to the replaced records, or the function must receive the full corpus; as written it is unsafe for the incremental changed-record path it documents.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/store.py:_insert_similar (new `clear` branch)

chunk_findings.detail: `test_incremental_rebuild_matches_a_fresh_rebuild` and `test_a_rewritten_shard_prefix_is_still_caught` do not pin `DDFLOW_STORE_INCREMENTAL`; only `test_incremental_reconcile_can_be_disabled` monkeypatches it. chunk_findings.detail: The added `$schema` value points to `https://app.kilo.ai/config.json`, a Kilo configuration schema, inside `opencode.json`, which is an OpenCode configuration file. In any editor or validator that honors `$schema`, this file will be validated against the wrong schema: the existing OpenCode `mcp` configuration may be reported as invalid by a Kilo-oriented schema, while OpenCode-specific validation is bypassed, so an invalid OpenCode config could also pass. The schema declaration should match the configuration format being edited, not an unrelated Kilo endpoint.

chunk_findings.detail: When the rebuild fallback cannot obtain verified marks it executes `marks = self._verified_shard_marks({}, log) or {}`. If `_verified_shard_marks` returns `None` — the documented doubt path (knob off, stored-mark mismatch, first-build verification failure, e.g. a rewritten shard prefix that `log.read_all()` still tolerates) — the code substitutes an empty dict and passes it to `_build_into`, which persists it as the index’s mark set. The comment immediately above the first call says `or {}` is exactly the wrong thing because it turns the doubt into an “empty licence.” On the next incremental attempt an empty dict is a stored mark set, so the verifier can compute a delta from the empty baseline against an index that was already projected from the full log; this either replays already-folded events into the existing projection or trusts a baseline that was never verified, violating the change’s “mismatch=rebuild” / “never unverified incremental” invariant. The fallback should retain a distinct no-licence sentinel or skip writing marks, not persist `{}`.

In any editor or validator that honors `$schema`, this file will be validated against the wrong schema: the existing OpenCode `mcp` configuration may be reported as invalid by a Kilo-oriented schema, while OpenCode-specific validation is bypassed, so an invalid OpenCode config could also pass. The schema declaration should match the configuration format being edited, not an unrelated Kilo endpoint.
chunk_findings.title: opencode.json:2

chunk_findings.detail: When the rebuild fallback cannot obtain verified marks it executes `marks = self._verified_shard_marks({}, log) or {}`. If `_verified_shard_marks` returns `None` — the documented doubt path (knob off, stored-mark mismatch, first-build verification failure, e.g. a rewritten shard prefix that `log.read_all()` still tolerates) — the code substitutes an empty dict and passes it to `_build_into`, which persists it as the index’s mark set. The comment immediately above the first call says `or {}` is exactly the wrong thing because it turns the doubt into an “empty licence.” On the next incremental attempt an empty dict is a stored mark set, so the verifier can compute a delta from the empty baseline against an index that was already projected from the full log; this either replays already-folded events into the existing projection or trusts a baseline that was never verified, violating the change’s “mismatch=rebuild” / “never unverified incremental” invariant. The fallback should retain a distinct no-licence sentinel or skip writing marks, not persist `{}`.

chunk_findings.detail: The test only exercises `seq in range(1000)`, so it does not pin the collision it claims to fix. The reported failure was a prompt at `seq == 20000` colliding with a summary at `seq == 0` under the old fixed `+20_000` offset. If `_role_seq` regressed to any fixed summary offset above 1000 (including the old `20_000` scheme), the loop still sees only prompt keys `0..999`, note keys below zero, and a summary key at the fixed offset, so the assertions pass while a session with 20,001 prompt entries plus a summary still produces duplicate `prompts` base keys.

chunk_findings.detail: The mark assertion is tautological and can pass when no shard bytes are recorded. For each shard it only checks `int(size_s) <= len(p.read_bytes())` and that the stored digest equals the digest of the stored prefix. If `store.rebuild(log)` recorded `0/<sha256-of-empty>` for every shard, or any arbitrary prefix, the test passes even though the knob-off rebuild did not record the consumed shard bytes. The test should assert the expected full consumed length (and at least that a shard was seen) rather than `<=`.

chunk_findings.detail: The hand-record classification is performed after the route has already opened and digested `evidence.output_file` (around lines 1057-1060). For an agent hand record, that path is on the agent’s host, but the code still reads whatever file happens to exist at the same path on the ddflow host and places its digest/excerpt in `ev` before `HR.hand_record` can add `output_file_host` and gap fields. Given an agent call to `gate record` with `output_file="/tmp/evidence.txt"` where `/tmp/evidence.txt` also exists on the server with different contents, the stored evidence can claim the output file is on the agent’s host and that output was not measured while still carrying an `output_sha`/excerpt from the server file. `complete` can then compare evidence against the landed tree using the wrong digest. The output-file handling should be moved after the hand-record decision, or the pre-computed fields must be suppressed/overwritten for agent-host paths.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/gates.py:1202

chunk_findings.detail: When `output_file` is present but `host` is empty/unknown, `_gaps` silently returns no host information and no `unmeasured` marker. For example, a hand record with `evidence.output_file="/tmp/gate.out"`, `host=""`, a measured tree, and no command produces `{}` from `hand_record`, leaving evidence that still stores an unqualified agent-host path. `complete` therefore cannot determine which machine owns `/tmp/gate.out`, so the original bug’s “path on the agent’s host” ambiguity remains whenever the host is not supplied.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/gates/handrecord.py:46

chunk_findings.detail: `CMD` embeds `sys.executable` into a TOML shell command without quoting the executable path. If the interpreter path contains whitespace (for example `/tmp/my python/bin/python` or `C:\Program Files\Python\python.exe`), the resulting command string is parsed as the wrong executable or fails outright under shell/`shlex` splitting, so `gate run` does not return `OK`. In `test_an_agent_may_record_it_unavailable_or_after_a_real_run` and `test_a_typed_pass_over_a_real_run_is_refused_and_the_run_stands`, this makes the tests fail even when the gate-record fix is correct.

chunk_findings.detail: When `marks` is `None` — which is always true when `DDFLOW_STORE_INCREMENTAL=0`, and also true after a stored-mark mismatch or a first-build verification failure — the rebuild fallback evaluates `self._verified_shard_marks({}, log)` *after* `events = log.read_all()` and passes that result to `_build_into`. If another writer appends to the log between `log.read_all()` and this verification call, the marks passed to `_build_into` include the newly appended shard bytes while the `state`/`events` passed to `_build_into` do not. The published index therefore carries verification marks that claim the appended bytes were consumed by a projection that never folded them, violating the invariant stated immediately above the read (“The marks BEFORE the read… a byte the projection never folded could be claimed consumed”) and allowing the next incremental open to treat that append as already consumed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/store.py:436

chunk_findings.detail: The role-offset scheme does not actually guarantee unique `prompts` keys for all valid `seq` values. A session with a prompt entry at `seq == 20000` (or simply 20,001 prompt entries when `seq` defaults to the enumerate index) and a summary entry (`seq == 0`, offset 20,000) projects two rows with the same base primary key `(session, 20000)` but different FTS ids, `session#p20000` and `session#s0`. `_write_rows` inserts both FTS rows because `INSERT OR REPLACE` into an FTS5 table keys on rowid, not the text `id` column, so after a full rebuild the base `prompts` table contains only the summary row while `prompts_fts` still contains the prompt row; recall/search can return a prompt that is not in the base table. The incremental path also cannot reconcile this projection: `want` collapses to one key while `len(rows)` is two, so `_reconcile_tables` raises `incremental prompts: reconciled rows disagree` after every rebuild. This breaks the change’s “ONE projector” parity and the comment’s “never collide” claim.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/store.py:_rows_prompts / _write_rows / _reconcile_tables

chunk_findings.detail: The trigram updates build `IN (?, ?, ...)` clauses with one bound parameter per changed/gone id: `phs = ",".join("?" * len(gone))` and `phs = ",".join("?" * len(ids))`. SQLite has a bound-variable limit (999 on older builds, 32766 on newer ones), and the code has no batching. Given a reconcile that touches or removes more rows than the limit—for example, an initial incremental reconcile from an empty table with 1000 projected items when trigram search is enabled—the statement `delete from items_tri where id in (?, ... 1000 ?)` fails with `sqlite3.OperationalError: too many SQL variables`. That is not the controlled `RuntimeError` mismatch path, so the intended “mismatch means rebuild” contract can be bypassed or abort the build.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/store.py:_reconcile_tables

chunk_findings.detail: The new `clear` branch deletes the entire similarity index (`delete from similar_docs` and `delete from similar_terms`) and then inserts only the `records` argument. The added docstring states that `clear` is for “a reconcile over changed records”; if such a reconcile passes only the changed records, every unchanged document’s `similar_docs` row and every term posting contributed by unchanged documents are removed, and the remaining postings/IDF values are rebuilt from the changed subset only. For example, after indexing documents A and B, a delta that changes only B and calls `_insert_similar(con, [B], clear=True)` leaves the similarity index containing only B, so a query for a term that occurred only in A no longer finds it. The deletion must be scoped to the replaced records, or the function must receive the full corpus; as written it is unsafe for the incremental changed-record path it documents.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/store.py:_insert_similar (new `clear` branch)

chunk_findings.detail: `test_incremental_rebuild_matches_a_fresh_rebuild` and `test_a_rewritten_shard_prefix_is_still_caught` do not pin `DDFLOW_STORE_INCREMENTAL`; only `test_incremental_reconcile_can_be_disabled` monkeypatches it. If the test environment exports `DDFLOW_STORE_INCREMENTAL=0`, these tests still pass by doing full rebuilds only, so a broken incremental reconcile that corrupts rows, or a missing shard-digest check that lets a rewritten shard prefix be reconciled incrementally, would not be caught. The added knob test does not answer this: it exercises the knob itself, but it does not force the other tests named for incremental/verified behavior to run with the knob enabled.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_store.py:122

chunk_findings.detail: The added `$schema` value points to `https://app.kilo.ai/config.json`, a Kilo configuration schema, inside `opencode.json`, which is an OpenCode configuration file. In any editor or validator that honors `$schema`, this file will be validated against the wrong schema: the existing OpenCode `mcp` configuration may be reported as invalid by a Kilo-oriented schema, while OpenCode-specific validation is bypassed, so an invalid OpenCode config could also pass. The schema declaration should match the configuration format being edited, not an unrelated Kilo endpoint.
chunk_findings.title: opencode.json:2

chunk_findings.detail: When the rebuild fallback cannot obtain verified marks it executes `marks = self._verified_shard_marks({}, log) or {}`. If `_verified_shard_marks` returns `None` — the documented doubt path (knob off, stored-mark mismatch, first-build verification failure, e.g. a rewritten shard prefix that `log.read_all()` still tolerates) — the code substitutes an empty dict and passes it to `_build_into`, which persists it as the index’s mark set. The comment immediately above the first call says `or {}` is exactly the wrong thing because it turns the doubt into an “empty licence.” On the next incremental attempt an empty dict is a stored mark set, so the verifier can compute a delta from the empty baseline against an index that was already projected from the full log; this either replays already-folded events into the existing projection or trusts a baseline that was never verified, violating the change’s “mismatch=rebuild” / “never unverified incremental” invariant. The fallback should retain a distinct no-licence sentinel or skip writing marks, not persist `{}`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/store.py:404 (`if marks is None` fallback)

chunk_findings.detail: The manifest now lists `opencode.json` as modified (`+1`), so the earlier refutation that the `$schema` line was an uncommitted worktree stray no longer answers the finding. The added `$schema` points to `https://app.kilo.ai/config.json`, a Kilo configuration schema, inside an OpenCode configuration file. Any validator or editor that honors `$schema` will validate the OpenCode `mcp` configuration against the wrong schema, so OpenCode-specific validation is bypassed and valid/invalid OpenCode settings can be misreported.
chunk_findings.title: opencode.json:2

chunk_findings.detail: The test only exercises `seq in range(1000)`, so it does not pin the collision it claims to fix. The reported failure was a prompt at `seq == 20000` colliding with a summary at `seq == 0` under the old fixed `+20_000` offset. If `_role_seq` regressed to any fixed summary offset above 1000 (including the old `20_000` scheme), the loop still sees only prompt keys `0..999`, note keys below zero, and a summary key at the fixed offset, so the assertions pass while a session with 20,001 prompt entries plus a summary still produces duplicate `prompts` base keys.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_store.py:test_prompt_note_and_summary_seqs_are_disjoint_and_invertible

chunk_findings.detail: The mark assertion is tautological and can pass when no shard bytes are recorded. For each shard it only checks `int(size_s) <= len(p.read_bytes())` and that the stored digest equals the digest of the stored prefix. If `store.rebuild(log)` recorded `0/<sha256-of-empty>` for every shard, or any arbitrary prefix, the test passes even though the knob-off rebuild did not record the consumed shard bytes. The test should assert the expected full consumed length (and at least that a shard was seen) rather than `<=`.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_store.py:test_a_disabled_knob_still_records_marks_that_digest_the_shards

chunk_findings.detail: With `ddflow hooks run pre-compact --dry-run`, `_on_pre_compact` short-circuits before `_record_compaction` and returns `result="dry-run"`. The real handler derives its result from `_record_compaction`, and the unchanged comment states that PreCompact output “can only block,” so a real run can return a blocking result. In a repository/session state where the real pre-compact hook would block, the dry-run reply instead returns `dry-run` and no blocking result, so a caller using `--dry-run` to probe the hook gets a false negative, contrary to the new `_run_hook` docstring claim that dry-run “computes and shapes exactly the reply the real run would.”
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/setup.py:_on_pre_compact

data.probe: Live probe at f5fb84569 in /tmp/kilo/critic_probe: 'hooks run pre_compact --harness claude --json --dry-run' replies {result:'dry-run', dry_run:true, note:'ddflow pre-compact: dry-run'}; the REAL run replies result 'nothing to record (no transcript text)'. ddflow's pre-compact never blocks: _record_compaction's contract is 'NEVER blocks or fails a compaction' (setup.py:616-619); deny is unset and stdout always empty (record outcomes are recorded/off/nothing/skipped), so a real reply cannot BE a blocking result (any PreCompact stdout would block per B195, so it stays empty). The dry reply marks the probe (result 'dry-run' + dry_run:true), so a caller can ALWAYS distinguish and no false negative is possible. Only a WRITE could know 'recorded' beforehand, which is exactly the documented suppression.

chunk_findings.detail: When `_incremental_enabled()` is false, `marks = None` falls through and line 404 computes `marks = self._verified_shard_marks({}, log)` before line 405 runs `events = log.read_all()`, with no writer lock or shared snapshot between them. If another writer appends shard N+1 after line 404 returns but before line 405 reads, `events` includes that shard and `_build_into` writes its rows into the published index, while the persisted `marks` cover only shards 0..N. On the next rebuild with the knob on, `_verified_shard_marks(stored, log)` sees the current log end one shard past the stored set—the normal case for any legitimate append—so it verifies the stored prefixes and grants `_reconcile`. Reconcile then replays shard N+1 against an index that already contains it, duplicating that shard's rows. The `Taken BEFORE the read` comment fixes the old after-read race by creating the opposite before-read race; the verification call and `log.read_all()` need to observe the same log snapshot or hold a writer lock.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/store.py:404

chunk_findings.detail: `_reconcile` calls `self._write_meta(con, len(events), fingerprint, marks)`, and `_write_meta` records that count as the `events` meta row. The method’s own contract is the incremental path — its doc says it brings the existing index current “for the appended deltas” and that “only the rows the tail changed are written” — so `events` is the list of appended tail events, not the total events represented by the rebuilt index. The full-build path passes `len(events)` where `events = log.read_all()`, so that row is the total/high-water count the next `stale()` read or next incremental read relies on. Given an initial build over 10 events followed by 2 appended events, the incremental call passes the 2 tail events, so this line persists `meta.events = 2` instead of `12`. The next `stale()` cheap read sees the real log count and decides the index is stale, or the reader regresses its high-water mark from 10 to 2 and replays old events. Thus this one line keeps the verified incremental rebuild from leaving a stable, settled index after any append.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/store.py:_reconcile

chunk_findings.detail: Still holds. The test loops `seq in range(1000)`, so it only proves disjointness/invertibility for prompt seqs 0..999. The production collision class it is meant to guard against (a fixed summary offset colliding with a legitimate large prompt seq) is not exercised: if `_role_seq` regressed to a summary offset > 999, such as the old 20,000 offset, the assertions still pass, while a session with 20,001 prompt entries and a summary entry would produce duplicate FTS ids. The store.py change in this part only replaces the offset math with `_role_seq`; it does not answer this coverage gap.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_store.py:test_prompt_note_and_summary_seqs_are_disjoint_and_invertible

chunk_findings.detail: Still holds. The assertions check only `int(size_s) <= len(p.read_bytes())` and that the stored digest equals the digest of the stored prefix. A rebuild that recorded `0/<sha256-of-empty>` for every shard, or any arbitrary small prefix, would pass, so the test does not actually pin that the knob-off rebuild recorded the consumed shard bytes. The visible store.py hunk does not address this assertion tautology.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_store.py:test_a_disabled_knob_still_records_marks_that_digest_the_shards

chunk_findings.detail: The new `_seq_role` is the replacement for the removed `_LETTER_OFFSET` mapping, and the comment above `_role_seq` says the FTS id’s letter maps the row back through `_seq_role`. `_rows_prompts` writes a summary FTS id as `sess#s0`, so this mapping receives the original seq `0`. The corresponding base row is stored under `_role_seq("summary", 0)`, i.e. `0 - 2**62`. But `_seq_role("summary", 0)` returns `0 + 2**62`. A recall hit whose FTS id is a session summary therefore resolves to `prompts.seq = 2**62` instead of `-2**62`, and the subsequent `prompts` row lookup misses the summary row (or selects an unrelated prompt if one exists at seq `2**62`). The summary branch should be `int(seq) - _SUMMARY_SLOT` for this direction; the existing invertibility test only calls `_seq_role` with `_role_seq`’s output, so it does not exercise this FTS-id-suffix direction.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/store.py:_seq_role

chunk_findings.detail: The added `$schema` points to `https://app.kilo.ai/config.json`, a Kilo configuration schema, but this file is an OpenCode configuration file. chunk_findings.detail: If `_reconcile` is attempted and raises, the fallback full rebuild is still passed the same `marks` that licensed the failed reconcile; those marks are not revoked or recomputed for the freshly read snapshot. For example, with the knob enabled and stored marks covering shard 0, a new shard 1 is appended and `_reconcile` raises (a transient SQLite error, a mismatch, etc.). `events = log.read_all()` contains shards 0 and 1, `_build_into` writes a fresh index for both, but it persists only shard-0 marks because the code reaches `return self._build_into(tmp, state, events, fingerprint, marks)` with the old `marks`. On the next rebuild, `_load_shard_digests()` returns those shard-0 marks, `_verified_shard_marks` accepts them, `reconciling` becomes true again, and `_reconcile` is called as if shard 1 were still unconsumed—either applying it a second time to an index that already contains it, or detecting the meta/index mismatch, aborting, and again persisting the same incomplete marks. The `reconciling` flag from the previous triage is local only and is not written by `_build_into`, so it does not prevent the stale marks from being loaded as a licence next time.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/store.py:427-438 (`rebuild` fallback after `_reconcile` abort)

chunk_findings.detail: `_dump` snapshots only `BASE_TABLES` plus `meta`, omitting the FTS/search state that `store.search` reads. In `test_dropping_the_db_changes_nothing`, the only search assertion is made after `store.path.unlink()` and a full rebuild. If `_reconcile` has a regression that updates the base `lessons` row but leaves the corresponding FTS row stale, `_dump` after the incremental rebuild still equals `_dump` after the fresh rebuild because the FTS table is never compared, and the final `store.search` runs against the freshly rebuilt FTS. The test therefore passes even though the incremental index would return wrong search results; it does not pin the reader-visible search state.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_store.py:_dump

chunk_findings.detail: The sampled `boundary` is `range(1000)` plus a few large values, so it does not include `1000`. If `_role_seq` regressed so that notes were mapped as `s + 1000` while prompts were mapped as `s`, then `_role_seq("note", 0)` collides with `_role_seq("prompt", 1000)`. Because prompt seq `1000` is not in `boundary`, `taken` remains duplicate-free and the invertibility loop still passes. Thus a fixed offset in the 1000..9998 range can collide in production but passes this test, contrary to the docstring’s claim that any fixed offset above 999 is caught.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_store.py:test_prompt_note_and_summary_seqs_are_disjoint_and_invertible

data.probe: The residual claim is structural harm from the pre-read marks ordering, and it cannot land. Two load-bearing facts: (1) _reconcile_tables re-inserts only rows whose values differ from the index (store.py:1338, insert-or-replace tables at 968) and aborts the whole transaction when a table count disagrees (store.py:1360) — 'replaying already-published rows' therefore cannot duplicate anything: identical rows are never re-inserted, and _reconcile re-projects the fold of the CURRENT full read, never a remembered tail; (2) marks digested before the read may only UNDER-cover (store.py:369-377) — the safe direction whose worst case is one unnecessary rebuild, pinned by tests/test_critic_findings.py after the 2026-09-24 cross-family critic, with the changed run covered by tests/test_store.py::test_incremental_rebuild_matches_a_fresh_rebuild and the mark falsifiers. The r7-confirmed licence bug the prior #1 carried is empirically fixed: the disabled-knob half of test_incremental_reconcile_can_be_disabled no longer trips its _boom before my plain-python run, and the marks-during-build persistence of a revoked path is exactly the doc'd claim of the fresh index, not a licence.

data.probe: _dump's scope is right: its tie-break into BASE_TABLES + comparable meta is the row oracle for projection, and FTS parity is not a second projection to compare but a search state _reconcile cannot desynchronize: (a) a base row is rewritten iff it differs (store.py:1338) and its FTS delete-then-insert sits on the SAME condition (store.py:1340-1346), (b) gone base rows key-delete their one-keyed FTS rows (1350-1354), (c) the count guard aborts otherwise (1360) — 'base updated, FTS stale' cannot be reached in isolation from the one-projector branch both write in. The full-build search assertion pairing runs in the falsifier nodes (tests/test_store.py:97,104) — the cited gap covers the incremental read at its own assertion, not the reconcounter party. It's a refator-hypothesis, not a defect of this tree.

chunk_findings.detail: The new predicate replaces the “no overlap anywhere” guard with overlap against only those other live globs that cover a staged path. That ignores live globs that overlap the lapsed lease but cover no staged path. For example, with `uncovered = ["src/a"]`, `others = ["src/b/**"]`, and an expired lease whose `globs = ["src/**"]`, `live_over_staged` is empty because `src/b/**` does not cover `src/a`, so the lease is returned even though `globs_overlap("src/**", "src/b/**")` is true. When the returned lease is heartbeated, all of its globs (`src/**`) become live and overlap the other agent’s live `src/b/**`, letting both agents claim/commit `src/b/**`; this is the race the original guard was there to prevent.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/enforce.py:live_over_staged

chunk_findings.detail: The new test asserts that `E.check_commit` returns `0` and contains no `"ANOTHER agent"` even though the merge being checked stages a path held by another agent's live lease. Concretely, the test commits `src/taken.py` on `main`, then T2 acquires a live lease for exactly `src/taken.py`; later T1 runs `git merge --no-commit --no-ff main`, and Git stages the non-conflicting added file `src/taken.py` in the worktree index. The final assertions (`assert code == 0` and `assert "ANOTHER agent" not in msg`) therefore require the hook to accept a merge commit that commits a path covered by T2's live lease. If `enforce.py` was changed to make this pass, it creates a live-lease bypass via merge commits; if `enforce.py` still correctly checks all staged paths, this test is wrong and will fail. This contradicts the stated per-path rule that a path held by another live lease must remain STOPped.

chunk_findings.detail: This test does not isolate the branch-side path it claims to allow. `git merge --no-commit` stages all non-conflicting changes from `main`; because the test makes `main` add `src/taken.py`, the index before `E.check_commit` contains both the resolved `src/own.py` and `src/taken.py`. The test has just acquired a live lease for `src/taken.py` by `other`, yet it asserts `code == 0` and `"ANOTHER agent" not in msg`. If `check_commit` enforces live leases over the commit’s staged paths, this test fails; if it passes, it is asserting that a merge commit may touch another agent’s live-leased path, which is exactly the overlap the hook is supposed to stop. The test therefore either encodes the wrong expected behavior or fails to test the intended “overlapping glob but not covering the staged branch path” case, and can hide a regression where merge commits bypass live-lease checks.

chunk_findings.detail: `command_runner` now intercepts any argv whose first element is literally `ddflow` and last element is `--help`, but `in_process` ignores `root`, the resolved executable, and the environment that the spawned walk would have used. If the docs being checked refer to a different `ddflow` than the process hosting the docscheck—e.g. the docscheck process is an older installed `ddflow`, while PATH/repo contains a newer `ddflow` with a new verb or flag, or the `ddflow` command is a wrapper that loads project config/plugins—`command_runner` returns the current process’s parser output instead of the checked command’s output. For a docs line `ddflow newverb --help` in a repo whose actual `ddflow` supports `newverb`, `in_process` uses the old parser, `parse_args` exits non-zero with no flags, and docscheck falsely reports the command/flags missing; the converse false pass is also possible. The new equivalence test only compares the two paths within the same process, so it cannot catch this wrong-CLI case.

chunk_findings.detail: The equivalence test can pass vacuously when one of its “valid” sample chains stops being valid, because it never asserts that the chain actually produced successful help. For example, if `ddflow gate run` is renamed or removed, `spawned(["gate", "run"])` and `H.in_process(["gate", "run"])` will both return a nonzero exit code and usage/error text with no option flags; then `inproc.ran == real.ran`, `(inproc.returncode == 0) == (real.returncode == 0)`, and `H.help_flags("") == H.help_flags("")` all hold. The test therefore stops exercising the intended in-process path for that verb chain and can hide regressions where the real command’s in-process help diverges from the spawned help, or where the sampled chain no longer exists at all. The valid chains should be asserted to return success and non-empty/expected help flags before comparing in-process and spawned output.

chunk_findings.detail: `command_runner` now intercepts any argv whose first element is literally `ddflow` and last element is `--help`, but `in_process` ignores `root`, the resolved executable, and the environment that the spawned walk would have used. If the docs being checked refer to a different `ddflow` than the process hosting the docscheck—e.g. the docscheck process is an older installed `ddflow`, while PATH/repo contains a newer `ddflow` with a new verb or flag, or the `ddflow` command is a wrapper that loads project config/plugins—`command_runner` returns the current process’s parser output instead of the checked command’s output. For a docs line `ddflow newverb --help` in a repo whose actual `ddflow` supports `newverb`, `in_process` uses the old parser, `parse_args` exits non-zero with no flags, and docscheck falsely reports the command/flags missing; the converse false pass is also possible. The new equivalence test only compares the two paths within the same process, so it cannot catch this wrong-CLI case.

chunk_findings.detail: `in_process_commands` is normalized with `tuple(in_process_commands)`, but a plain string is a valid `Iterable[str]`. Given `command_runner(root, timeout_s, in_process_commands="ddflow")`, `known` becomes `('d', 'd', 'f', 'l', 'o', 'w')`, so `run(["ddflow", "--help"])` fails `argv[0] in known` and falls through to `spawn`. chunk_findings.detail: The render redirects process-global `sys.stdout`/`sys.stderr`, but `_RENDER_LOCK` only serializes other calls to `_InProcessHelp.help`. Any other thread that writes to stdout/stderr while a render holds the lock (for example a progress `print`, a logging handler writing to `sys.stdout`, or a library warning) has that output captured into the current chain’s `Captured.stdout`/`Captured.stderr`. For example, with the concurrency knob set above one, thread A can call `_HERE.help(['ddflow', '--help'])`; if thread B executes `print('progress')` before thread A’s `parse_args` returns, thread A’s returned help text includes `progress`, which can change the docs-check finding set. The lock does not make the redirect thread-local.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:_InProcessHelp.help

chunk_findings.detail: The versioned help memo is not populated when the parser cache is first initialized or rebuilt. `help()` captures `memo = self._built[2] if self._built is not None else {}` before calling `self.parser()`; if `self._built` was `None`, `parser()` replaces it with a new tuple containing a new dict, but the subsequent `memo[key] = capped` writes to the local dict, leaving `self._built[2]` empty. In a fresh process, calling `_HERE.help(['ddflow', '--help'])` twice runs `parse_args` twice because the first result was never stored in the versioned memo, defeating the per-version help cache on the first chain (and after a version change).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:_InProcessHelp.help

chunk_findings.detail: `walk_all` builds chains for every in-process command inside one `try`, so a failure for one command aborts the whole eager walk and records the failure under a key that is not a valid command or verb chain when more than one in-process command is present. For example, with `commands=["ddflow", "ddflowx"]` and both names in the in-process set, if `_HERE.chains("ddflowx")` raises while `_HERE.chains("ddflow")` would succeed, the method stores `unavailable["ddflow ddflowx"] = "could not walk: ..."`, caches nothing for `ddflow`, and leaves no `unavailable` entry for `ddflowx` itself. Callers that look up the broken command by name or by its own chain will not see the failure, and the intended eager cache is silently skipped for the good command.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:walk_all

chunk_findings.detail: For a non-root chain whose help process runs but exits non-zero, the method caches `None` but records neither `unavailable` nor `_broken`. The class documents `unavailable` as “one note each (command or verb chain -> reason)”, yet `walk_all` only adds a non-zero-exit note when `len(key) == 1`. Given a registry chain `("ddflow", "docs", "check")` where `_HERE.help(["ddflow", "docs", "check", "--help"])` returns `ran=True, returncode=2`, `walk_all` sets `self._cache[("ddflow", "docs", "check")] = None` but leaves `unavailable` without `"ddflow docs check"`, so the reason that this verb chain could not be walked is lost.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:walk_all

chunk_findings.detail: The timeout test does not actually create a stalled help command. Given the command list `[sys.executable, "-c", "import time; time.sleep(30)", "--help"]`, CPython parses the trailing `--help` as an interpreter option (unless separated by `--`), so the subprocess prints Python usage and exits successfully before executing the `-c` code. Therefore `H.command_runner(_ROOT, 1, in_process_commands=())(stall)` returns a non-timeout capture with `returncode == 0`, and the assertion `done.timed_out and done.returncode is None` fails; the test exercises neither the timeout knob nor a stalled spawned tool.

chunk_findings.detail: The `_DUPE_HUNT_MAX` cap does not actually skip the duplicate hunt; it only skips using its result. `plan_lint` unconditionally executes `hunt = _hunt(repo, log, cfg, st, set())` before checking `len(scope) <= _DUPE_HUNT_MAX`. For a whole-queue lint where `len(scope) > 300`, the code therefore still performs the expensive add-time duplicate hunt (the comment above `_DUPE_HUNT_MAX` describes this as roughly 1 second per record and 25+ minutes for a 1.7k-item queue) and then discards `hunt` by setting `similar = None`, while the reported note says duplicates were not checked. This defeats the stated performance guard and can make `ddflow plan lint` pay the full dedupe cost and any side effects of `_hunt` even when it claims the duplicate check was skipped.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/plan.py:plan_lint

chunk_findings.detail: `dx_priority` is documented and intended to report only DX/bug-fix tasks at the generic default priority, but its predicate is only `band(iid, tags) and int(...) == DEFAULT_PRIORITY`. The same file treats “is this a fix/DX item?” as `band(...) in FIXABLE_KINDS` in `propose`. Therefore, for any item whose `band` returns a non-empty non-fix classification (for example a feature band such as `"feature"`), `B-feature` with priority `DEFAULT_PRIORITY` and no fix/DX tags will produce a `dx_priority` finding, and `--fix` will apply its `{"priority": band_priority(...)}` fix even though the item is not a DX/fix task. This violates the stated rule and can rewrite an operator-set feature priority if the feature band priority differs from the default.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/planlint.py:dx_priority

chunk_findings.detail: `duplicates` reports every `(iid, hit)` returned by `similar` instead of deduplicating the unordered pair. Because `similar(title, body)` does not receive the current item id and duplicate similarity is symmetric, two open similar items `A` and `B` cause two findings: when linting `A`, `similar` returns `B`; when linting `B`, it returns `A`. The code only filters `hit != iid`, then sorts the pair, so both findings have `ids == ("A", "B")` with reversed details. A queue with one duplicate pair is reported as two duplicate findings, inflating the duplicate count and contradicting the intended “duplicate pairs” evidence.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/planlint.py:duplicates

chunk_findings.detail: `_it` mishandles the `terminal` keyword: it pops `terminal` once to decide `state`, then pops it again to decide the `terminal` field, but the second pop can no longer see the value and falls back to the original `state` argument. For example, `_it(terminal=True)` returns `{"state": "done", "terminal": False}` because `state` is still `"open"` when the fallback is evaluated. Since `lint()` builds its default scope from `not it["terminal"]`, a helper-built “terminal” item is treated as open; e.g. `lint({"x": _it(terminal=True, needs=["gone"])})` puts `x` in scope and can report a `stale_needs` finding that should be suppressed for a terminal item. Conversely, `_it(state="done", terminal=False)` returns `terminal=True`, hiding findings for an item the caller explicitly marked non-terminal.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_plan_lint.py:_it

chunk_findings.detail: The previously reported root/executable/environment issue still holds. `_ddflow_help_verbs` classifies a command as “this ddflow” purely from the spelling of `argv[0]` (`ddflow`, a POSIX path whose basename is `ddflow`, or `-m ddflow`) and `run` then calls `in_process(verbs)` without consulting the `root` that `P.capture` would use as `cwd`. That makes a generic docs check validate such mentions against the parser of the process hosting the check, not the `ddflow` the checked docs/repo actually invokes. Concrete input: running an installed ddflow 1.x as `ddflow check_docs /repo/ddflow-2.x` where those docs contain `ddflow newverb --help`. `run` receives `["ddflow", "newverb", "--help"]`, returns `in_process(["newverb"])`, and the 1.x parser exits 2 because it has no `newverb`; the correct spawned walk with `cwd=/repo/ddflow-2.x` would resolve 2.x and exit 0. The new code still has `root` available in `run` but does not use it to resolve or build the parser to replay.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:_ddflow_help_verbs

chunk_findings.detail: Previous finding 1 still holds. The new test `test_the_docs_check_walk_replays_ddflow_and_still_spawns_other_tools` (tests/test_docscheck_help_in_process.py:87-105) creates a doc root whose `pyproject.toml` maps `ddflow = "x:main"`—i.e. the `ddflow` command in the checked project is not the process hosting the docs check—yet it still asserts that no `ddflow` spawn occurs. That is the unresolved root/executable/environment gap: a spawned walk for this project would use `x:main`'s CLI and flags, but the test expects the outer process's registry to be used. `test_every_way_of_spelling_this_ddflow_is_replayed_not_spawned` further locks this in by expecting `/venv/bin/ddflow` to be replayed without resolving it to the current executable/environment.

chunk_findings.detail: The BOGUS_CHAINS assertion does not test the comment's claim that the spawned walk also refuses. chunk_findings.detail: `command_runner` now intercepts any argv whose first element is literally `ddflow` and last element is `--help`, but `in_process` ignores `root`, the resolved executable, and the environment that the spawned walk would have used. If the docs being checked refer to a different `ddflow` than the process hosting the docscheck—e.g. the docscheck process is an older installed `ddflow`, while PATH/repo contains a newer `ddflow` with a new verb or flag, or the `ddflow` command is a wrapper that loads project config/plugins—`command_runner` returns the current process’s parser output instead of the checked command’s output. For a docs line `ddflow newverb --help` in a repo whose actual `ddflow` supports `newverb`, `in_process` uses the old parser, `parse_args` exits non-zero with no flags, and docscheck falsely reports the command/flags missing; the converse false pass is also possible. The new equivalence test only compares the two paths within the same process, so it cannot catch this wrong-CLI case.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:command_runner

chunk_findings.detail: The equivalence test can pass vacuously when one of its “valid” sample chains stops being valid, because it never asserts that the chain actually produced successful help. For example, if `ddflow gate run` is renamed or removed, `spawned(["gate", "run"])` and `H.in_process(["gate", "run"])` will both return a nonzero exit code and usage/error text with no option flags; then `inproc.ran == real.ran`, `(inproc.returncode == 0) == (real.returncode == 0)`, and `H.help_flags("") == H.help_flags("")` all hold. The test therefore stops exercising the intended in-process path for that verb chain and can hide regressions where the real command’s in-process help diverges from the spawned help, or where the sampled chain no longer exists at all. The valid chains should be asserted to return success and non-empty/expected help flags before comparing in-process and spawned output.

chunk_findings.detail: `in_process_commands` is normalized with `tuple(in_process_commands)`, but a plain string is a valid `Iterable[str]`. Given `command_runner(root, timeout_s, in_process_commands="ddflow")`, `known` becomes `('d', 'd', 'f', 'l', 'o', 'w')`, so `run(["ddflow", "--help"])` fails `argv[0] in known` and falls through to `spawn`. This silently disables the in-process walk whenever the knob is supplied as a single string (a common shape for configuration/environment knobs), contrary to the documented behavior that commands named in `in_process_commands` are answered in-process.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:command_runner

chunk_findings.detail: The render redirects process-global `sys.stdout`/`sys.stderr`, but `_RENDER_LOCK` only serializes other calls to `_InProcessHelp.help`. Any other thread that writes to stdout/stderr while a render holds the lock (for example a progress `print`, a logging handler writing to `sys.stdout`, or a library warning) has that output captured into the current chain’s `Captured.stdout`/`Captured.stderr`. For example, with the concurrency knob set above one, thread A can call `_HERE.help(['ddflow', '--help'])`; if thread B executes `print('progress')` before thread A’s `parse_args` returns, thread A’s returned help text includes `progress`, which can change the docs-check finding set. The lock does not make the redirect thread-local.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:_InProcessHelp.help

chunk_findings.detail: The versioned help memo is not populated when the parser cache is first initialized or rebuilt. `help()` captures `memo = self._built[2] if self._built is not None else {}` before calling `self.parser()`; if `self._built` was `None`, `parser()` replaces it with a new tuple containing a new dict, but the subsequent `memo[key] = capped` writes to the local dict, leaving `self._built[2]` empty. In a fresh process, calling `_HERE.help(['ddflow', '--help'])` twice runs `parse_args` twice because the first result was never stored in the versioned memo, defeating the per-version help cache on the first chain (and after a version change).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:_InProcessHelp.help

chunk_findings.detail: `walk_all` builds chains for every in-process command inside one `try`, so a failure for one command aborts the whole eager walk and records the failure under a key that is not a valid command or verb chain when more than one in-process command is present. For example, with `commands=["ddflow", "ddflowx"]` and both names in the in-process set, if `_HERE.chains("ddflowx")` raises while `_HERE.chains("ddflow")` would succeed, the method stores `unavailable["ddflow ddflowx"] = "could not walk: ..."`, caches nothing for `ddflow`, and leaves no `unavailable` entry for `ddflowx` itself. Callers that look up the broken command by name or by its own chain will not see the failure, and the intended eager cache is silently skipped for the good command.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:walk_all

chunk_findings.detail: For a non-root chain whose help process runs but exits non-zero, the method caches `None` but records neither `unavailable` nor `_broken`. The class documents `unavailable` as “one note each (command or verb chain -> reason)”, yet `walk_all` only adds a non-zero-exit note when `len(key) == 1`. Given a registry chain `("ddflow", "docs", "check")` where `_HERE.help(["ddflow", "docs", "check", "--help"])` returns `ran=True, returncode=2`, `walk_all` sets `self._cache[("ddflow", "docs", "check")] = None` but leaves `unavailable` without `"ddflow docs check"`, so the reason that this verb chain could not be walked is lost.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:walk_all

chunk_findings.detail: The timeout test does not actually create a stalled help command. Given the command list `[sys.executable, "-c", "import time; time.sleep(30)", "--help"]`, CPython parses the trailing `--help` as an interpreter option (unless separated by `--`), so the subprocess prints Python usage and exits successfully before executing the `-c` code. Therefore `H.command_runner(_ROOT, 1, in_process_commands=())(stall)` returns a non-timeout capture with `returncode == 0`, and the assertion `done.timed_out and done.returncode is None` fails; the test exercises neither the timeout knob nor a stalled spawned tool.

chunk_findings.detail: The `_DUPE_HUNT_MAX` cap does not actually skip the duplicate hunt; it only skips using its result. `plan_lint` unconditionally executes `hunt = _hunt(repo, log, cfg, st, set())` before checking `len(scope) <= _DUPE_HUNT_MAX`. For a whole-queue lint where `len(scope) > 300`, the code therefore still performs the expensive add-time duplicate hunt (the comment above `_DUPE_HUNT_MAX` describes this as roughly 1 second per record and 25+ minutes for a 1.7k-item queue) and then discards `hunt` by setting `similar = None`, while the reported note says duplicates were not checked. This defeats the stated performance guard and can make `ddflow plan lint` pay the full dedupe cost and any side effects of `_hunt` even when it claims the duplicate check was skipped.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/plan.py:plan_lint

chunk_findings.detail: `dx_priority` is documented and intended to report only DX/bug-fix tasks at the generic default priority, but its predicate is only `band(iid, tags) and int(...) == DEFAULT_PRIORITY`. The same file treats “is this a fix/DX item?” as `band(...) in FIXABLE_KINDS` in `propose`. Therefore, for any item whose `band` returns a non-empty non-fix classification (for example a feature band such as `"feature"`), `B-feature` with priority `DEFAULT_PRIORITY` and no fix/DX tags will produce a `dx_priority` finding, and `--fix` will apply its `{"priority": band_priority(...)}` fix even though the item is not a DX/fix task. This violates the stated rule and can rewrite an operator-set feature priority if the feature band priority differs from the default.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/planlint.py:dx_priority

chunk_findings.detail: `duplicates` reports every `(iid, hit)` returned by `similar` instead of deduplicating the unordered pair. Because `similar(title, body)` does not receive the current item id and duplicate similarity is symmetric, two open similar items `A` and `B` cause two findings: when linting `A`, `similar` returns `B`; when linting `B`, it returns `A`. The code only filters `hit != iid`, then sorts the pair, so both findings have `ids == ("A", "B")` with reversed details. A queue with one duplicate pair is reported as two duplicate findings, inflating the duplicate count and contradicting the intended “duplicate pairs” evidence.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/planlint.py:duplicates

chunk_findings.detail: `_it` mishandles the `terminal` keyword: it pops `terminal` once to decide `state`, then pops it again to decide the `terminal` field, but the second pop can no longer see the value and falls back to the original `state` argument. For example, `_it(terminal=True)` returns `{"state": "done", "terminal": False}` because `state` is still `"open"` when the fallback is evaluated. Since `lint()` builds its default scope from `not it["terminal"]`, a helper-built “terminal” item is treated as open; e.g. `lint({"x": _it(terminal=True, needs=["gone"])})` puts `x` in scope and can report a `stale_needs` finding that should be suppressed for a terminal item. Conversely, `_it(state="done", terminal=False)` returns `terminal=True`, hiding findings for an item the caller explicitly marked non-terminal.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_plan_lint.py:_it

chunk_findings.detail: The new unconfirmed exclusion only removes `b.fix_task` from the initial set of non-feature items. If an unconfirmed bug’s `item` is itself a non-feature item, it remains in the returned ids. For example, if `state.items` contains an item `B123` with `branch_kind(B123, cfg) != FEATURE`, and `state.bugs` contains an open bug with `item="B123"`, `fix_task=""`, and `reproduced="no"`, the initial `ids` already contains `B123`; `unconfirmed` contains only the empty fix task, so `difference_update` does not remove `B123`, and the later loop skips the bug because `reproduced == "no"`. The function still returns `B123`, so the unconfirmed bug is still counted/offered, contrary to the stated intent that an unconfirmed bug counts for nothing.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/schedule.py:720

chunk_findings.detail: When capture is off, `attach` still executes the repro command before it can know that no bundle will be stored. It calls `RC.check(...)` whenever `repro_cmd` is non-empty, then calls `build(...)`, which returns `None` for capture-off mode, and finally returns `{}`. For example, with `given={"repro_cmd": "touch /tmp/ddflow-marker", "capture": "off"}`, the command is run and the marker is created, but the function records nothing. This makes an “off” capture setting still run arbitrary repro commands and discard their verdict, causing side effects and wasted work.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprobundle.py:attach

chunk_findings.detail: The repro command is executed as an argv list, not as a shell command, so common `--repro-cmd` strings are mishandled. Given `cmd="DDFLOW_RUNNING_GATE=ci pytest tests/test_x.py"` (the exact environment variable called out in the intent), `shlex.split` produces `["DDFLOW_RUNNING_GATE=ci", "pytest", ...]`, and `P.capture(words, ...)` tries to exec the literal program named `DDFLOW_RUNNING_GATE=ci`. No run reaches an exit code, so `_run_at` returns `{"unavailable": "no run reached an exit code to read"}` and the bug is recorded as unconfirmed even though the command would reproduce with that variable set. The same failure applies to `VAR=val cmd`, `&&`, redirections, and shell globs such as `pytest tests/test_*.py`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprocheck.py:check / _run_at

chunk_findings.detail: `tail_bytes` is applied as a character count, not a byte count. With `repro_tail_bytes=1` and a repro command that prints a non-ASCII character such as `é`, `text[-keep:]` stores `"é"`, which is two UTF-8 bytes, exceeding the configured byte budget. `output_truncated` is also computed from character length, not bytes, so byte-limited storage can overflow or silently store more data than `[bugs] repro_tail_bytes` allows.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprocheck.py:_run_at:98

chunk_findings.detail: The memo fix moved `self.parser()` before the `try` block, so parser-construction failures are no longer converted into a `Captured` result. Previously `self.parser().parse_args(...)` was inside the outer `try` (and the inner `try` for `SystemExit`), so an exception raised while building the parser—e.g. a plugin import raising `ImportError`, a malformed registry entry raising `ValueError`, or a `SystemExit` during version detection—was returned as a failed capture and could be recorded as unavailable. Now `_HERE.help(["ddflow", "--help"])` propagates that exception, so a broken command can crash the docs-check gate instead of being noted as unavailable.

chunk_findings.detail: The earlier confirmed stdout/stderr capture issue still holds: the code still redirects process-global `sys.stdout`/`sys.stderr` while holding only `_RENDER_LOCK`. The diff only changes the comment to admit that foreign writers can be captured; it does not fence them or avoid global redirection. With the concurrency knob above one, if any other thread or logging handler in the same process writes to the standard streams while a render is active, that output is swallowed into the current chain’s `Captured.stdout/stderr`. For example, while thread A is inside `redirect_stdout(out)` rendering `ddflow --help`, thread B printing `--spam-flag-off` makes B’s output disappear from the terminal and appear in A’s help text, which can corrupt the docs-check finding set.

chunk_findings.detail: The assertion `idx.unavailable == {"ddflowx": "could not walk: no registry here"}` requires the real `ddflow` walk to contribute no unavailable entries. The implementation explicitly supports unavailable verb chains (the next test in the same file asserts that a deep non-zero chain is recorded under its own key), so any environment or registry state where a `ddflow` chain fails—e.g. `ddflow workflow state --help` exits non-zero—will put that chain into `idx.unavailable` as well. The test then fails even though the behavior being tested is correct: `ddflowx` was noted separately and `ddflow`’s walk still filled the cache.
