chunk_findings.detail: The classifier decides “this ddflow” from argv spelling alone, so it can redirect a different executable to the current process’s parser. If the checked `root` contains `./ddflow` (or `/other/venv/bin/ddflow`) and the docs mention `./ddflow gate --help`, `argv[0].rsplit("/", 1)[-1] == "ddflow"` makes `run` call `in_process(["gate"])` and never call `P.capture(..., cwd=root)`. If the root-local `ddflow` has a `gate` command or flags absent from the process hosting the check, the docs check can mark the docs as broken, or vice versa. The `-m` branch has the same overreach: `["pytest", "-m", "ddflow", "--help"]` is accepted because only `argv[1:3]` is checked, so a pytest chain is replayed as ddflow’s root help. The earlier PATH probe only addresses bare `ddflow`; it does not cover paths or a named interpreter/executable that selects a different binary/environment.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:_ddflow_help_verbs

chunk_findings.detail: The test claims to prove that `check_docs` really uses the in-process walk and judges `ddflow gate skip --reason x`, but it only proves that no `ddflow` argv is spawned. If `check_docs` silently dropped `ddflow` mentions (or filtered `ddflow` out before calling the runner), all assertions would still pass: the monkeypatched capture would record only the `nix` spawn, `rep.findings` would be empty, `rep.notes` would still be `["help"]` for the `nix` spawn, and `rep.clean` would be true. Thus the test passes even when the `ddflow` mention is not checked at all; it should assert a ddflow help note or make a bogus ddflow flag produce a finding.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_docscheck_help_in_process.py:test_the_docs_check_walk_replays_ddflow_and_still_spawns_other_tools

chunk_findings.detail: `c` is a list of argv elements, so `"ddflow" in c` tests exact list membership, not substring/path matching. If `command_runner` regressed to spawn a path-spelled ddflow command such as `["/venv/bin/ddflow", "gate", "--help"]`, `spawned_calls` would contain that list and the assertion would still pass, even though a ddflow-shaped command spawned. Use substring/verb classification (e.g. `any("ddflow" in arg for arg in c)` or `H._ddflow_help_verbs(c)`) if the intent is to catch any spelling.

chunk_findings.detail: When the scoped live-work count exceeds `_DUPE_HUNT_MAX` (300), `plan_lint` passes `similar=None` to `PL.lint`, and the code comment states that this skips the duplicate check. If there are no other findings, `report.findings` is empty and the function returns `O.ok("plan.lint", ...)`, i.e. a successful lint. Given a queue of 301 live work items where two items have identical title/body (a duplicate pair) and there are no overlap, glob, priority, or stale-reference findings, `ddflow plan lint` exits 0 and reports no duplicate findings, even though the stated intent is to lint the whole open queue for duplicates. The note says the check was skipped, but the machine-readable result is still success with no duplicate findings, and the note’s “duplicates: 0 when skipped” is false: duplicates are unknown, not zero.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/plan.py:plan_lint

chunk_findings.detail: The `dx_priority` check is gated only on `band(iid, tags)` being truthy, not on the band being one of `FIXABLE_KINDS` (`"dx"`/`"bug"`). The module's own `propose` uses `ka in FIXABLE_KINDS`, which means `band` is expected to be able to return non-empty non-fix classifications such as `"feature"`. Given a scoped feature with `band(...) == "feature"` and `priority == DEFAULT_PRIORITY`, this code files a `dx_priority` finding and attaches `fix={"priority": band_priority(iid, tags)}`. Because `--fix` applies `dx_priority` fixes, this can misreport a feature as a DX/bug-priority defect or, if the feature band priority differs, silently change the feature's priority even though the intended check is only for DX/bug tasks at the generic default priority.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/planlint.py:dx_priority

chunk_findings.detail: The renderer assumes every finding kind is one of the hard-coded `_LINT_KINDS` and does `by[f["kind"]].append(f)`. The command passes the service’s `findings` straight to this renderer, and the intent requires reporting cycle-checked proposed edges and needs-rule violations; those can have kinds such as `cycle` or `needs_rule` that are not in `_LINT_KINDS`. Given a report containing `{"findings": [{"kind": "cycle", "ids": ["A", "B"], "detail": "..."}]}`, `_lint_text` raises `KeyError` before printing any output, so `ddflow plan lint` crashes instead of showing the cycle/rule finding.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/plan.py:_lint_text

chunk_findings.detail: The test asserts that two overlapping open tasks `a` and `b` produce no overlap finding because `a` needs a done task `x` and `x` needs `b`. But `a`’s edge to `x` is exactly a “needs naming a settled item” case, which the same file elsewhere (`test_a_needs_naming_a_settled_item_is_stale_and_fixable`) says is stale and fixable by removing `needs`. Given the test’s own items (`a` open needs `x`, `x` done needs `b`, both `a` and `b` glob `docs/a.md`), treating `a -> x` as a live ordering edge is wrong: after `--fix` drops the stale `a -> x` edge, `a` and `b` remain overlapping with no ordering edge. The test codifies the incorrect expectation that a stale settled-item edge can suppress an overlap, allowing a `--fix` run to leave an unreported unordered overlap.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_plan_lint.py:test_an_order_THROUGH_a_settled_item_is_an_order

data.reason: 4 finding(s)

chunk_findings.detail: `in_process_commands` is normalized with `tuple(in_process_commands)`, but a plain string is a valid `Iterable[str]`. Given `command_runner(root, timeout_s, in_process_commands="ddflow")`, `known` becomes `('d', 'd', 'f', 'l', 'o', 'w')`, so `run(["ddflow", "--help"])` fails `argv[0] in known` and falls through to `spawn`. This silently disables the in-process walk whenever the knob is supplied as a single string (a common shape for configuration/environment knobs), contrary to the documented behavior that commands named in `in_process_commands` are answered in-process.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:command_runner

chunk_findings.detail: The render redirects process-global `sys.stdout`/`sys.stderr`, but `_RENDER_LOCK` only serializes other calls to `_InProcessHelp.help`. Any other thread that writes to stdout/stderr while a render holds the lock (for example a progress `print`, a logging handler writing to `sys.stdout`, or a library warning) has that output captured into the current chain’s `Captured.stdout`/`Captured.stderr`. For example, with the concurrency knob set above one, thread A can call `_HERE.help(['ddflow', '--help'])`; if thread B executes `print('progress')` before thread A’s `parse_args` returns, thread A’s returned help text includes `progress`, which can change the docs-check finding set. The lock does not make the redirect thread-local.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:_InProcessHelp.help

chunk_findings.detail: The versioned help memo is not populated when the parser cache is first initialized or rebuilt. `help()` captures `memo = self._built[2] if self._built is not None else {}` before calling `self.parser()`; if `self._built` was `None`, `parser()` replaces it with a new tuple containing a new dict, but the subsequent `memo[key] = capped` writes to the local dict, leaving `self._built[2]` empty. In a fresh process, calling `_HERE.help(['ddflow', '--help'])` twice runs `parse_args` twice because the first result was never stored in the versioned memo, defeating the per-version help cache on the first chain (and after a version change).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:_InProcessHelp.help

chunk_findings.detail: `walk_all` builds chains for every in-process command inside one `try`, so a failure for one command aborts the whole eager walk and records the failure under a key that is not a valid command or verb chain when more than one in-process command is present. For example, with `commands=["ddflow", "ddflowx"]` and both names in the in-process set, if `_HERE.chains("ddflowx")` raises while `_HERE.chains("ddflow")` would succeed, the method stores `unavailable["ddflow ddflowx"] = "could not walk: ..."`, caches nothing for `ddflow`, and leaves no `unavailable` entry for `ddflowx` itself. Callers that look up the broken command by name or by its own chain will not see the failure, and the intended eager cache is silently skipped for the good command.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:walk_all

chunk_findings.detail: For a non-root chain whose help process runs but exits non-zero, the method caches `None` but records neither `unavailable` nor `_broken`. The class documents `unavailable` as “one note each (command or verb chain -> reason)”, yet `walk_all` only adds a non-zero-exit note when `len(key) == 1`. Given a registry chain `("ddflow", "docs", "check")` where `_HERE.help(["ddflow", "docs", "check", "--help"])` returns `ran=True, returncode=2`, `walk_all` sets `self._cache[("ddflow", "docs", "check")] = None` but leaves `unavailable` without `"ddflow docs check"`, so the reason that this verb chain could not be walked is lost.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:walk_all

chunk_findings.detail: The timeout test does not actually create a stalled help command. Given the command list `[sys.executable, "-c", "import time; time.sleep(30)", "--help"]`, CPython parses the trailing `--help` as an interpreter option (unless separated by `--`), so the subprocess prints Python usage and exits successfully before executing the `-c` code. Therefore `H.command_runner(_ROOT, 1, in_process_commands=())(stall)` returns a non-timeout capture with `returncode == 0`, and the assertion `done.timed_out and done.returncode is None` fails; the test exercises neither the timeout knob nor a stalled spawned tool.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_docs_check_speed.py:88-96

chunk_findings.detail: The memo fix moved `self.parser()` before the `try` block, so parser-construction failures are no longer converted into a `Captured` result. Previously `self.parser().parse_args(...)` was inside the outer `try` (and the inner `try` for `SystemExit`), so an exception raised while building the parser—e.g. a plugin import raising `ImportError`, a malformed registry entry raising `ValueError`, or a `SystemExit` during version detection—was returned as a failed capture and could be recorded as unavailable. Now `_HERE.help(["ddflow", "--help"])` propagates that exception, so a broken command can crash the docs-check gate instead of being noted as unavailable.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:_InProcessHelp.help

chunk_findings.detail: The earlier confirmed stdout/stderr capture issue still holds: the code still redirects process-global `sys.stdout`/`sys.stderr` while holding only `_RENDER_LOCK`. The diff only changes the comment to admit that foreign writers can be captured; it does not fence them or avoid global redirection. With the concurrency knob above one, if any other thread or logging handler in the same process writes to the standard streams while a render is active, that output is swallowed into the current chain’s `Captured.stdout/stderr`. For example, while thread A is inside `redirect_stdout(out)` rendering `ddflow --help`, thread B printing `--spam-flag-off` makes B’s output disappear from the terminal and appear in A’s help text, which can corrupt the docs-check finding set.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:_InProcessHelp.help

chunk_findings.detail: The assertion `idx.unavailable == {"ddflowx": "could not walk: no registry here"}` requires the real `ddflow` walk to contribute no unavailable entries. The implementation explicitly supports unavailable verb chains (the next test in the same file asserts that a deep non-zero chain is recorded under its own key), so any environment or registry state where a `ddflow` chain fails—e.g. `ddflow workflow state --help` exits non-zero—will put that chain into `idx.unavailable` as well. The test then fails even though the behavior being tested is correct: `ddflowx` was noted separately and `ddflow`’s walk still filled the cache.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_docs_check_speed.py:test_one_in_process_command_cannot_blanket_the_others

chunk_findings.detail: The new early `memo` lookup bypasses the version/rebuild check. `memo` is taken from `self._built` before `self.parser()` is called, and if the key is present the method returns immediately. Since `self.parser()` is the operation that detects a new tool version and replaces `self._built` with a new memo, a cached chain from version A is returned after the tool changes to version B, or after any state change that would require the parser to be rebuilt. For example, the first `_HERE.help(['ddflow', '--help'])` call caches the version-A help; if the version source then changes, the second call with the same argv returns the version-A `Captured` instead of rebuilding and reporting the new help or a build error, producing stale findings and hiding a newly broken registry.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:_InProcessHelp.help

chunk_findings.detail: The `threading.active_count() > 1` gate over-refuses whenever the help walk is actually concurrent. If the concurrency knob runs `_HERE.help` on worker threads, then as soon as more than one worker thread is alive, every in-process render reaches the gate and returns `Captured(error=RuntimeError(...))`, even though no other thread wrote to stdio. Given `concurrency=2`, a worker thread calling `_HERE.help(['ddflow', '--help'])` sees `threading.active_count()` equal to at least 2 and discards a clean capture, so the in-process walk cannot return ddflow help while the knob is above one; it records unavailable or falls back to the spawning path the change was meant to avoid.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:_InProcessHelp.help

chunk_findings.detail: The same gate under-refuses threads that exit during the render. It calls `threading.active_count()` only after the redirected render has finished, so a background thread that writes to `sys.stdout` while the redirect is active and then exits before the count is taken is invisible. For example, while the main thread is inside `_HERE.help`, another thread starts, prints `--phantom-flag` to stdout during the argparse render, and exits before the render returns; `threading.active_count()` then returns 1, so the mixed capture containing the phantom flag is returned and cached, exactly the failure the comment says is prevented.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:_InProcessHelp.help

chunk_findings.detail: The new test does not actually prove that foreign writers are fenced; it only proves that phantom text is not *returned as ddflow’s output* when `capped.ran` is true. In the “refused” path described by the test comment, `_InProcessHelp.help` has already redirected process-global `sys.stdout`/`sys.stderr` and run the render; any `print` from `spammer` during that window is written into the render’s captured `StringIO`, and the refusal discards that `StringIO`. The test then stops the thread and skips its only assertion because `capped.ran` is false, so it passes even though the spammer’s bytes were silently swallowed instead of reaching the real stdout/stderr. In a real run, a concurrent progress `print` or logging handler writing to `sys.stdout` while an in-process help render is active can therefore lose its output; the test should force at least one foreign write inside the redirect window and assert that the write is either not captured or is forwarded to the real streams.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_docs_check_speed.py:test_a_render_shared_with_another_thread_is_never_returned_mixed

chunk_findings.detail: `_ddflow_help_verbs` decides that an argv names *this* ddflow from the basename alone or from any `["-m", "ddflow"]` pair, without checking that the named executable/module is the one hosting the docscheck. For example, if the docs being checked mention `/other/venv/bin/python -m ddflow gate --help` (or `/other/venv/bin/ddflow gate --help`), the function returns `["gate"]`, so `command_runner` calls `in_process` and replays the current process's parser. A spawned walk would have executed the explicit interpreter/binary, whose `ddflow` may be a different version or a wrapper around another CLI, so the reported help flags are wrong. The earlier PATH-resolution refutation does not cover this spelling: subprocess resolves explicit paths directly, not through PATH.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:_ddflow_help_verbs

chunk_findings.detail: The guard `assert not any("ddflow" in c for c in spawned_calls)` does not actually reject a spawned ddflow path spelling. `spawned_calls` is a list of argv lists, so `"ddflow" in c` tests exact list-element equality, not substring/basename matching. If `D.check_docs` or the command resolver invokes the runner with a path spelling such as `["/venv/bin/ddflow", "gate", "skip", "--help"]` (or `ddflow.exe`/`ddflow.bat` on Windows) and `H.command_runner` regresses to spawning it, this assertion still passes because `"/venv/bin/ddflow" != "ddflow"`. The test therefore can report success while the docs-check walk has spawned ddflow, contrary to its stated purpose and the path-spelling guarantee.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_docscheck_help_in_process.py (`test_the_docs_check_walk_replays_ddflow_and_still_spawns_other_tools`)

chunk_findings.detail: When the scoped live-work count exceeds `_DUPE_HUNT_MAX` (300), `plan_lint` passes `similar=None` to `PL.lint`, and the code comment states that this skips the duplicate check. If there are no other findings, `report.findings` is empty and the function returns `O.ok("plan.lint", ...)`, i.e. a successful lint. Given a queue of 301 live work items where two items have identical title/body (a duplicate pair) and there are no overlap, glob, priority, or stale-reference findings, `ddflow plan lint` exits 0 and reports no duplicate findings, even though the stated intent is to lint the whole open queue for duplicates. The note says the check was skipped, but the machine-readable result is still success with no duplicate findings, and the note’s “duplicates: 0 when skipped” is false: duplicates are unknown, not zero.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/plan.py:plan_lint

chunk_findings.detail: The `dx_priority` check is gated only on `band(iid, tags)` being truthy, not on the band being one of `FIXABLE_KINDS` (`"dx"`/`"bug"`). The module's own `propose` uses `ka in FIXABLE_KINDS`, which means `band` is expected to be able to return non-empty non-fix classifications such as `"feature"`. Given a scoped feature with `band(...) == "feature"` and `priority == DEFAULT_PRIORITY`, this code files a `dx_priority` finding and attaches `fix={"priority": band_priority(iid, tags)}`. Because `--fix` applies `dx_priority` fixes, this can misreport a feature as a DX/bug-priority defect or, if the feature band priority differs, silently change the feature's priority even though the intended check is only for DX/bug tasks at the generic default priority.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/planlint.py:dx_priority

chunk_findings.detail: The renderer assumes every finding kind is one of the hard-coded `_LINT_KINDS` and does `by[f["kind"]].append(f)`. The command passes the service’s `findings` straight to this renderer, and the intent requires reporting cycle-checked proposed edges and needs-rule violations; those can have kinds such as `cycle` or `needs_rule` that are not in `_LINT_KINDS`. Given a report containing `{"findings": [{"kind": "cycle", "ids": ["A", "B"], "detail": "..."}]}`, `_lint_text` raises `KeyError` before printing any output, so `ddflow plan lint` crashes instead of showing the cycle/rule finding.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/plan.py:_lint_text

chunk_findings.detail: The test asserts that two overlapping open tasks `a` and `b` produce no overlap finding because `a` needs a done task `x` and `x` needs `b`. But `a`’s edge to `x` is exactly a “needs naming a settled item” case, which the same file elsewhere (`test_a_needs_naming_a_settled_item_is_stale_and_fixable`) says is stale and fixable by removing `needs`. Given the test’s own items (`a` open needs `x`, `x` done needs `b`, both `a` and `b` glob `docs/a.md`), treating `a -> x` as a live ordering edge is wrong: after `--fix` drops the stale `a -> x` edge, `a` and `b` remain overlapping with no ordering edge. The test codifies the incorrect expectation that a stale settled-item edge can suppress an overlap, allowing a `--fix` run to leave an unreported unordered overlap.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_plan_lint.py:test_an_order_THROUGH_a_settled_item_is_an_order

chunk_findings.detail: The classifier claims to replay only “this interpreter’s module” (`python -m ddflow`), but `_is_a_python` accepts any executable whose basename looks like Python, including slash-spelled absolute interpreters such as `/other/venv/bin/python`. Given docs that mention `/other/venv/bin/python -m ddflow gate --help`, `run` returns `in_process(["gate"])` and never spawns the named interpreter. If that named interpreter has a different ddflow install, the docs check can accept a flag that exists only in the current process or reject a flag that exists only in the named one; the earlier slash-spelled `ddflow` case was fixed, but this slash-spelled Python case was not.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:_ddflow_help_verbs

chunk_findings.detail: `_is_a_python` says it recognizes `python.exe` on Windows, but it only splits the program name on `/`. Given a Windows command spelled `C:\Python\python.exe -m ddflow gate --help`, the basename remains `c:\python\python.exe`, `removeprefix("python")` does not apply, and the function returns False, so the intended `python -m ddflow` in-process path is not used. This is a concrete platform omission in the new classifier.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:_is_a_python

chunk_findings.detail: This test still does not prove that `check_docs` actually uses the in-process ddflow walk or that it validates `ddflow gate skip --reason x` against that walk. It only patches `P.capture` and asserts that no spawned argv contains the exact list element `"ddflow"`. If `D.check_docs` regressed to filter out or ignore mentions whose first token is `ddflow` before calling the runner, the first call would still record only the `nix` spawn, `rep.notes` would still be `["help"]`, `rep.findings` would be empty, and the second call’s monkeypatched `nix` help would make `rep.clean` true. All assertions would pass even though the ddflow mention was never checked by `H.in_process`.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_docscheck_help_in_process.py:test_the_docs_check_walk_replays_ddflow_and_still_spawns_other_tools

chunk_findings.detail: `assert not any("ddflow" in c for c in spawned_calls)` uses list membership, so it only catches an argv element exactly equal to `"ddflow"`. If the runner regressed to spawn a path-spelled ddflow command such as `["./ddflow", "gate", "--help"]` or `["/venv/bin/ddflow", "gate", "--help"]`, the assertion still passes because neither list contains the exact element `"ddflow"`. This allows a ddflow-shaped spawn to go undetected despite the test’s stated intent.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_docscheck_help_in_process.py:test_the_docs_check_walk_replays_ddflow_and_still_spawns_other_tools

data.reason: 4 finding(s)

chunk_findings.detail: `in_process_commands` is normalized with `tuple(in_process_commands)`, but a plain string is a valid `Iterable[str]`. Given `command_runner(root, timeout_s, in_process_commands="ddflow")`, `known` becomes `('d', 'd', 'f', 'l', 'o', 'w')`, so `run(["ddflow", "--help"])` fails `argv[0] in known` and falls through to `spawn`. This silently disables the in-process walk whenever the knob is supplied as a single string (a common shape for configuration/environment knobs), contrary to the documented behavior that commands named in `in_process_commands` are answered in-process.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:command_runner

chunk_findings.detail: The render redirects process-global `sys.stdout`/`sys.stderr`, but `_RENDER_LOCK` only serializes other calls to `_InProcessHelp.help`. Any other thread that writes to stdout/stderr while a render holds the lock (for example a progress `print`, a logging handler writing to `sys.stdout`, or a library warning) has that output captured into the current chain’s `Captured.stdout`/`Captured.stderr`. For example, with the concurrency knob set above one, thread A can call `_HERE.help(['ddflow', '--help'])`; if thread B executes `print('progress')` before thread A’s `parse_args` returns, thread A’s returned help text includes `progress`, which can change the docs-check finding set. The lock does not make the redirect thread-local.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:_InProcessHelp.help

chunk_findings.detail: The versioned help memo is not populated when the parser cache is first initialized or rebuilt. `help()` captures `memo = self._built[2] if self._built is not None else {}` before calling `self.parser()`; if `self._built` was `None`, `parser()` replaces it with a new tuple containing a new dict, but the subsequent `memo[key] = capped` writes to the local dict, leaving `self._built[2]` empty. In a fresh process, calling `_HERE.help(['ddflow', '--help'])` twice runs `parse_args` twice because the first result was never stored in the versioned memo, defeating the per-version help cache on the first chain (and after a version change).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:_InProcessHelp.help

chunk_findings.detail: `walk_all` builds chains for every in-process command inside one `try`, so a failure for one command aborts the whole eager walk and records the failure under a key that is not a valid command or verb chain when more than one in-process command is present. For example, with `commands=["ddflow", "ddflowx"]` and both names in the in-process set, if `_HERE.chains("ddflowx")` raises while `_HERE.chains("ddflow")` would succeed, the method stores `unavailable["ddflow ddflowx"] = "could not walk: ..."`, caches nothing for `ddflow`, and leaves no `unavailable` entry for `ddflowx` itself. Callers that look up the broken command by name or by its own chain will not see the failure, and the intended eager cache is silently skipped for the good command.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:walk_all

chunk_findings.detail: For a non-root chain whose help process runs but exits non-zero, the method caches `None` but records neither `unavailable` nor `_broken`. The class documents `unavailable` as “one note each (command or verb chain -> reason)”, yet `walk_all` only adds a non-zero-exit note when `len(key) == 1`. Given a registry chain `("ddflow", "docs", "check")` where `_HERE.help(["ddflow", "docs", "check", "--help"])` returns `ran=True, returncode=2`, `walk_all` sets `self._cache[("ddflow", "docs", "check")] = None` but leaves `unavailable` without `"ddflow docs check"`, so the reason that this verb chain could not be walked is lost.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:walk_all

chunk_findings.detail: The timeout test does not actually create a stalled help command. Given the command list `[sys.executable, "-c", "import time; time.sleep(30)", "--help"]`, CPython parses the trailing `--help` as an interpreter option (unless separated by `--`), so the subprocess prints Python usage and exits successfully before executing the `-c` code. Therefore `H.command_runner(_ROOT, 1, in_process_commands=())(stall)` returns a non-timeout capture with `returncode == 0`, and the assertion `done.timed_out and done.returncode is None` fails; the test exercises neither the timeout knob nor a stalled spawned tool.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_docs_check_speed.py:88-96

chunk_findings.detail: The memo fix moved `self.parser()` before the `try` block, so parser-construction failures are no longer converted into a `Captured` result. Previously `self.parser().parse_args(...)` was inside the outer `try` (and the inner `try` for `SystemExit`), so an exception raised while building the parser—e.g. a plugin import raising `ImportError`, a malformed registry entry raising `ValueError`, or a `SystemExit` during version detection—was returned as a failed capture and could be recorded as unavailable. Now `_HERE.help(["ddflow", "--help"])` propagates that exception, so a broken command can crash the docs-check gate instead of being noted as unavailable.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:_InProcessHelp.help

chunk_findings.detail: The earlier confirmed stdout/stderr capture issue still holds: the code still redirects process-global `sys.stdout`/`sys.stderr` while holding only `_RENDER_LOCK`. The diff only changes the comment to admit that foreign writers can be captured; it does not fence them or avoid global redirection. With the concurrency knob above one, if any other thread or logging handler in the same process writes to the standard streams while a render is active, that output is swallowed into the current chain’s `Captured.stdout/stderr`. For example, while thread A is inside `redirect_stdout(out)` rendering `ddflow --help`, thread B printing `--spam-flag-off` makes B’s output disappear from the terminal and appear in A’s help text, which can corrupt the docs-check finding set.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:_InProcessHelp.help

chunk_findings.detail: The assertion `idx.unavailable == {"ddflowx": "could not walk: no registry here"}` requires the real `ddflow` walk to contribute no unavailable entries. The implementation explicitly supports unavailable verb chains (the next test in the same file asserts that a deep non-zero chain is recorded under its own key), so any environment or registry state where a `ddflow` chain fails—e.g. `ddflow workflow state --help` exits non-zero—will put that chain into `idx.unavailable` as well. The test then fails even though the behavior being tested is correct: `ddflowx` was noted separately and `ddflow`’s walk still filled the cache.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_docs_check_speed.py:test_one_in_process_command_cannot_blanket_the_others

chunk_findings.detail: The new early `memo` lookup bypasses the version/rebuild check. `memo` is taken from `self._built` before `self.parser()` is called, and if the key is present the method returns immediately. Since `self.parser()` is the operation that detects a new tool version and replaces `self._built` with a new memo, a cached chain from version A is returned after the tool changes to version B, or after any state change that would require the parser to be rebuilt. For example, the first `_HERE.help(['ddflow', '--help'])` call caches the version-A help; if the version source then changes, the second call with the same argv returns the version-A `Captured` instead of rebuilding and reporting the new help or a build error, producing stale findings and hiding a newly broken registry.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:_InProcessHelp.help

chunk_findings.detail: The `threading.active_count() > 1` gate over-refuses whenever the help walk is actually concurrent. If the concurrency knob runs `_HERE.help` on worker threads, then as soon as more than one worker thread is alive, every in-process render reaches the gate and returns `Captured(error=RuntimeError(...))`, even though no other thread wrote to stdio. Given `concurrency=2`, a worker thread calling `_HERE.help(['ddflow', '--help'])` sees `threading.active_count()` equal to at least 2 and discards a clean capture, so the in-process walk cannot return ddflow help while the knob is above one; it records unavailable or falls back to the spawning path the change was meant to avoid.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:_InProcessHelp.help

chunk_findings.detail: The same gate under-refuses threads that exit during the render. It calls `threading.active_count()` only after the redirected render has finished, so a background thread that writes to `sys.stdout` while the redirect is active and then exits before the count is taken is invisible. For example, while the main thread is inside `_HERE.help`, another thread starts, prints `--phantom-flag` to stdout during the argparse render, and exits before the render returns; `threading.active_count()` then returns 1, so the mixed capture containing the phantom flag is returned and cached, exactly the failure the comment says is prevented.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:_InProcessHelp.help

chunk_findings.detail: The new test does not actually prove that foreign writers are fenced; it only proves that phantom text is not *returned as ddflow’s output* when `capped.ran` is true. In the “refused” path described by the test comment, `_InProcessHelp.help` has already redirected process-global `sys.stdout`/`sys.stderr` and run the render; any `print` from `spammer` during that window is written into the render’s captured `StringIO`, and the refusal discards that `StringIO`. The test then stops the thread and skips its only assertion because `capped.ran` is false, so it passes even though the spammer’s bytes were silently swallowed instead of reaching the real stdout/stderr. In a real run, a concurrent progress `print` or logging handler writing to `sys.stdout` while an in-process help render is active can therefore lose its output; the test should force at least one foreign write inside the redirect window and assert that the write is either not captured or is forwarded to the real streams.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_docs_check_speed.py:test_a_render_shared_with_another_thread_is_never_returned_mixed

chunk_findings.detail: The version check and the memo binding are not atomic, so the “never serve another version’s replay” fix is still wrong under the supported concurrency knob. `parser = self.parser()` can return a parser built for version A; before the next statement reads `self._built[2]`, another thread can call `parser()`, detect version B, and replace `self._built` with B’s parser and empty memo. The first thread then binds B’s memo, misses the key, renders with A’s parser, and stores A’s help into B’s memo. A later call for the same chain sees version B, binds B’s memo, and returns A’s help. The interleaving is: thread A `parser()` returns A-parser; thread B `parser()` rebuilds to B and replaces `_built`; thread A `memo = self._built[2]` gets B’s memo; thread A runs the A-parser and caches A’s output under B. This is a concrete stale-version finding-set corruption whenever a version change is observed by another concurrent help call.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:_InProcessHelp.help

chunk_findings.detail: `_RoutedTo` replaces `sys.stdout`/`sys.stderr` during a render but implements only `write` and `flush`. Any code executed inside the render that introspects the stream now fails with `AttributeError`: for example, `sys.stdout.isatty()` for TTY/color detection raises instead of returning `False`, and `sys.stdout.fileno()` inside an `except OSError` block raises `AttributeError` instead of the `UnsupportedOperation`/`OSError` that the previous `io.StringIO` capture produced. Given a verb whose help code checks `sys.stdout.isatty()`, the in-process render aborts instead of producing help.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:_RoutedTo

chunk_findings.detail: The test starts a non-daemon thread that blocks on `letgo.wait()` with no timeout and does not release it if setup fails. If the `with redirect_stdout(H._RoutedTo(real, sink, threading.get_ident())):` setup raises before `letgo.set()` is reached (for example, `_RoutedTo` is removed or its constructor fails), the foreign thread remains blocked forever; because it is non-daemon, Python/pytest waits for it at shutdown and the test suite hangs instead of failing cleanly.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_docs_check_speed.py:test_a_render_never_serves_a_mix_of_a_foreign_threads_print

chunk_findings.detail: This is the earlier finding still unresolved: `_ddflow_help_verbs` treats any `python`-like program plus `-m ddflow` as naming this ddflow, even when the interpreter is a slash-spelled binary from another environment. Given a docs command `/other/venv/bin/python -m ddflow gate --help`, `_is_a_python("/other/venv/bin/python")` returns true and `argv[1:3] == ["-m", "ddflow"]`, so `_ddflow_help_verbs` returns `["gate"]` and `command_runner.run` calls `in_process(["gate"])`, replaying the current process's parser. If the other venv’s `ddflow` lacks `gate` or exposes different flags, the spawned walk would exit non-zero / report different help, but the in-process replay can exit 0 / report the current parser’s flags, producing a false pass or false fail. The added `_is_a_python` does not check that the interpreter is the current interpreter or that `ddflow` resolves to the hosting package, so it does not answer the earlier finding.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:_ddflow_help_verbs

chunk_findings.detail: The assertion `assert not any("ddflow" in c for c in spawned_calls)` does not prove “nothing spawned for a ddflow mention”; for a list `c`, `"ddflow" in c` is exact-element membership, not substring/basename matching. If `D.check_docs` or command resolution passes a path-spelled ddflow argv to the runner—e.g. `["/venv/bin/ddflow", "gate", "skip", "--help"]` or `["ddflow.exe", ...]`—the assertion passes even though the ddflow help walk spawned, and `test_every_way_of_spelling_this_ddflow_is_replayed_not_spawned` at lines 78-80 explicitly shows such a path-spelled argv is expected to be spawned by `H.command_runner`. Thus the new test still fails to guard the regression reported earlier: a ddflow mention can spawn via a path spelling while the test still reports success.

chunk_findings.detail: The in-process helper is ddflow-only, but its public methods accept an arbitrary command name/`argv[0]` and silently ignore it. `_require_walk` returns the root parser for any one-element chain, and `help()` caches on `tuple(argv[1:])`. Given the in-process knob containing a non-ddflow command, e.g. `_HERE.chains("ddflowx")`, the method yields ddflow’s verb chains prefixed by `ddflowx`; `_HERE.help(["ddflowx", "--help"])` parses `["--help"]` against ddflow’s parser and returns ddflow root help. The memo key also collides with `["ddflow", "--help"]`, so the first cached ddflow help is served for the other command. This silently produces the wrong finding set for any non-ddflow command routed through the in-process path.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:_InProcessHelp.chains/help

chunk_findings.detail: The `SystemExit` replay maps `SystemExit(None)` to returncode `1`: `code = exc.code if isinstance(exc.code, int) else 1`. A spawned process exits `0` when `sys.exit()` is called with no code. Given a verb whose custom help/action calls `sys.exit()` after printing help, `_HERE.help(["ddflow", "verb", "--help"])` returns a non-zero capture, so the chain is treated as failed/unavailable even though the real command succeeded.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:_InProcessHelp.help

chunk_findings.detail: `memo[key] = capped` is performed outside the `with _RENDER_LOCK:` block, despite the comment claiming build-to-cache is one critical section. With the concurrency knob above one and an uncached chain, thread A can render, release the lock, and be descheduled before the cache write; thread B then acquires the lock, sees the memo still missing, and renders the same chain again. This breaks the “replayed once per chain then cached” behavior and can duplicate side effects of `parse_args` under concurrency.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:_InProcessHelp.help

chunk_findings.detail: `walk_all` promises that “a broken command notes itself and stops only ITS OWN walk,” but the try around `_HERE.chains(cmd)` catches only `Exception`. The same code path can raise `SystemExit` (the earlier review already accepted `SystemExit` from registry/version detection as a build failure). Given a registry whose build calls `sys.exit(2)`, constructing `HelpIndex` with an in-process command enters `walk_all`, the `except Exception` misses `SystemExit`, and the exception propagates out of `__init__`, crashing the docs check instead of recording `unavailable[cmd] = "could not walk: ..."`. The per-command try added for the earlier “one broken command aborts the whole walk” finding does not answer this case because it did not broaden the caught exception type.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:walk_all

chunk_findings.detail: `idx.unavailable == {}` requires the real `ddflow` registry walk to have zero unavailable chains. The implementation (and `test_a_verb_chain_that_exits_nonzero_is_noted_chain_by_chain`) deliberately records unavailable entries for any verb chain whose help exits non-zero, so if any legitimate chain fails in the test environment — for example a plugin or config-dependent chain such as `ddflow workflow state --help` exiting 2 — `walk_all` adds that chain to `idx.unavailable` and the speed test fails even though the in-process walk is fast and behaving as specified. This is the same over-strict exact-unavailable assumption that was fixed in `test_one_in_process_command_cannot_blanket_the_others`; this test still couples the speed regression to the whole tree being perfectly healthy.

chunk_findings.detail: The returned runner is no longer safe for concurrent use because `in_process` replaces the process-wide `sys.stdout` and `sys.stderr` while parsing. If two `command_runner(...)` calls overlap, one call’s `parse_args` output can be captured into another call’s `Captured.out`/`err`. For example, thread A calls `runner(["ddflow", "gate", "--help"])` while thread B calls `runner(["ddflow", "bug", "--help"])`; because `contextlib.redirect_stdout(out)` is global and not atomic, A’s help text may be written into B’s `StringIO` and vice versa, so the docs check can see flags from the wrong verb (or unrelated stdout writes) and pass/fail the wrong mention. The previous `P.capture` path used subprocess pipes and did not have this cross-thread capture problem.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:in_process

chunk_findings.detail: The assertions meant to prove that the `check_docs` walk never spawns ddflow only inspect `argv[0]`. If the walk still calls `P.capture` with the current interpreter spelling, e.g. `[sys.executable, "-m", "ddflow", "gate", "skip", "--help"]` (or `["ddflow.exe", ...]` on Windows), the three checks pass: `c[0].endswith("/ddflow")` is false, `c[0] == "ddflow"` is false, and `c[0] != "ddflow" and "/ddflow" not in c[0]` is true. Thus a regression that still spawns ddflow help—while perhaps still using the in-process result for checking—can pass this test even though the stated goal is that a ddflow mention spawns nothing. The test should inspect the full argv (e.g. reject any `*-m ddflow` or basename `ddflow`/`ddflow.exe`) or assert that the only spawned call is the `nix` chain.

chunk_findings.detail: The new runner routes any command named in `in_process_commands` to `_HERE.help` whenever the argv ends in `--help`, even though `_HERE` is the ddflow-only in-process helper. The earlier fix to `_HERE.chains`/`walk_all` does not cover this path: `run()` calls `_HERE.help(argv)` directly and has no check that the command is the registry’s own prog, no fallback to `spawn`, and no conversion to a failed capture. For example, `runner = command_runner(root, 1, in_process_commands=["ddflow-mcp"]); runner(["ddflow-mcp", "--help"])` will not spawn `ddflow-mcp`; it will invoke the ddflow helper. If `_HERE.help` still parses `argv[1:]` against ddflow’s parser, the check silently receives ddflow’s root help for a different tool; if `_HERE.help` was hardened to raise, the runner raises instead of returning `P.Captured`/a note, breaking the runner contract and the “missing/unavailable tool is a note” behavior.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:command_runner

chunk_findings.detail: The earlier fix only guarded `chains`; `help` still ignores `argv[0]` and caches on `tuple(argv[1:])`. Given `_HERE.help(["ddflowx", "--help"])`, the method parses `["--help"]` against ddflow’s root parser and returns ddflow’s root help, caching it under `("--help",)`. A non-ddflow command routed directly to this helper (or any future `walk_all` path that calls `help` without first going through the guarded `chains`) is therefore answered with ddflow’s tree, which is the exact behavior the confirmed finding reported.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:_InProcessHelp.help

chunk_findings.detail: It returns the `choices` of the first `_SubParsersAction` found in `parser._actions`. Argparse allows multiple subparsers actions on one parser; given a root parser with `sub1.add_parser("a")` and `sub2.add_parser("b")`, `chains("ddflow")` yields only `["ddflow", "a"]` and never `["ddflow", "b"]`. Docs check then silently omits every verb/flag from the second subparser table, so the “declared command registry already knows every verb” premise is wrong for parsers with more than one subparsers action.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:_subcommands

chunk_findings.detail: `_RoutedTo` unconditionally reads `real.fileno` (and `real.isatty`) when wrapping `sys.stdout`/`sys.stderr`. If the process’s stdout or stderr is a plain `StringIO` or any stream object without `fileno` (common when another tool or test replaces `sys.stdout`), constructing `_RoutedTo` raises `AttributeError`; in `_InProcessHelp.help` that exception is caught by the outer `except Exception` and turned into `Captured(error=...)`. Thus every in-process help chain is marked failed/unavailable even though spawning `ddflow --help` would have succeeded.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:_RoutedTo.__init__

chunk_findings.detail: The method does not faithfully reproduce stderr for non-argparse exits. For zero exit it returns `Captured(0, out.getvalue() or err.getvalue(), "")`, so a custom help action that prints `--foo` to stdout and `--bar` to stderr and exits 0 loses `--bar` from the capture. Likewise, if a custom action calls `sys.exit("bad help")`, the method maps the exit to returncode 1 but leaves stderr empty, whereas the spawned process would print `"bad help"` to stderr. Both inputs make the in-process capture differ from the spawn the method claims to replay.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:_InProcessHelp.help

chunk_findings.detail: The test times `idx.walk_all()` only after `H.HelpIndex(...)` has already been constructed, but the rest of the file treats construction as performing the walk (`test_one_in_process_command_cannot_blanket_the_others` and `test_a_verb_chain_that_exits_nonzero_is_noted_chain_by_chain` assert `idx.unavailable` / `idx._cache` immediately after construction without calling `walk_all`). Given a regression where the help walk again spawns once per verb chain, the constructor can spend minutes walking the tree; the timed `idx.walk_all()` then returns the already-built/cached chain set and can easily be `< 10` seconds. Thus the intended cold-walk speed regression can pass while the actual walk is still too slow.

chunk_findings.detail: The `_capture_lock` only serializes calls to `in_process`; it does not make replacing the process-wide `sys.stdout`/`sys.stderr` safe against unrelated writers. While `in_process` holds the lock and redirects the streams, any other thread (logging, progress output, a background ACP handler, etc.) that writes to `sys.stdout`/`sys.stderr` has that output captured into this run’s `Captured.out`/`err`. For example, during a docs-help walk, a background thread can log `--foo` while `_parser.parse_args(['gate', '--help'])` is running; `help_flags` then sees `--foo` and the check can falsely believe that flag exists, or the help text can otherwise be corrupted. The prior lock fix does not answer this because the interfering thread does not call `in_process` and therefore does not acquire `_capture_lock`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:in_process

chunk_findings.detail: `in_process` bypasses the normal captured subprocess path but only catches `SystemExit`. If the deferred `build_parser()` import fails, or if parsing raises a non-`SystemExit` exception (for example a custom argparse action raising `ValueError`, or `argparse` configured with `exit_on_error=False` raising `ArgumentError`), the exception propagates out of `command_runner.run` and aborts `check_docs`. This violates the module’s stated behavior that a tool that cannot run should become a note rather than a passed/failed flag check. A concrete failing environment is one where `ddflow.surfaces.cli` raises `ImportError` because an optional CLI dependency is missing: the old runner would call `P.capture` and receive a non-zero/missing-tool captured result, while the new code crashes the docs check.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:in_process

chunk_findings.detail: The test explicitly requires a path-spelled `ddflow` invocation to keep spawning: it calls `H.command_runner(ROOT, 60)(["/venv/bin/ddflow", "gate", "--help"])`, asserts `not path_spelled.ran`, and asserts `spawned_calls == [["/venv/bin/ddflow", "gate", "--help"]]`. In the common virtualenv layout where the test interpreter is `/venv/bin/python` and the package under test provides the console script `/venv/bin/ddflow`, that path is this ddflow, not a non-ddflow tool. The stated intent is that only non-ddflow tools keep spawning, and the prior triage treats path-spelled ddflow spawns as the regression to prevent. This test therefore pins the wrong behavior: if `command_runner` correctly resolves `/venv/bin/ddflow` to the current ddflow and replays it in-process, the assertion fails; if it continues to spawn the slow ddflow help, the test passes. Because the path is hardcoded rather than derived from `sys.executable`, the test also fails to cover the path spelling of the *current* ddflow on environments where the venv is not literally `/venv`.

chunk_findings.detail: `run` treats any argv whose first element is the literal string `"ddflow"` as “this process”, so it never runs that argv in `root` and never uses `timeout_s`. Given a docs check invoked by one ddflow install on a repo whose `ddflow` executable resolved from `root`/`PATH` is a different install (or is absent), a docs line such as `ddflow gate skip --reason x --help` yields argv `["ddflow", "gate", "skip", "--reason", "x", "--help"]`; `_ddflow_help_verbs` returns the verbs, `run` calls `in_process`, and the docs check validates the command against the checking process’s parser. It can therefore accept `--reason` when the repo’s actual `ddflow` has no such flag (or pass a command whose executable is missing), contrary to the runner contract that argv naming another tool is run in `root`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:command_runner.run / _ddflow_help_verbs

chunk_findings.detail: In the `BOGUS_CHAINS` loop, the assertions accept “the command did not run” as “the command refused the invalid verb.” If both the spawned subprocess and `H.in_process` fail with an error/timeout capture (e.g. `P.capture` returns a `Captured` with an error and a non-zero or missing return code, and `H.in_process` also returns an error capture), then `inproc.ran == real.ran` can be true, `inproc.returncode != 0 and real.returncode != 0` can be true for an error return code such as `None`/timeout code, and the `help_flags` comparison can pass if both outputs are empty or otherwise equal. The test then passes without demonstrating that either the spawned CLI or the in-process walk actually rejected the invalid verb. It should require that both actually ran and returned an integer non-zero exit code.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_docscheck_help_in_process.py:test_the_in_process_help_flags_match_the_spawned_walk

chunk_findings.detail: This test infers that the second run is blocked on `H._capture_lock` merely from `t.join(timeout=5)` leaving the thread alive. If `H.in_process` does not acquire `_capture_lock` (or acquires a different lock) but is simply slow, the test can still pass. For example, if `H.in_process(["gate"])` takes about 6 seconds without using `_capture_lock`, the first `join(timeout=5)` returns with the thread alive, the test releases the held lock, the second `join(timeout=5)` then succeeds, and the final assertions pass even though there was no serialization. The test should verify lock acquisition/serialization directly rather than using a timeout as a proxy.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_docscheck_help_in_process.py:test_in_process_serializes_overlapping_runs

chunk_findings.detail: The new runner routes any command named in `in_process_commands` to `_HERE.help` whenever the argv ends in `--help`, even though `_HERE` is the ddflow-only in-process helper. The earlier fix to `_HERE.chains`/`walk_all` does not cover this path: `run()` calls `_HERE.help(argv)` directly and has no check that the command is the registry’s own prog, no fallback to `spawn`, and no conversion to a failed capture. For example, `runner = command_runner(root, 1, in_process_commands=["ddflow-mcp"]); runner(["ddflow-mcp", "--help"])` will not spawn `ddflow-mcp`; it will invoke the ddflow helper. If `_HERE.help` still parses `argv[1:]` against ddflow’s parser, the check silently receives ddflow’s root help for a different tool; if `_HERE.help` was hardened to raise, the runner raises instead of returning `P.Captured`/a note, breaking the runner contract and the “missing/unavailable tool is a note” behavior.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:command_runner

chunk_findings.detail: The earlier fix only guarded `chains`; `help` still ignores `argv[0]` and caches on `tuple(argv[1:])`. Given `_HERE.help(["ddflowx", "--help"])`, the method parses `["--help"]` against ddflow’s root parser and returns ddflow’s root help, caching it under `("--help",)`. A non-ddflow command routed directly to this helper (or any future `walk_all` path that calls `help` without first going through the guarded `chains`) is therefore answered with ddflow’s tree, which is the exact behavior the confirmed finding reported.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:_InProcessHelp.help

chunk_findings.detail: It returns the `choices` of the first `_SubParsersAction` found in `parser._actions`. Argparse allows multiple subparsers actions on one parser; given a root parser with `sub1.add_parser("a")` and `sub2.add_parser("b")`, `chains("ddflow")` yields only `["ddflow", "a"]` and never `["ddflow", "b"]`. Docs check then silently omits every verb/flag from the second subparser table, so the “declared command registry already knows every verb” premise is wrong for parsers with more than one subparsers action.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:_subcommands

chunk_findings.detail: `_RoutedTo` unconditionally reads `real.fileno` (and `real.isatty`) when wrapping `sys.stdout`/`sys.stderr`. If the process’s stdout or stderr is a plain `StringIO` or any stream object without `fileno` (common when another tool or test replaces `sys.stdout`), constructing `_RoutedTo` raises `AttributeError`; in `_InProcessHelp.help` that exception is caught by the outer `except Exception` and turned into `Captured(error=...)`. Thus every in-process help chain is marked failed/unavailable even though spawning `ddflow --help` would have succeeded.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:_RoutedTo.__init__

chunk_findings.detail: The method does not faithfully reproduce stderr for non-argparse exits. For zero exit it returns `Captured(0, out.getvalue() or err.getvalue(), "")`, so a custom help action that prints `--foo` to stdout and `--bar` to stderr and exits 0 loses `--bar` from the capture. Likewise, if a custom action calls `sys.exit("bad help")`, the method maps the exit to returncode 1 but leaves stderr empty, whereas the spawned process would print `"bad help"` to stderr. Both inputs make the in-process capture differ from the spawn the method claims to replay.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:_InProcessHelp.help

chunk_findings.detail: The test times `idx.walk_all()` only after `H.HelpIndex(...)` has already been constructed, but the rest of the file treats construction as performing the walk (`test_one_in_process_command_cannot_blanket_the_others` and `test_a_verb_chain_that_exits_nonzero_is_noted_chain_by_chain` assert `idx.unavailable` / `idx._cache` immediately after construction without calling `walk_all`). Given a regression where the help walk again spawns once per verb chain, the constructor can spend minutes walking the tree; the timed `idx.walk_all()` then returns the already-built/cached chain set and can easily be `< 10` seconds. Thus the intended cold-walk speed regression can pass while the actual walk is still too slow.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_docs_check_speed.py:test_the_ddflow_help_walk_is_in_process_and_under_ten_seconds

chunk_findings.detail: [r-lock-cycle-selfheal] The change adds a blocking polling wait: it imports `sleep`, defines `_POLL_S = 5.0`, and documents that `wait_job` polls `roborev list --json` in a loop. The project rule says agents never poll-wait or hold while waiting; in the stated standards-gate use, an agent invoking this helper would sleep/hold in a loop instead of adding needs edges or otherwise letting ddflow heal the wait, which is the behavior this rule exists to prevent.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/roborev.py: sleep/_POLL_S/wait_job polling

chunk_findings.detail: After `sleep(min(_POLL_S, left))`, the loop restarts and calls `_read_list()` before any deadline check. `left` was set to `deadline - monotonic()`, so the sleep ends at or after `deadline`; the subsequent `_read_list` consumes additional time (bounded only by `_TIMEOUT_S`). This can make `wait_job` block for `wait_s + _TIMEOUT_S`, not “up to wait_s seconds.” Example: `wait_s=5`, `_POLL_S=0.1`; at `t=4.9` it sleeps `0.1` and wakes at `t=5.0`, then `_read_list` hangs for 30 s; `wait_job` returns `live` at `t=35`. It should re-check `monotonic() >= deadline` before the next `_read_list` when `wait_s > 0`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/roborev.py:wait_job

chunk_findings.detail: The fallback note expression `f"{w.error or 'timed out' or f'exit {w.returncode}'}"` is broken: because `'timed out'` is truthy, the `f'exit {w.returncode}'` arm is unreachable. When `roborev wait --job N` exits with code 3 and `w.error` is `None`/`w.timed_out` is `False`, the returned note says “timed out” even though it did not time out, hiding the real exit code from the operator.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/roborev.py:_done

chunk_findings.detail: The new `wait_job` function polls `roborev list --json` in a loop until a bound (as exercised by `tests/test_roborev_wait.py::test_the_trap_primitives_are_never_called_while_the_list_says_queued`, which asserts repeated `list` calls). This is a poll-wait inside ddflow and directly violates [r-lock-cycle-selfheal]: “agents never poll-wait or hold while waiting.” A queued job makes `ddflow gate run standards` block for the configured bound (observed 10+ minutes), recreating the blockage/circular-wait situation the rule requires ddflow to resolve by adding needs edges, not by holding.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/roborev.py:wait_job

data.probe: Advisory rule names ddflow's ITEM waits (its remedy: needs edges between queue items); a roborev daemon job is an external queue, no item id exists to edge. wait_job is bounded by standards_wait_s, re-news the caller's lease via on_tick each poll, and returns a live verdict at the bound: a bounded returning wait, not a hold. The item body is the operator's direction to wrap the wait with a bound + lease renewal.

chunk_findings.detail: [r-lock-cycle-selfheal] The change adds a blocking polling wait: it imports `sleep`, defines `_POLL_S = 5.0`, and documents that `wait_job` polls `roborev list --json` in a loop. The project rule says agents never poll-wait or hold while waiting; in the stated standards-gate use, an agent invoking this helper would sleep/hold in a loop instead of adding needs edges or otherwise letting ddflow heal the wait, which is the behavior this rule exists to prevent.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/roborev.py: sleep/_POLL_S/wait_job polling

chunk_findings.detail: After `sleep(min(_POLL_S, left))`, the loop restarts and calls `_read_list()` before any deadline check. `left` was set to `deadline - monotonic()`, so the sleep ends at or after `deadline`; the subsequent `_read_list` consumes additional time (bounded only by `_TIMEOUT_S`). This can make `wait_job` block for `wait_s + _TIMEOUT_S`, not “up to wait_s seconds.” Example: `wait_s=5`, `_POLL_S=0.1`; at `t=4.9` it sleeps `0.1` and wakes at `t=5.0`, then `_read_list` hangs for 30 s; `wait_job` returns `live` at `t=35`. It should re-check `monotonic() >= deadline` before the next `_read_list` when `wait_s > 0`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/roborev.py:wait_job

chunk_findings.detail: The fallback note expression `f"{w.error or 'timed out' or f'exit {w.returncode}'}"` is broken: because `'timed out'` is truthy, the `f'exit {w.returncode}'` arm is unreachable. When `roborev wait --job N` exits with code 3 and `w.error` is `None`/`w.timed_out` is `False`, the returned note says “timed out” even though it did not time out, hiding the real exit code from the operator.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/roborev.py:_done

chunk_findings.detail: The new `wait_job` function polls `roborev list --json` in a loop until a bound (as exercised by `tests/test_roborev_wait.py::test_the_trap_primitives_are_never_called_while_the_list_says_queued`, which asserts repeated `list` calls). This is a poll-wait inside ddflow and directly violates [r-lock-cycle-selfheal]: “agents never poll-wait or hold while waiting.” A queued job makes `ddflow gate run standards` block for the configured bound (observed 10+ minutes), recreating the blockage/circular-wait situation the rule requires ddflow to resolve by adding needs edges, not by holding.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/roborev.py:wait_job

chunk_findings.detail: When `[agent].family` / `DDFLOW_AGENT_FAMILY` is configured but the agent’s latest session has already recorded a model id, `_author_model` still returns that session model before it ever considers the configured family (`if found: return found, "session"`). For example, with `DDFLOW_AGENT_FAMILY=deepseek`, a session model of `deepseek-chat`, and no `--model`, `_author_model` returns `("deepseek-chat", "session")`, so `family_only` is false and both the returned `base` and the completion event record `author_model: "deepseek-chat"`. That writes the exact model id into the committed event log / commit evidence even though an author family was configured, contrary to the stated requirement that a configured family be stored as `author_family` only and that `complete` no longer need to write a model id.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/complete.py:_author_model

chunk_findings.detail: `reviewer_independence` calls `router_set(author_model, cfg.agent.routers)` before deciding whether `author_model` is a configured family, and then forces `author_fam` to `""` whenever `routed` is not `None`. With `[agent].family = "deepseek"` (so `cfg.agent.families` contains `deepseek`) and `[agent].routers = {"deepseek": ["other"]}`, `author_model="deepseek"` makes `router_set` return `["other"]`, so the new `family_name_of` branch is skipped and `author_fam` is empty. A review evidence `model="deepseek-chat"` is resolved by `_reviewer_fams` to family `deepseek`; because `author_fam` is empty and `deepseek` is not in `routed`, the author-family rejection cannot fire. Thus a configured author family can be bypassed by a router key collision, contrary to the change's intent that `[agent].family` is the author's identity. If the router entry is empty (`{"deepseek": []}`), the same input instead returns the router error rather than using the family.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/gates/reviewers.py:150

chunk_findings.detail: The CLI integration tests do not isolate the documented `DDFLOW_AGENT_FAMILY` environment knob. `test_agent_family_is_a_knob_with_env_and_default_off` shows that this environment variable is a supported source for the author family, but `_done` and `test_gate_record_refuses_the_configured_family_without_a_session_model` run `ddflow` with whatever environment the test runner has. For example, if `DDFLOW_AGENT_FAMILY=alibaba` is set, `test_complete_with_a_configured_family_records_the_family_only` writes `agent.family=deepseek` but the CLI may resolve the author family from the environment, so the completion event records `alibaba` (or a non-`config` source) and the assertion `data.get("author_family") == "deepseek"` fails. Likewise, the gate-record test expects a refusal because the configured author family is `deepseek`, but an inherited `DDFLOW_AGENT_FAMILY=alibaba` would make the first `--model deepseek` command independent and cause `assert code == REFUSED` to fail. These tests should clear the variable (or otherwise pass a controlled environment) before invoking the CLI.

chunk_findings.detail: The change adds `from time import sleep` and `_POLL_S = 5.0`, and its module docstring explicitly says `wait_job` polls `roborev list --json` in a loop. This is a poll-wait/hold inside ddflow and violates [r-lock-cycle-selfheal] (“agents never poll-wait or hold while waiting”). The prior refutation does not answer it: the fact that a roborev daemon job is an external queue with no ddflow item id only explains why a needs edge cannot be created here; it does not make a bounded `sleep` loop not a poll-wait. A standards gate run that calls this helper on a queued job still holds the agent for the configured bound, which is the blockage the rule exists to prevent.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/roborev.py:_POLL_S

chunk_findings.detail: When `_read_list` reports `status == "done"`, `wait_job` calls `_done` without checking the remaining `deadline` and without calling `on_tick`. `_done` then runs `proc.capture([exe, "wait", ...], timeout=_TIMEOUT_S)` and `proc.capture([exe, "show", ...], timeout=_TIMEOUT_S)` sequentially. Given `wait_s=1` and a job whose `roborev wait`/`show` commands hang, `wait_job` returns after as much as `2*_TIMEOUT_S` seconds (e.g. 60s), not “up to wait_s seconds,” and the caller’s lease is not renewed on this path, defeating the bound and lease-renewal purpose for the standards-gate wait.

chunk_findings.detail: The test’s name and docstring promise that `wait_job(repo, 7, 0)` reads the status once and reports it live, but it never inspects `log`. With the fake clock returning an additional second on each `monotonic` call, a `wait_job` implementation that checks the bound at the top of the loop returns `live=True` before ever invoking `_read_list`, so the test passes even if no status read occurs. It therefore does not enforce the behavior it is named for.

chunk_findings.detail: When `[agent].family` / `DDFLOW_AGENT_FAMILY` is configured but the agent’s latest session has already recorded a model id, `_author_model` still returns that session model before it ever considers the configured family (`if found: return found, "session"`). For example, with `DDFLOW_AGENT_FAMILY=deepseek`, a session model of `deepseek-chat`, and no `--model`, `_author_model` returns `("deepseek-chat", "session")`, so `family_only` is false and both the returned `base` and the completion event record `author_model: "deepseek-chat"`. That writes the exact model id into the committed event log / commit evidence even though an author family was configured, contrary to the stated requirement that a configured family be stored as `author_family` only and that `complete` no longer need to write a model id.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/complete.py:_author_model

chunk_findings.detail: `reviewer_independence` calls `router_set(author_model, cfg.agent.routers)` before deciding whether `author_model` is a configured family, and then forces `author_fam` to `""` whenever `routed` is not `None`. With `[agent].family = "deepseek"` (so `cfg.agent.families` contains `deepseek`) and `[agent].routers = {"deepseek": ["other"]}`, `author_model="deepseek"` makes `router_set` return `["other"]`, so the new `family_name_of` branch is skipped and `author_fam` is empty. A review evidence `model="deepseek-chat"` is resolved by `_reviewer_fams` to family `deepseek`; because `author_fam` is empty and `deepseek` is not in `routed`, the author-family rejection cannot fire. Thus a configured author family can be bypassed by a router key collision, contrary to the change's intent that `[agent].family` is the author's identity. If the router entry is empty (`{"deepseek": []}`), the same input instead returns the router error rather than using the family.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/gates/reviewers.py:150

chunk_findings.detail: The CLI integration tests do not isolate the documented `DDFLOW_AGENT_FAMILY` environment knob. `test_agent_family_is_a_knob_with_env_and_default_off` shows that this environment variable is a supported source for the author family, but `_done` and `test_gate_record_refuses_the_configured_family_without_a_session_model` run `ddflow` with whatever environment the test runner has. For example, if `DDFLOW_AGENT_FAMILY=alibaba` is set, `test_complete_with_a_configured_family_records_the_family_only` writes `agent.family=deepseek` but the CLI may resolve the author family from the environment, so the completion event records `alibaba` (or a non-`config` source) and the assertion `data.get("author_family") == "deepseek"` fails. Likewise, the gate-record test expects a refusal because the configured author family is `deepseek`, but an inherited `DDFLOW_AGENT_FAMILY=alibaba` would make the first `--model deepseek` command independent and cause `assert code == REFUSED` to fail. These tests should clear the variable (or otherwise pass a controlled environment) before invoking the CLI.

chunk_findings.detail: The refusal check treats any non-`None` `routed` value as a usable author identity, but it does not require that value to be non-empty. If `[agent].routers` maps the author model to an empty family list (for example `[agent].routers = {"author-model": []}`), `_author_identity` can return `routed=[]` and `author_fam=""`. `_author_no_identity_refusal` then sees `routed is not None`, returns no refusal, and `reviewer_independence` proceeds as if the author’s family set is known and empty. A reviewer from any family, including one that is actually the same unknown author family, will therefore be counted as independent even though the author’s pretraining family was never established.

chunk_findings.detail: The new regression test intended to prove that a session-declared model id does not reach the completion log only asserts that `author_model` is absent; it omits the `assert "model" not in data` guard used by the adjacent completion tests. chunk_findings.detail: Changing `ruff-check` and `ruff-format` to `pass_filenames: true` makes Ruff receive explicit file paths. Ruff, by default, checks explicitly supplied paths even if they match `exclude`/`extend-exclude` or `.gitignore`; the previous `ruff check .` / `ruff format --check .` respected the project’s Ruff exclusion configuration. With this change, if the repository has any intentionally excluded Python file (for example generated `*_pb2.py`, vendored code, or migrations containing an unused import), a diff-scoped run or `pre-commit run --all-files` that passes that path to `uv run ruff check` will now report the error and fail the push/CI, whereas it was skipped before. The same applies to `ruff format --check` at `.pre-commit-config.yaml:44`. Add `--force-exclude` to both entries (or otherwise filter excluded paths) to preserve the previous semantics.
chunk_findings.title: .pre-commit-config.yaml:38

chunk_findings.detail: `scope_to_diff` validates `since` with `W.rev(tree, since)` but then interpolates the original `since` directly into the shell command string: `command.replace(" --all-files", f" --from-ref {since} --to-ref HEAD", 1)`. If `since` is a ref name containing shell metacharacters (for example a Git ref such as `foo$(touch /tmp/pwn)` or `foo;touch /tmp/pwn`, which can be valid ref names), `W.rev` can resolve it, so the function returns a command like `pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --from-ref foo$(touch /tmp/pwn) --to-ref HEAD`. When the CI runner executes that command through a shell (as the surrounding command forms, including `SKIP=` prefixes and the previous `rc=0; ...; exit $rc` pattern, require), the shell expands/executes the injected content on the CI machine. The safe value is the commit hash returned by `W.rev`, or the ref must be quoted with `shlex.quote` before interpolation.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:scope_to_diff

chunk_findings.detail:
The test’s lint hook swallows non-“BAD found” grep failures. `SCRIPT` is `#!/bin/sh
if grep -q BAD "$@"; then exit 1; fi
exit 0
`, so it only exits 1 when `grep` exits 0 (marker found). If `grep` exits 2 because a passed file is missing/unreadable, or exits 127 because `grep` is not available, or misparses a filename beginning with `-` as an option, the `if` condition is false and the script falls through to `exit 0`. For example, `scripts/lint.sh deleted.py` returns 0 even though it could not check the file; a diff-scoped pre-commit run that passes a deleted or oddly named file could therefore see the hook “pass” when it did not actually lint the input.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_ci_diff_scope.py:SCRIPT

chunk_findings.detail: Changing these hooks to `pass_filenames: true` makes ruff receive explicit file paths instead of `.`. Ruff does not apply its `exclude`/`extend-exclude` patterns to explicitly passed paths unless `--force-exclude` is supplied. The new entries (`uv run ruff check` and `uv run ruff format --check`) omit that flag. Thus, if the repository’s ruff configuration excludes a tracked Python path (e.g. `[tool.ruff] exclude = ["ddflow/_vendor"]`) and a branch modifies a file under that path, pre-commit will pass it explicitly to ruff and ruff will lint/format-check it, potentially failing the push even though the previous `ruff check .` / `ruff format --check .` invocation would have skipped the excluded file.
chunk_findings.title: .pre-commit-config.yaml:ruff-check

chunk_findings.detail: The new scoping drops the environment’s `SKIP` whenever the command already carries its own leading `SKIP=` assignment. The removed implementation explicitly merged the inherited `SKIP` with the command’s own skip (`SKIP="${SKIP:+$SKIP,}..."`), because a shell command-prefix assignment overrides the inherited environment. Now, given environment `SKIP=slow-tests` and `command="SKIP=lint pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --all-files"` with a valid `since`, `scope_to_diff` returns `SKIP=lint pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --from-ref <since> --to-ref HEAD`. When run through the shell, `SKIP` is exactly `lint`, so the `slow-tests` hook is not skipped even though the selected-tests plan set it; the old behavior would have skipped both `slow-tests` and `lint`. This can cause CI to run hooks that were meant to be skipped (or fail because a skipped hook now runs).
chunk_findings.title: `ddflow/services/ci.py:scope_to_diff`

chunk_findings.detail: The regression test’s pre-commit hook will not run in the pre-push stage, so the second test fails (and the first passes vacuously). In `pre-commit`, a hook’s `stages` defaults to `[commit]` unless specified, while `CI.run`’s default command is the pre-push command `pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push`. In `test_the_branchs_own_bad_python_still_fails_the_push`, the branch diff contains `mine.py` with `BAD = 2`, but the hook `changed-python-clean` is not selected for the `pre-push` stage, so pre-commit exits successfully without executing the script; `res.status` is `"passed"`, causing the assertion expecting `"failed"` to fail. If `pre-commit` is not installed, the whole file skips, so the intended regression gate may also be silently skipped.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_ci_diff_scope.py:31

chunk_findings.detail: The assertion `assert " --to-ref HEAD" in cmd` is an unanchored substring check, so it also matches `--to-ref HEAD~1` (or `--to-ref HEAD^`). If `scope_to_diff` returned `SKIP=frozen-workflow-files pre-commit run --from-ref base --to-ref HEAD~1`, the test would pass even though the CI diff excludes the pushed `HEAD` commit and could miss errors in the tip. The test should require the target ref to be exactly `HEAD`, not merely start with that text.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_ci_tripwire_hooks.py:test_the_commands_own_skip_applies_to_the_diff_scoped_run_too

chunk_findings.detail: The done path still does not honor the caller’s `wait_s` bound. In `wait_job`, when the job is seen as `done`, `timeout` is set to `_TIMEOUT_S` and is only reduced if `left = deadline - monotonic()` is positive; if `_read_list` or `on_tick` has already consumed the bound, `timeout` remains `_TIMEOUT_S`. `_done` then runs `roborev wait --job` and `roborev show --job` sequentially, each with `max(1.0, timeout)`, and it does not reduce the second timeout by the time spent in the first ask. For example, with `wait_s=30`, a job that is already `done`, and `roborev wait --job` hanging for 30s, `_done` still invokes `roborev show --job` with another 30s timeout, so `wait_job` returns after about 60s, not “up to 30s.” With `wait_s=1` and an `on_tick` that takes 10s, `left <= 0`, so `timeout` remains `_TIMEOUT_S` (e.g. 30s), and the wait can return after roughly `10 + 2*_TIMEOUT_S` seconds. The prior fix (“each verdict ask is capped at the remaining bound”) does not answer this: it does not cap the total bound, it ignores zero/negative remaining time, and `_done`’s `max(1.0, timeout)` also defeats a sub-second remaining bound.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/roborev.py:wait_job / _done

chunk_findings.detail: The test only asserts that `FAKE_LOG` contains exactly one line; it never checks that the logged command is a `roborev list --json` read. If `wait_job(repo, 7, 0)` made a single non-list roborev call (for example `roborev show --job 7`) and returned `live=True` with a canned “still queued” note, the log would still contain one line and the test would pass, even though the status was never read from `roborev list --json`. Thus the zero-bound test still does not pin the list poll it is named for; it should assert the logged line starts with `list`.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_roborev_wait.py:test_zero_bound_reads_the_status_once_and_reports_it_live
