chunk_findings.detail: The regression test’s pre-commit hook will not run in the pre-push stage, so the second test fails (and the first passes vacuously). In `pre-commit`, a hook’s `stages` defaults to `[commit]` unless specified, while `CI.run`’s default command is the pre-push command `pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push`. In `test_the_branchs_own_bad_python_still_fails_the_push`, the branch diff contains `mine.py` with `BAD = 2`, but the hook `changed-python-clean` is not selected for the `pre-push` stage, so pre-commit exits successfully without executing the script; `res.status` is `"passed"`, causing the assertion expecting `"failed"` to fail. If `pre-commit` is not installed, the whole file skips, so the intended regression gate may also be silently skipped.

chunk_findings.detail: The assertion `assert " --to-ref HEAD" in cmd` is an unanchored substring check, so it also matches `--to-ref HEAD~1` (or `--to-ref HEAD^`). If `scope_to_diff` returned `SKIP=frozen-workflow-files pre-commit run --from-ref base --to-ref HEAD~1`, the test would pass even though the CI diff excludes the pushed `HEAD` commit and could miss errors in the tip. The test should require the target ref to be exactly `HEAD`, not merely start with that text.

chunk_findings.detail: The new leading-`SKIP=` parser assumes the assignment value is a single non-whitespace token optionally wrapped in one quote layer. A valid shell command such as `SKIP='lint, slow' pre-commit run --all-files` with a valid `since` matches only `SKIP='lint,` because `\S+` stops at the space; `lead.end()` then leaves `slow'` in `run`. The returned command becomes `SKIP="${SKIP:+$SKIP,}'lint," slow' pre-commit run --from-ref <commit> --to-ref HEAD`, which the shell parses as an unmatched quoted word (`slow'`) instead of invoking `pre-commit`, so the CI command is corrupted rather than preserving the original quoted `SKIP`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_LEADING_SKIP

chunk_findings.detail: The double-quote branch of `_leading_skip` does not implement shell escaping: inside a double-quoted `SKIP` value it treats a backslash as an ordinary character and the following `"` as a closing quote. For the valid shell command `SKIP="lint\"slow" pre-commit run --all-files` with an inherited environment `SKIP=slow-tests`, the parser closes the quote at `\"`, then treats the real closing quote as opening a new quote and returns `None` because it ends inside a quote. `scope_to_diff` then emits the original assignment unchanged except for the `--all-files` rewrite, e.g. `SKIP="lint\"slow" pre-commit run --from-ref <commit> --to-ref HEAD`. The shell sets `SKIP` to `lint"slow`, shadowing `slow-tests`, so the inherited skip is not merged and the skipped hook/test runs. The same escaping bug can also split a valid command inside a quoted value (`SKIP="\" --all-files" ...`) and rewrite the `--all-files` that belongs to the `SKIP` value, producing a malformed command.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_leading_skip

chunk_findings.detail: The new regression test only checks prefixes for the `lint, slow` and empty-`SKIP` cases, and only checks the scoped suffix for the `$(echo pwn)` case; it never asserts that `--all-files` has been removed for any of the new inputs. Thus a `scope_to_diff` implementation that returned, for example, `SKIP="${SKIP:+$SKIP,}"'lint, slow' pre-commit run --all-files` or `SKIP="" pre-commit run --all-files` would satisfy the assertions even though the command would still lint the whole tree, which is the behavior the change is supposed to prevent. It should assert `--all-files` absence and the exact `--from-ref <since> --to-ref HEAD` suffix for all three quoted/empty-`SKIP` cases.

chunk_findings.detail: The new double-quote scanner still does not implement shell backslash escapes. Inside `"..."` it appends a backslash as an ordinary character and then processes the following character as if it were unescaped. For the valid command text `SKIP="a\\b" pre-commit run --all-files` (two backslash characters between the quotes), the shell would resolve the assignment value to `a\b`, but `_leading_skip` returns `a\\b` with `active=False`, so the surrounding `scope_to_diff` path rebuilds a single-quoted literal containing two backslashes and the CI run receives a different SKIP value. The same branch also treats `SKIP="lint\$slow" ...` as active even though `\$` is a literal `$`, causing the inherited SKIP not to be merged. This contradicts the docstring’s “value the shell would resolve it to” and the earlier requirement to merge a parseable leading SKIP with the environment’s SKIP.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_leading_skip

chunk_findings.detail: The new double-quote escape handling and the unquoted backslash handling do not account for backslash-newline line continuation. In shell, an unquoted `\<newline>` removes both characters, and inside double quotes a backslash also retains special meaning before a newline (not only before `$`, backtick, `"` and `\`). Given a multi-line CI command such as `SKIP=a\` + newline + `b pre-commit run --all-files`, the shell parses the assignment value as `ab` and the command as `pre-commit ...`, but `_leading_skip` appends the newline as part of the value and returns `a\nb`; `scope_to_diff` then rebuilds a single-quoted value containing a newline, changing the command. The same corruption occurs inside double quotes, e.g. `SKIP="a\` + newline + `b" ...`, where the expected value is `ab` but the parser keeps both the backslash and the newline.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_leading_skip

chunk_findings.detail: The added double-backslash assertion only checks a prefix ending at `pre-commit run `. A returned command such as `SKIP="${SKIP:+$SKIP,}"'a\b' pre-commit run --all-files` satisfies the `startswith` assertion even though `--all-files` was not replaced by `--from-ref/--to-ref`. The test would therefore pass while the CI run still lints the whole tree, which is the failure mode the diff-scoping change is meant to prevent.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_ci_tripwire_hooks.py:240

chunk_findings.detail: `_scope_the_run` uses `run.rpartition(" --all-files")` but does not guard against the marker being absent. If `run` contains no literal ` --all-files`, `rpartition` returns `head == ""` and `tail == run`, so the function returns ` --from-ref <commit> --to-ref HEAD` concatenated in front of the original run. For example, given `scope_to_diff("pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push", tree, "base")` (or a `SKIP=...` variant with the same run), the result is something like ` --from-ref base --to-ref HEADpre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push` (or `SKIP="..." --from-ref base --to-ref HEAD pre-commit run ...`), which is not the original command and is not a valid shell command. The previous `run.replace(..., 1)` behavior left a command without `--all-files` unchanged; this change makes that path malformed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_scope_the_run

chunk_findings.detail: Choosing the **last** literal ` --all-files` can replace the wrong occurrence and leave an actual `--all-files` flag in the run. For input `command="SKIP=lint && pre-commit run --all-files # see --all-files"`, `_scope_the_run` finds the ` --all-files` in the trailing comment, not the flag passed to `pre-commit`, and returns a command equivalent to `SKIP="lint" && pre-commit run --all-files # see --from-ref <commit> --to-ref HEAD`. The CI command still runs `pre-commit run --all-files`, so the whole tree is linted despite the diff-scoping change.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_scope_the_run

chunk_findings.detail: Outside quotes the escape handling treats `\<char>` as an escape pair for every following character, but in shell a backslash outside quotes is literal unless followed by `$`, `` ` ``, `"`, `\`, or newline. Given shell command text `SKIP=a\bc pre-commit run --all-files`, the shell assignment value is `a\bc`, but `_leading_skip` drops the backslash and produces the parsed value `abc`; the rebuilt command then skips `abc` instead of `a\bc`, changing the skip list.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_leading_skip

chunk_findings.detail: The new backslash-newline case checks only the rebuilt prefix and that `--all-files` is absent; unlike the adjacent `a\b` case, it does not check that the diff range was appended. Given the test input `SKIP="foo\<newline>bar" pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --all-files`, a `scope_to_diff` implementation that correctly parses the continuation but returns `SKIP="${SKIP:+$SKIP,}"'foobar' pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push` (or `... --from-ref HEAD --to-ref HEAD`) satisfies all assertions for that case. CI would then not scope the run to the branch diff, potentially linting nothing, while the regression test still passes.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_ci_tripwire_hooks.py:244

chunk_findings.detail: When `_leading_skip` declines a double-quoted `SKIP` assignment containing shell expansion, `scope_to_diff` passes the whole command (including that verbatim assignment) to `_scope_the_run`. Given `SKIP="$(echo pre-commit run --all-files)" pre-commit run --all-files` with a valid `since`, `run.find("pre-commit run")` matches the text inside the double-quoted assignment, and the first ` --all-files` after that match is also inside that assignment. The function returns `SKIP="$(echo pre-commit run --from-ref <sha> --to-ref HEAD)" pre-commit run --all-files`. The operator’s assignment is no longer verbatim, and the real `pre-commit run` still receives `--all-files`, so the CI run still lints the whole tree. This is a regression from the previous last-occurrence behavior, which would have selected the real trailing flag.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_scope_the_run

chunk_findings.detail: The “first ` --all-files` after `pre-commit run`” heuristic is not quote-aware, so a quoted file argument before the real flag can capture the replacement. Given `pre-commit run --files ' --all-files' --all-files` with a valid `since`, `at=0` and the first literal ` --all-files` in `run[at:]` is the one inside the quoted `--files` argument. The returned command is `pre-commit run --files ' --from-ref <sha> --to-ref HEAD' --all-files`, leaving the actual `--all-files` flag on the run (so the whole tree is still checked) and inserting the diff range into a file argument. The added test only covers the opposite order, where the real flag appears before the quoted argument.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:_scope_the_run

chunk_findings.detail: The new “only the default phrase” logic still uses plain substring replacement: `if DEFAULT_COMMAND in run: run.replace(DEFAULT_COMMAND, ..., 1)`. That replaces the first textual occurrence of the default phrase anywhere in the command, not necessarily the actual `pre-commit run` invocation. For example, with a valid `since=abc`, input `pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --files 'pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --all-files' --all-files` contains `DEFAULT_COMMAND` only inside the quoted `--files` argument. The function returns `pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --files 'pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --from-ref abc --to-ref HEAD' --all-files`, so the real pre-commit run still receives `--all-files` and still lints the whole merged tree (and the quoted file argument is corrupted). The added test uses only a partial quoted marker (`' --all-files'`), so it does not cover a quoted argument containing the full default phrase.

chunk_findings.detail: `_add_globs_arg` treats `glob.escape()` as if it makes every glob metacharacter literal, but the standard library explicitly does not escape the two-character sequence `**`. If a staged path literally contains `**` (for example `src/**.py`, stageable with `git add -- ':(literal)src/**.py'`), the advice prints `ddflow update <ID> --add-globs '["src/**.py"]'`. Running that adds the glob `src/**.py`, which under fnmatch/glob semantics also matches other paths such as `src/ab.py` (and `src/**/file.py` can match nested files), so the lease is widened beyond the literal staged path. The earlier probe only tested `src/a[b].py` and a comma path; it does not answer the `**` case.

chunk_findings.detail: The advice is built with `glob.escape()` (the new test asserts the exact `shlex.quote(json.dumps([glob.escape(p) ...]))` form), and Python’s `glob.escape()` deliberately does **not** escape the two-character sequence `**`. Given a staged path whose literal name contains `**`, e.g. `src/**.py`, the hook prints advice like `ddflow update <ID> --add-globs '["src/**.py"]'`. If an agent runs that, `src/**.py` is treated as a glob, not as the literal path, and can cover other files (e.g. `src/x.py`), silently widening the lease — the exact failure this change is supposed to prevent. The earlier refutation probe only staged `src/a[b].py`; it does not exercise a literal `**` path, so it does not answer this case.

The `PROPOSE` contract says the plan shows the exact command; this string is not an exact/executable command (the trailing parenthetical is shell syntax, not a comment) and does not identify the item. If an operator copies the shown command, it fails or does the wrong thing rather than running the intended recovery command.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/recovery_plan.py:_recovery_actions

chunk_findings.detail: The `requeue` branch calls the global `MQ.requeue_orphans(repo)` without passing `a.item` or any action-specific filter, and then emits a row with `"item": ""`. This breaks the stated one-row-per-action/per-action-precondition contract. For example, given a plan action for queue entry `A` with effect `requeue`, if `A` has already moved but another orphaned queue entry `B` exists, `MQ.requeue_orphans(repo)` can return `B`; the row reports `applied=True` for the `A` action even though `A` was not the thing requeued. If `B` was only PROPOSE/OPERATOR, the branch has also applied an action the plan was not supposed to perform.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/recovery.py:apply (requeue branch)

chunk_findings.detail: When `--all --plan` is run with no actions but the kill switch is on (`out.data = {"_render": {"plan": True, "actions": []}, "paused": True}`), `_render_plan` returns `""` before it ever checks `paused`. `ddflow recover --all --plan` then prints nothing, so the operator cannot tell from the plan output that recovery is paused and `--apply` would refuse. The kill-switch status is shown only when there is at least one action, hiding a safety-relevant state in the empty-plan case.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/parsers/reporting.py:_render_plan

chunk_findings.detail: The test does not verify that the kill switch actually prevented the SAFE_AUTO action from being applied. It only asserts that the first `RP.recover(..., apply=True)` returns exit `3`, then removes the switch and asserts that a later apply succeeds. A buggy `services.recovery` that ignored `.ddflow/local/recovery.stop`, recorded the `lease.expired` event, and still returned exit `3` would pass every assertion: first apply exit `3`, plan dry run still non-empty, second apply exit `0`, and `lease.expired_at` true. The test should assert immediately after the first apply while the switch exists that `fold(...).items["T1"].lease.expired_at` is falsy.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_recovery_plan.py:test_apply_records_a_clean_expiry_and_the_kill_switch_stops_apply_only

chunk_findings.detail: The test claims that `apply` never touches the dirty worktree, but after applying it only checks that the lease was not expired. If `recover(apply=True)` incorrectly executed the proposed `ddflow claim T1 --force` action, the lease could be replaced by a fresh non-expired lease and the assertion `not lease.expired_at` would still pass, while the proposed action had in fact been done. The test should assert that the proposed action did not run (for example, that the worktree/`work.py` is unchanged and the lease holder/claim state was not changed), not merely that the lease is not expired.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_recovery_plan.py:test_plan_flags_the_work_and_apply_never_touches_it

chunk_findings.detail: In the `expired_lease` branch, `spent[r["item"]] = spent.get(r["item"], 0) + 1` runs even when the emitted action is `_capped(...)`, which returns an `OPERATOR` action that is only shown and never applied. Given `limits.max_attempts=1`, `facts.attempts={"T1": 1}`, and two `expired_lease` rows for `T1`, the first row emits an `OPERATOR` capped action and then increments `spent`; the second row sees `attempts=2` and emits another capped action whose reason says “2 recovery attempt(s), the cap is 1”. No second recovery attempt occurred, so the plan misreports the recovery-attempt count and can make the operator believe the cap was exceeded.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/recovery_plan.py:_recovery_actions

chunk_findings.detail: When `.ddflow/local/recovery.stop` already exists before the first action, the loop enters, `kill_switch(repo, cfg)` returns True at `i == 0`, and the code emits rows for every remaining action with the note “the kill switch was pulled mid-pass”. No action has been attempted and the switch was not pulled during the pass; it was on before the pass began. The previous behavior distinguished this case with “the kill switch is on: nothing ran”. This inaccurate note can mislead an operator into believing the apply pass started and was stopped partway, rather than never running, which is safety-relevant for a kill switch.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/recovery.py:apply (kill-switch branch)

chunk_findings.detail: The added assertions still verify only the reported `applied_rows`, not an independent observable effect. If `recover(..., apply=True)` executes the proposed `ddflow claim T1 --force` action but still constructs the row with `applied=False` and `note="shown only"` (or otherwise fails to report the side effect), the test still passes: the required `T1` row is present, every row reports `applied is False`, and the lease can be a fresh non-expired replacement lease. The test’s stated contract is that PROPOSE is shown and never done, so it should assert non-execution through observable state (e.g. unchanged worktree/lease identity or absence of a claim event), not rely solely on the same report that could be wrong.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_recovery_plan.py:test_plan_flags_the_work_and_apply_never_touches_it

chunk_findings.detail: The tail file is opened by path after the repro command has run, and the command can replace that path with a symlink to any file the user can read. `_one_run` writes to predictable files such as `0.out` under a directory created by `tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="ddflow-repro-")`, and `_tail_from_file` later calls `open(path, "rb")` without `O_NOFOLLOW` or a saved descriptor. In a default environment (`TMPDIR` unset), a repro command such as `for f in /tmp/ddflow-repro-*/0.out; do ln -sf "$HOME/.ssh/id_rsa" "$f"; done; true` with `tail_bytes=4096` causes `_tail_from_file` to follow the new symlink and store the tail of the SSH private key in `record["output"]`; with `runs>1`, the next shell redirection follows the same symlink and can overwrite the target, and a symlink to a FIFO can block the filing. The command can also discover the exact tail path from its command line or open file descriptors.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprocheck.py:_tail_from_file

chunk_findings.detail: `tail_bytes` bounds only the bytes read back and stored, not the bytes written during capture. `_one_run` redirects the entire run to `tail_file` with no size cap, and `_run_at` accumulates every per-run tail in `out` before joining them. Given `repro_cmd="yes"` and any non-zero timeout, the run can fill the temp filesystem before the timeout expires, causing the repro run to fail for an unrelated reason or affecting other ddflow operations even though `repro_tail_bytes` may be small. Given `repro_runs=100000` and `repro_tail_bytes=1_000_000`, if each run produces 1 MB, `out` and `joined` allocate roughly 100 GB before the final byte cut, so the bug filing can OOM; the capture pipeline should be bounded, not just the final record field.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprocheck.py:_one_run

chunk_findings.detail: Shell-level failures are counted as reproduced runs. `_one_run` only treats `could_not_run`, `timed_out`, or `code is None` as unreached, but a shell syntax error, command-not-found, or redirection error produces a non-zero exit code and is placed in `codes`. For example, with `repro_cmd="echo hi )"`, the wrapped line becomes `( echo hi ) ) > file 2>&1`; the shell exits 2 before executing `echo hi`, yet `_run_at` records `reproduced: "yes"` and `failures: 1`, confirming a bug that was never exercised. The same false confirmation occurs for `repro_cmd="this-command-does-not-exist"` (exit 127) or when a previous run deleted the tails directory so the next redirection fails.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/reprocheck.py:_one_run

chunk_findings.detail: The expected rendered tail is the head-byte cut, not the tail-byte cut. With `repro_tail_bytes = 3` and output `é`*5, the UTF-8 bytes are `c3 a9 c3 a9 c3 a9 c3 a9 c3 a9`. A true byte tail of length 3 is the last three bytes `a9 c3 a9`, which decode with `errors="replace"` as `U+FFFDé`, not `éU+FFFD`. The later test at line 191 pins the same budget as a tail of the joined output (`"-marker\n"`, the last 8 bytes of `run-marker\n`), so a tail implementation will fail line 180, while changing the implementation to take the first 3 bytes to satisfy line 180 would make line 191 wrong.

chunk_findings.detail: The new advice builder assumes `glob.escape()` makes a staged path literal, but CPython's `glob.escape()` deliberately does **not** escape the two-character sequence `**`. Given a staged path whose name literally contains `**`, e.g. `src/**.py` (stageable via `git add -- ':(literal)src/**.py'`), `_add_globs_arg` prints advice like `ddflow update <ID> --add-globs '["src/**.py"]'`. If the agent runs that, ddflow adds the glob `src/**.py`; under fnmatch/glob/pathspec-style wildcard semantics it also matches other paths such as `src/a.py` (`fnmatch.fnmatch('src/a.py', 'src/**.py')` is true), so the lease is silently widened beyond the staged path. The added test asserts the exact `glob.escape` form and does not cover this documented exception, so the earlier untriaged findings still apply.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/enforce.py:_add_globs_arg

chunk_findings.detail: The new advice/test path constructs the `--add-globs` value with `glob.escape()`; `tests/test_enforce.py:test_the_refusal_advice_keeps_a_comma_path_whole` explicitly asserts the form `shlex.quote(json.dumps([glob.escape(p) for p in paths]))`. `glob.escape()` deliberately does not escape the two-character sequence `**`, so a staged path whose literal name contains `**` (for example `src/**.py`, stageable with `git add -- ':(literal)src/**.py'`) produces advice such as `ddflow update <ID> --add-globs '["src/**.py"]'`. If an agent follows that, `--add-globs` stores `src/**.py` as a glob rather than the literal path, and under fnmatch/glob matching it can cover other files such as `src/ab.py`, so the hook advice can still widen the lease instead of adding only the uncovered path. The new comma/bracket test locks in this unsafe formula and does not cover literal `**`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/enforce.py:_add_globs_arg

chunk_findings.detail: When `item` is non-empty, the new plan path sets `queue = []` instead of filtering `MQ.entries(repo)` by that item. For example, if the only orphaned work is a running merge-queue entry with `e.item == "X"` and there are no lease/worktree, dead-run, or job rows, then `recover(repo, item="X", all=True, plan=True)` builds `Facts(queue=())`, triage returns no actions, and the function returns `O.nothing(...)` even though there is a recoverable queue entry for `X`. The same omission makes `recover --all --apply --item X` report nothing to recover when a running queue entry for `X` exists.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/reporting/health.py:recover

chunk_findings.detail: Given `Facts(recoveries=({"item": "X", "kind": "expired_lease", "salvageable": False, "holder": "A", "age_s": 10},), attempts={"X": 2})`, `triage(..., Limits(max_attempts=2))` returns an `Action` with `cls="safe_auto"` and `attempts=2` from `_expiry`. The `Facts.attempts` documentation says this counter is the `lease.expired` count today, and the action’s effect is `expire`, so applying it would be the third lease-expiry recovery attempt despite the cap. `_resume` correctly downgrades to `OPERATOR` when `attempts >= limits.max_attempts`, but `_expiry` ignores `Limits`; thus `recover --all --plan` advertises a `SAFE_AUTO` action beyond the configured cap (and with `Limits(max_attempts=0)` it would still advertise `SAFE_AUTO`).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/recovery_plan.py:134

chunk_findings.detail: `apply` is the documented entry point that should refuse when the kill switch is on, but it never calls `kill_switch` after acquiring the recovery flock (or at all). If `.ddflow/local/recovery.stop` exists, or is created after a caller’s pre-check and before this function is called, `apply(repo, log, agent, [action])` still enters the lock and executes SAFE_AUTO effects such as `L.expire(...)`; if the pass takes time, creating the marker after the first action does not stop later actions either. The emergency brake is therefore not enforced by the code that actually performs recovery.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/recovery.py:apply

chunk_findings.detail: When `MQ.integrator` yields True (the integrator lock was acquired) and `MQ.requeue_orphans(repo)` returns an empty collection because there are no orphaned queue entries, the row note is “the integrator lock is held; the next integrator run takes them”. That statement is false: the lock was acquired, and the correct reason is that there were no entries to requeue. It misreports lock contention to the operator.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/recovery.py:apply (requeue branch)

chunk_findings.detail: When the kill switch is enabled (`out.data["paused"]` is truthy) and the plan contains at least one action, `_render_plan` emits both “PAUSED: the kill switch is on; nothing will run.” and the unconditional line “`ddflow recover --all --apply` performs only SAFE_AUTO.” That is contradictory and misleading: the same output tells the operator that nothing will run while also telling them that an `--apply` run will perform SAFE_AUTO actions. The apply hint should be suppressed or reworded when paused.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/parsers/reporting.py:_render_plan

chunk_findings.detail: The test claims to verify behavior with the kill switch enabled, but it calls `_facts()`, which defaults to `kill_switch=False`. Thus the test only proves that an empty fact set produces no actions; it does not exercise the kill-switch path. For example, if `triage` were changed to ignore `kill_switch` and still return actions for `_facts(kill_switch=True, recoveries=[_row(salvageable=False)])`, this test would still pass because its actual input has the switch off.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_recovery_plan.py:test_nothing_in_means_no_actions_even_with_a_kill_switch

chunk_findings.detail: The new cap check is evaluated per recovery row against the current `facts.attempts[item]`, not against the number of SAFE_AUTO actions already emitted for that item in the same `triage` pass. If `facts.recoveries` contains two expired-lease, non-salvageable rows for the same item `X` and `facts.attempts["X"] == limits.max_attempts - 1`, the loop takes the `else` branch for both rows and returns two `SAFE_AUTO` actions with effect `expire`. Applying both would perform two lease-expiry recoveries, taking the item from one attempt below the cap to one attempt above it. The cap should account for actions emitted in this pass or otherwise limit SAFE_AUTO expire actions per item, not just inspect the starting counter for each row.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/recovery_plan.py:137

chunk_findings.detail: The kill-switch fix only samples the switch once after the recovery flock is acquired (as described by the triage probe: “right after the flock is taken”). If `apply` is called with several SAFE_AUTO actions, the pass can start while the switch is off, perform the first action, then the operator creates `.ddflow/local/recovery.stop`; because the switch is not rechecked between actions, the remaining SAFE_AUTO actions still run while the kill switch is on. That contradicts the contract that `apply` refuses when the switch is on and the intent that the operator can pull the brake.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/recovery.py:apply

chunk_findings.detail: The refactor removed the per-action exception handling that previously guaranteed one failing SAFE_AUTO step would be reported instead of aborting the pass. `_one_safe` only wraps the requeue path via `_requeue`; the `expire`, `record_unavailable`, and `job_end` branches run unguarded, and `apply` calls `_one_safe` without catching exceptions. For example, given a `safe_auto` action with `evidence["effect"] == "expire"` where `L.expire(log, a.item, reason=...)` raises (e.g., a permission or I/O error on the log), `recover --all --apply` propagates the exception, aborts the recovery pass, and returns no result rows for the remaining actions even though earlier SAFE_AUTO side effects may already have been performed. This contradicts the function’s own “never sinks” contract and the previous behavior.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/recovery.py:_one_safe

chunk_findings.detail: The new assertion `all(r["applied"] is False and "shown only" in r["note"] for r in rec.data["applied_rows"])` is vacuously true when `rec.data["applied_rows"]` is empty. The test does not assert that the apply result actually contains a row for the proposed `ddflow claim T1` action (or even that `applied_rows` is non-empty). Therefore, if `recover(repo, all=True, apply=True, agent="op")` regresses to returning `applied_rows=[]` while still exiting `0` and leaving the lease unexpired, the test still passes even though the operator is not shown the PROPOSE action. That contradicts the test’s stated contract and the intent that PROPOSE actions are shown, never done.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_recovery_plan.py:test_plan_flags_the_work_and_apply_never_touches_it

chunk_findings.detail: The final cap branch (`elif attempts >= limits.max_attempts: out.append(_capped(r["item"], attempts, limits))`) does not add the item to `capped`, unlike the expired-lease cap branch. Given two recovery rows for the same item with `kind != "expired_lease"`, `salvageable=True`, and current attempts at the cap—e.g. `facts.recoveries = ({"item": "X", "kind": "stale_run", "salvageable": True}, {"item": "X", "kind": "stale_run", "salvageable": True})`, `facts.attempts = {"X": 2}`, `Limits(max_attempts=2)`—the first iteration emits one `_capped` OPERATOR action but leaves `capped` empty. The second iteration passes the `if r["item"] in capped` guard and emits a second `_capped` action for the same item. Thus `triage`/`recover --all --plan --json` can report duplicate capped actions for one item, violating the intended “one capped line per item” behavior and making the final cap path inconsistent with the expired-lease cap path.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/recovery_plan.py:_recovery_actions

chunk_findings.detail: Changing `ruff-check` and `ruff-format` to `pass_filenames: true` makes Ruff receive explicit file paths. Ruff, by default, checks explicitly supplied paths even if they match `exclude`/`extend-exclude` or `.gitignore`; the previous `ruff check .` / `ruff format --check .` respected the project’s Ruff exclusion configuration. With this change, if the repository has any intentionally excluded Python file (for example generated `*_pb2.py`, vendored code, or migrations containing an unused import), a diff-scoped run or `pre-commit run --all-files` that passes that path to `uv run ruff check` will now report the error and fail the push/CI, whereas it was skipped before. The same applies to `ruff format --check` at `.pre-commit-config.yaml:44`. Add `--force-exclude` to both entries (or otherwise filter excluded paths) to preserve the previous semantics.
chunk_findings.title: .pre-commit-config.yaml:38

chunk_findings.detail: `scope_to_diff` validates `since` with `W.rev(tree, since)` but then interpolates the original `since` directly into the shell command string: `command.replace(" --all-files", f" --from-ref {since} --to-ref HEAD", 1)`. If `since` is a ref name containing shell metacharacters (for example a Git ref such as `foo$(touch /tmp/pwn)` or `foo;touch /tmp/pwn`, which can be valid ref names), `W.rev` can resolve it, so the function returns a command like `pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --from-ref foo$(touch /tmp/pwn) --to-ref HEAD`. When the CI runner executes that command through a shell (as the surrounding command forms, including `SKIP=` prefixes and the previous `rc=0; ...; exit $rc` pattern, require), the shell expands/executes the injected content on the CI machine. The safe value is the commit hash returned by `W.rev`, or the ref must be quoted with `shlex.quote` before interpolation.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:scope_to_diff

chunk_findings.detail:
The test’s lint hook swallows non-“BAD found” grep failures. `SCRIPT` is `#!/bin/sh
if grep -q BAD "$@"; then exit 1; fi
exit 0
`, so it only exits 1 when `grep` exits 0 (marker found). If `grep` exits 2 because a passed file is missing/unreadable, or exits 127 because `grep` is not available, or misparses a filename beginning with `-` as an option, the `if` condition is false and the script falls through to `exit 0`. For example, `scripts/lint.sh deleted.py` returns 0 even though it could not check the file; a diff-scoped pre-commit run that passes a deleted or oddly named file could therefore see the hook “pass” when it did not actually lint the input.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_ci_diff_scope.py:SCRIPT

chunk_findings.detail: The new SKIP-merging path rebuilds the leading assignment by inserting the raw captured `SKIP` value inside double quotes, so shell quoting in the original value is not preserved. Given `command = "SKIP='lint' pre-commit run --all-files"` and a resolvable `since`, `_LEADING_SKIP` captures `'lint'` and the function returns `SKIP="${SKIP:+$SKIP,}'lint'" pre-commit run --from-ref <sha> --to-ref HEAD`. When this is run through the shell, `SKIP` becomes the literal `'lint'` (or `inherited,'lint'` if `SKIP` was set), not `lint`; pre-commit therefore does not skip the `lint` hook, whereas the previous command preserved `SKIP='lint'` and did skip it. This can cause a hook the command intended to skip to run, potentially failing CI, whenever a leading `SKIP=` assignment uses single quotes or otherwise depends on shell quoting.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:scope_to_diff

chunk_findings.detail: The new quote-stripping step only checks that the captured `SKIP` token starts and ends with the same quote character; it does not check that those quotes form a single balanced layer around the whole value. For the valid shell command `SKIP='lint','format' pre-commit run --all-files`, the captured raw token is `'lint','format'`. The code strips the first and last single quotes, producing `lint','format`, and rebuilds the command as `SKIP="${SKIP:+$SKIP,}lint','format" pre-commit run ...`. When executed by a shell, pre-commit receives a `SKIP` value such as `lint','format` (or `inherited,lint','format`), which splits into hook IDs `lint'` and `'format`, not `lint` and `format`, so the intended hooks are not skipped.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci.py:scope_to_diff

chunk_findings.detail: Changing these hooks to `pass_filenames: true` makes ruff receive explicit file paths instead of `.`. Ruff does not apply its `exclude`/`extend-exclude` patterns to explicitly passed paths unless `--force-exclude` is supplied. The new entries (`uv run ruff check` and `uv run ruff format --check`) omit that flag. Thus, if the repository’s ruff configuration excludes a tracked Python path (e.g. `[tool.ruff] exclude = ["ddflow/_vendor"]`) and a branch modifies a file under that path, pre-commit will pass it explicitly to ruff and ruff will lint/format-check it, potentially failing the push even though the previous `ruff check .` / `ruff format --check .` invocation would have skipped the excluded file.

chunk_findings.detail: The new scoping drops the environment’s `SKIP` whenever the command already carries its own leading `SKIP=` assignment. The removed implementation explicitly merged the inherited `SKIP` with the command’s own skip (`SKIP="${SKIP:+$SKIP,}..."`), because a shell command-prefix assignment overrides the inherited environment. Now, given environment `SKIP=slow-tests` and `command="SKIP=lint pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --all-files"` with a valid `since`, `scope_to_diff` returns `SKIP=lint pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push --from-ref <since> --to-ref HEAD`. When run through the shell, `SKIP` is exactly `lint`, so the `slow-tests` hook is not skipped even though the selected-tests plan set it; the old behavior would have skipped both `slow-tests` and `lint`. This can cause CI to run hooks that were meant to be skipped (or fail because a skipped hook now runs).

chunk_findings.detail: The regression test’s pre-commit hook will not run in the pre-push stage, so the second test fails (and the first passes vacuously). In `pre-commit`, a hook’s `stages` defaults to `[commit]` unless specified, while `CI.run`’s default command is the pre-push command `pre-commit run --hook-stage pre-push`. In `test_the_branchs_own_bad_python_still_fails_the_push`, the branch diff contains `mine.py` with `BAD = 2`, but the hook `changed-python-clean` is not selected for the `pre-push` stage, so pre-commit exits successfully without executing the script; `res.status` is `"passed"`, causing the assertion expecting `"failed"` to fail. chunk_findings.detail: The double-quote branch of `_leading_skip` does not implement shell escaping: inside a double-quoted `SKIP` value it treats a backslash as an ordinary character and the following `"` as a closing quote.
